systems.name: Big Five (Five-Factor Model, OCEAN)
systems.statusNote: The Big Five has strong empirical support and is regarded as the scientific consensus model of personality structure in academic psychology. The Five-Factor Model was consolidated by Costa & McCrae (1992), building on Goldberg's (1990) lexical research.
systems.blurb: The Big Five, or Five-Factor Model, describes personality along five broad, statistically independent dimensions summarised by the acronym OCEAN. It emerged from the lexical tradition (Goldberg) and was formalised by Costa and McCrae from the 1980s onward, sorting people by where they fall on each trait rather than into fixed types. Our free course walks through all five traits, shows you how to read high and low scores, and closes with an honest look at the model's evidence and limits.
systems.source: Lewis Goldberg (lexical tradition) and Paul Costa & Robert McCrae, 1980s-1990s

dimensions.name: Openness to Experience
dimensions.desc: Scoring high means being curious, imaginative, and drawn to novelty, art, and abstract ideas, while scoring low means preferring the familiar, practical, and routine.

dimensions.name: Conscientiousness
dimensions.desc: Scoring high means being organised, disciplined, and goal-directed, while scoring low means being more easygoing, flexible, and spontaneous about plans and details.

dimensions.name: Extraversion
dimensions.desc: Scoring high means being outgoing, energetic, and energised by social interaction, while scoring low means being more reserved, quiet, and comfortable in solitude.

dimensions.name: Agreeableness
dimensions.desc: Scoring high means being compassionate, cooperative, and trusting of others, while scoring low means being more sceptical, competitive, and willing to put one's own interests first.

dimensions.name: Neuroticism
dimensions.desc: Scoring high means experiencing anxiety, mood swings, and stress more readily, while scoring low (emotional stability) means staying calm, resilient, and even-tempered under pressure.

systems.name: HEXACO model
systems.statusNote: HEXACO is an empirically supported personality model derived from lexical studies across many languages, and is well regarded in academic personality psychology. Proposed by Ashton & Lee (2004), it adds an Honesty–Humility dimension to the Big Five.
systems.blurb: The HEXACO model is a six-factor framework of personality developed by Kibeom Lee and Michael Ashton in the early 2000s from cross-language lexical research. It sorts people along six broad dimensions, adding an Honesty-Humility factor — sincerity, fairness and modesty versus manipulation and greed — not captured by the older Big Five. Our free course walks through all six traits, shows why researchers added the sixth, and helps you read your own profile.

dimensions.name: Conscientiousness
dimensions.desc: High scorers are organised, disciplined, careful, and goal-driven, while low scorers are more impulsive, easygoing, and tolerant of disorder and error.

dimensions.name: Openness to Experience
dimensions.desc: High scorers are imaginative, curious, and drawn to art, ideas, and the unconventional, while low scorers prefer the familiar, practical, and conventional.

systems.name: Eysenck PEN model
systems.statusNote: An influential, biologically rooted trait theory; the Extraversion and Neuroticism dimensions are well replicated across studies, while Psychoticism remains more contested. The three-factor PEN model was set out by Eysenck & Eysenck (1976).
systems.blurb: The PEN model is a biologically grounded theory of personality developed by Hans Eysenck (with later work alongside Sybil Eysenck) from the 1940s through the 1970s. It sorts people along three broad, independent dimensions—Psychoticism, Extraversion, and Neuroticism—that Eysenck linked to underlying differences in nervous-system arousal and reactivity. Our free course places Eysenck in the history of trait theory, explains the three dimensions and their biological basis, and looks at his famous theory of the criminal personality.
systems.source: Hans J. Eysenck (with Sybil B. G. Eysenck), 1940s–1970s

dimensions.name: Neuroticism
dimensions.desc: High scorers are emotionally reactive, anxious, and prone to negative moods, while low (stable) scorers are calm, even-tempered, and resilient under stress.

systems.name: Cattell 16 Personality Factors (16PF)
systems.statusNote: The 16PF derives from factor-analytic research and remains a psychometrically validated instrument, though some of Cattell's sixteen factors show overlap and are widely summarised by the broader five-factor model. First published by Cattell (1949).
systems.blurb: The 16 Personality Factors is a trait model and questionnaire developed by psychologist Raymond Cattell in the 1940s using factor analysis of language and behaviour. It sorts people along sixteen primary trait dimensions, each scored as a continuous position between two opposing poles; the dimensions are correlated rather than fully independent, which is why they cluster into about five broader global factors. Our free course explains Cattell's source-trait approach, the sixteen factors, and how the 16PF relates to the other major trait models including the Big Five.
systems.source: Raymond B. Cattell, 1949 (first edition of the 16PF questionnaire)

systems.name: Dark Triad / Dark Tetrad
systems.statusNote: These are empirically studied personality constructs measured with validated self-report scales; high scores describe normal-range tendencies and are not a clinical diagnosis. The 'Dark Triad' term was introduced by Paulhus & Williams (2002).
systems.blurb: The Dark Triad is a cluster of three socially aversive but subclinical personality traits, named by Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams in 2002. It sorts people by their levels of Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy; a fourth trait, sadism, extends it to the Dark Tetrad. Our free course explains all four constructs, how they differ and overlap, and how they show up in everyday behaviour — while being clear that a high score is a normal-range tendency, not a clinical diagnosis.
systems.source: Paulhus & Williams (2002); Sadism added c. 2009-2013 (Dark Tetrad)

dimensions.name: Machiavellianism
dimensions.desc: High scorers favour calculated manipulation, cynicism about others' motives, and a strategic, ends-focused approach, while low scorers tend toward straightforwardness and trust.

dimensions.name: Narcissism
dimensions.desc: High scorers show grandiosity, a sense of entitlement, and a strong need for admiration, while low scorers are more modest and less reliant on external validation.

dimensions.name: Psychopathy
dimensions.desc: High scorers display callousness, impulsivity, and low empathy, while low scorers are more emotionally responsive to others and more behaviourally controlled.

dimensions.name: Sadism
dimensions.desc: High scorers derive enjoyment from inflicting or witnessing others' suffering, while low scorers find such cruelty unpleasant or distressing.

systems.name: Light Triad
systems.statusNote: The Light Triad Scale (Kaufman, Yaden, Hyde & Tsukayama, 2019) is a validated measure of a benevolent orientation toward others — the positive counterpart to the Dark Triad, built from three facets.
systems.blurb: The Light Triad is a cluster of three personality traits describing a loving, benevolent orientation towards other people — proposed by Scott Barry Kaufman and colleagues in 2019 as the positive counterpart to the Dark Triad. Measured by the 12-item Light Triad Scale, it comprises Kantianism (treating people as ends in themselves rather than means), Humanism (valuing the inherent dignity and worth of each person), and Faith in Humanity (believing people are fundamentally good). Higher scores tend to track life satisfaction, compassion, and a sense of personal growth. The light and dark triads are distinct dimensions rather than opposite ends of one scale, so a strong light orientation is not merely the absence of a dark one.

dimensions.name: Humanism
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you value the dignity and worth of every individual.

dimensions.name: Faith in humanity
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you believe people are, at heart, fundamentally good.

systems.name: Emotional intelligence
systems.statusNote: The four-branch model (Salovey & Mayer, 1990; Mayer & Salovey, 1997) is the dominant scientific account of emotional intelligence, defining it as four related abilities: perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions. It is measured two ways — as a mental ability with performance tests such as the MSCEIT (Mayer, Salovey, Caruso & Sitarenios, 2003), and as a self-reported trait with questionnaires such as the TEIQue (Petrides & Furnham, 2001). This reflective self-rating reflects the self-perceived (trait) side, not a formal score.
systems.blurb: Emotional intelligence (EI) is the set of skills for working with emotion — recognising it, harnessing it, understanding it and regulating it. The most-cited scientific account, the Mayer and Salovey four-branch model, splits it into perceiving emotions (reading feelings in faces, voices and yourself), using emotions (letting the right mood power your thinking and creativity), understanding emotions (grasping how feelings blend, shift and what sparks them) and managing emotions (steering your own and others' feelings without bottling them up or being swept away). You can be strong in some branches while still growing in others, so this maps the shape of your emotional skill rather than a single score. Researchers measure EI two ways — as a mental ability tested with performance tasks (the MSCEIT) and as a self-perceived trait reported on questionnaires (trait EI, the TEIQue) — and a quick self-rating like this one reflects the self-perceived side.
systems.source: Four-branch model of emotional intelligence (Mayer & Salovey)

dimensions.name: Perceiving emotions
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you quickly and accurately pick up emotions — in faces, voices, body language and in yourself; leaning low means feelings often pass you by until they are spelled out.

dimensions.name: Using emotions
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you let the right mood power your thinking — using enthusiasm to create, or a flicker of unease to double-check your work; leaning low means you tend to keep emotion and reasoning in separate boxes.

dimensions.name: Understanding emotions
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you understand where feelings come from and how they blend and shift over time — how disappointment can harden into resentment; leaning low means emotional cause and effect is harder to trace.

dimensions.name: Managing emotions
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you can stay open to a feeling yet steer it — soothing yourself or others without bottling up or blowing up; leaning low means strong emotions are more likely to carry you along.

systems.name: Temperament & Character Inventory (Cloninger)
systems.statusNote: A research-based psychobiological model with peer-reviewed support, though its proposed links between dimensions and specific neurotransmitter systems remain debated and only partially confirmed. From Cloninger's Temperament and Character Inventory (Cloninger, Svrakic & Przybeck, 1993).
systems.blurb: The Temperament and Character Inventory is a personality model developed by psychiatrist C. Robert Cloninger in the early 1990s. It sorts people across seven continuous dimensions: four heritable, emotion-based temperaments (Novelty Seeking, Harm Avoidance, Reward Dependence, Persistence) and three learned, self-concept-based character traits (Self-Directedness, Cooperativeness, Self-Transcendence). Our free course introduces the model, its psychobiological structure, and Cloninger's own account of the genetics behind personality.
systems.source: C. Robert Cloninger, 1993 (building on his 1987 Tridimensional model)

dimensions.name: Harm Avoidance

dimensions.name: Self-Directedness

dimensions.name: Cooperativeness
dimensions.desc: High scorers are empathic, tolerant, and helpful toward others, while low scorers are self-absorbed, critical, and indifferent to others' rights and needs.

dimensions.name: Self-Transcendence
dimensions.desc: High scorers feel connected to something larger than themselves and accept ambiguity, while low scorers are practical, materialistic, and prefer clear control over their world.

systems.name: Fisher Temperament (neurochemical)
systems.statusNote: A popular model linking temperament to brain chemistry; partly research-informed but not a settled scientific typology.
systems.blurb: Biological anthropologist Helen Fisher proposed four broad temperaments — Explorer, Builder, Director, and Negotiator — each linked to a brain-chemistry system (dopamine, serotonin, testosterone, and estrogen). Measured by her Temperament Inventory, the model emerged from large-scale online-dating data and is studied in relationship and attraction research.

systems.name: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)
systems.statusNote: Extremely popular but scientifically criticised: it shows low test-retest reliability and its four discrete dichotomies are not supported by trait research, which finds personality varies continuously rather than in categories.
systems.blurb: The MBTI is a personality framework that sorts people into 16 types built from four dichotomies: Introversion/Extraversion (I/E), Sensing/Intuition (S/N), Thinking/Feeling (T/F), and Judging/Perceiving (J/P). It was created by Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers in the mid-20th century, drawing loosely on Carl Jung's theory of psychological types. Our free course tours all 16 types and the Jungian cognitive functions beneath them, then closes with an honest look at why psychologists question the test's reliability — so you can use your type as a mirror, not a verdict.
systems.source: Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers, developed from the 1940s onward, based on Carl Jung's typology

systems.name: Jungian cognitive functions
systems.statusNote: The eight-function model is influential in popular type communities but is not an empirically validated framework, and the function constructs lack consistent scientific support.
systems.blurb: A model of eight cognitive functions derived from Carl Jung's 1921 work Psychological Types and elaborated by later type theorists. Each function pairs a mental activity (sensing, intuition, thinking, or feeling) with an orientation (extraverted or introverted), and people are sorted by which functions they most rely on. Our free course introduces all eight functions, shows how they stack into a type, and watches them in action — a richer lens beneath the Myers-Briggs letters, though an influential type-community model rather than a validated framework.
systems.source: Carl Jung, Psychological Types (1921); expanded by later type theory

systems.name: Socionics (Information Metabolism Types)
systems.statusNote: Socionics is a post-Jungian framework popular mainly in Eastern Europe; it is not empirically validated by mainstream psychology and is regarded as pseudoscientific.
systems.blurb: Socionics is a theory of personality and information metabolism developed by Lithuanian economist and sociologist Aushra Augustinaviciute in the 1970s. Building on Carl Jung's typology and Antoni Kepinski's idea of information metabolism, it sorts people into sixteen types defined by how they perceive and process information. It parallels but is distinct from MBTI, and the four-letter codes do not map one-to-one. Our free course introduces the theory, the idea of information metabolism, and how socionics differs from MBTI — a lens popular in Eastern European type communities rather than validated science.

options.label: ESE — Enthusiast (Hugo)

options.label: LII — Analyst (Robespierre)

options.label: SEE — Politician (Napoleon)

options.label: ILI — Critic (Balzac)

options.label: LIE — Entrepreneur (Jack London)

options.label: ESI — Guardian (Dreiser)

systems.name: Keirsey Temperament Sorter
systems.statusNote: Like the MBTI it draws on, the Keirsey Temperament Sorter is a popular self-report instrument that is not considered scientifically validated by mainstream personality psychology.
systems.blurb: The Keirsey Temperament Sorter is a self-assessment that sorts people into four temperaments — Artisan, Guardian, Idealist and Rational, names Keirsey drew from Plato's four kinds of character — each subdivided into four role variants that map onto the 16 MBTI types. American psychologist David Keirsey introduced the model in the 1978 book Please Understand Me (co-written with Marilyn Bates) and expanded it in Please Understand Me II (1998), grouping people by their observable behaviour, values and communication. Our free course helps you find your temperament and see how it relates to the MBTI letters — a popular self-report tool rather than a validated test.

options.label: Idealist

options.label: Rational

options.label: Phlegmatic
options.desc: Associated with phlegm, the phlegmatic temperament is calm, easy-going, and reliable.

systems.blurb: The Enneagram of Personality is a model that sorts people into nine interconnected types, each defined by a characteristic core motivation and core fear. It was popularised in the 1970s by Oscar Ichazo and Claudio Naranjo, who drew on earlier esoteric and psychological ideas. Our free course walks through all nine types, their wings and core fears, and how to find your own — closing with an honest look at what a personality test can and cannot tell you, since the Enneagram is a tool for reflection rather than a validated scientific test.

options.label: Type 3 — The Achiever

options.label: Type 4 — The Individualist

options.label: Type 5 — The Investigator

options.label: Type 6 — The Loyalist

options.label: Type 7 — The Enthusiast
options.desc: Motivated by a desire to be satisfied and free through new experiences, while fearing being deprived, trapped, or in pain.

options.label: Type 8 — The Challenger
options.desc: Motivated by a desire to protect themselves and stay in control, while fearing being harmed, controlled, or made vulnerable by others.

options.label: Type 9 — The Peacemaker
options.desc: Motivated by a desire for inner and outer peace and harmony, while fearing loss, separation, and conflict.

systems.name: Type A / Type B personality
systems.statusNote: The original A/B distinction grew out of mid-20th-century cardiology research and entered popular culture, but the claimed link to heart disease has been largely weakened by later studies, and the model is not regarded as a validated personality framework.
systems.blurb: A behavioural typology proposed by cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman in the 1950s, which sorts people by their characteristic pattern of competitiveness, time-urgency, and stress response. The original Type A and Type B pair was later extended with Type C and Type D as researchers described further coping and affect styles. Our free course explains all four patterns and tells the honest story of the model's cardiology origins — including why the once-claimed link between Type A and heart disease has largely weakened.
systems.source: Friedman & Rosenman, 1950s (Type A/B); Type C and Type D added by later researchers (late 20th century)

options.label: Type A

options.label: Type B
options.desc: Relaxed, easy-going, and reflective, with less urgency and competitiveness than Type A (the other half of the original pair).

options.label: Type C
options.desc: Cooperative and detail-focused, tending to suppress emotions rather than express them (added to the model after the original A/B pair).

options.label: Type D
options.desc: The 'distressed' type, combining negative affectivity with social inhibition, so distressing feelings are felt strongly but held back from others (a later addition to the model).

systems.blurb: True Colors is a four-colour temperament model created by Don Lowry in 1978, adapting David Keirsey's four temperaments into accessible colour metaphors. It sorts people by their dominant motivational style, values, and behavioural strengths into one of four colours: Blue, Gold, Green, or Orange.

systems.name: Lüscher Color Test
systems.statusNote: A historic colour-preference test devised by the Swiss psychotherapist Max Lüscher (first presented in 1947; English edition translated and edited by Ian Scott, Random House, 1969). It has been used in clinical and commercial settings, but it is not supported by scientific evidence: independent studies have not confirmed its construct or predictive validity (Braün & Bonta, 1979), and it features among the techniques rated 'discredited' in an expert Delphi poll (Norcross, Koocher & Garofalo, 2006). Popular belief, not science — best treated as a reflective self-ID, not a measure.
systems.blurb: The Lüscher Color Test is a colour-preference personality test devised by the Swiss psychotherapist Max Lüscher and first presented in 1947. You rank eight colours from most to least liked, and Lüscher read that order as a portrait of your psychological state and needs. At its heart sit four 'basic colours', each standing for a basic need: dark blue for calm and contentment, blue-green for self-assertion and will, orange-red for drive and excitement, and bright yellow for hope and spontaneity. This asks which of the four draws you most. Widely used in popular and some clinical settings, the test is not backed by scientific evidence — independent research finds no construct validity and it appears on published lists of discredited assessments — so take it as a reflective prompt, not a measure.
systems.source: Max Lüscher, The Lüscher Color Test (trans. & ed. Ian Scott), Random House, 1969; first presented 1947

systems.statusNote: An influential developmental framework popular in coaching and organisational circles, but not a mainstream-validated psychometric instrument.
systems.blurb: Spiral Dynamics is a model of developmental value systems, or 'vMemes', that describes how individuals and cultures move through successive worldviews in response to changing life conditions. It was derived from the work of psychologist Clare W. Graves and developed by Don Beck and Christopher Cowan in the 1990s, who labelled each stage by colour. It sorts people by the underlying value system through which they make sense of the world.

options.label: Green — Community
options.desc: An egalitarian, communitarian worldview that emphasises human bonds, consensus, inclusion, feelings, and the wellbeing of the whole group.

options.label: Yellow — Integrative

systems.name: The 12 Archetypes (Jungian)

systems.blurb: A set of twelve universal character archetypes — the Hero, Sage, Explorer, Outlaw and more — derived from Carl Jung's concept of the collective unconscious and popularised by Carol S. Pearson, then applied to brand and identity work by Margaret Mark and Carol Pearson around 2001. It sorts people by their core motivations, desires, and the recurring role they play in their own life narrative. Our free course traces the twelve from Jung's psychology to modern branding and storytelling, and helps you find your own dominant archetypes.

options.desc: 1F Physics (confident) · 2V Will (flexible) · 3E Emotion (insecure) · 4L Logic (unbothered)

options.label: FLVE
options.desc: 1F Physics (confident) · 2L Logic (flexible) · 3V Will (insecure) · 4E Emotion (unbothered)

options.label: FLEV
options.desc: 1F Physics (confident) · 2L Logic (flexible) · 3E Emotion (insecure) · 4V Will (unbothered)

options.label: FEVL
options.desc: 1F Physics (confident) · 2E Emotion (flexible) · 3V Will (insecure) · 4L Logic (unbothered)

options.label: FELV
options.desc: 1F Physics (confident) · 2E Emotion (flexible) · 3L Logic (insecure) · 4V Will (unbothered)

systems.name: Objective Personality — your Animal
systems.statusNote: The Objective Personality System (Dave & Shannon Powers) extends Jungian typing into a 512-type framework built by observing behaviour. Its four 'Animals' describe what most energises you. A popular online (YouTube) framework, not scientifically validated.
systems.blurb: Your dominant 'Animal' in the Objective Personality System — what most drives and energises you.

options.label: Play
options.desc: Energised by people and the moment — interaction, fun, and doing things together.

options.label: Sleep
options.desc: Energised by depth and solitude — your inner world, focus, and rest.

options.label: Blast
options.desc: Energised by impact — pushing your ideas and will out into the world.

options.label: Consume
options.desc: Energised by taking things in — learning and gathering information and resources.

systems.name: The Four Tendencies (Gretchen Rubin)
systems.statusNote: A self-help framework popularised through Rubin's books and quiz; it is not an academically validated personality model and has not been established through peer-reviewed psychometric research.
systems.blurb: The Four Tendencies is a personality framework created by writer Gretchen Rubin (introduced around 2015 and expanded in her 2017 book of the same name). It sorts people by how they respond to two kinds of expectations: outer expectations imposed by others and inner expectations they set for themselves.
systems.source: Gretchen Rubin, 2015 (formalised in The Four Tendencies, 2017)

options.label: Upholder
options.desc: Readily meets both outer expectations from others and inner expectations they set for themselves.

options.label: Questioner
options.desc: Meets inner expectations they judge to be justified, but questions outer expectations and complies only once convinced of the reasoning.

options.label: Obliger
options.desc: Readily meets outer expectations from others but struggles to meet the inner expectations they set for themselves.

options.label: Rebel
options.desc: Resists both outer and inner expectations, preferring to act from a sense of freedom, choice, and personal identity.

systems.name: Introvert, Extrovert or Ambivert
systems.statusNote: Introversion–extraversion is a well-supported trait dimension (here as a simple everyday self-label).
systems.blurb: The most everyday personality split of all: where you fall on the introversion–extraversion spectrum — chiefly, what recharges you. Our free course covers the science of the difference, its roots in Carl Jung's work, how to tell introvert from extrovert from ambivert, and Susan Cain's landmark talk on the power of introverts.

options.label: Introvert
options.desc: Recharges in solitude, prefers depth, and can be drained by too much stimulation.

options.label: Extrovert
options.desc: Recharges around other people and is energised by social activity and stimulation.

options.label: Ambivert
options.desc: A balance of both, shifting with mood and context.

systems.name: Birth order
systems.statusNote: Alfred Adler's theory that birth order shapes personality is popular; the evidence for large, lasting effects is weak.
systems.blurb: A theory from Alfred Adler that your position among your siblings shapes your character. A widely used self-identification, though research finds the effects small at best.

options.label: Firstborn
options.desc: Often responsible, conscientious, and achievement-oriented — the natural leader.

options.label: Middle child
options.desc: Often diplomatic, adaptable, and peace-making, used to negotiating.

options.label: Youngest
options.desc: Often outgoing, charming, and willing to take risks for attention.

options.label: Only child
options.desc: Often mature, self-reliant, and comfortable in their own company.

options.label: Twin or multiple
options.desc: Raised as one of a set, often with a strong sense of sharing and partnership.

systems.name: Chronotype (body clock)
systems.blurb: Your natural body-clock timing — whether you wake, peak and wind down early (a 'lark'), late (an 'owl'), or somewhere in between. It's set largely by your internal circadian rhythm, not just by habit.
systems.statusNote: Morningness–eveningness (chronotype) is a validated trait in sleep science, measured by instruments such as the Horne–Östberg Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (1976). Pop 'animal' chronotype quizzes, by contrast, are not validated. A reflective self-ID.

options.label: Early bird
options.desc: Wakes and peaks early; fades in the evening.

options.label: Intermediate
options.desc: Neither strongly morning nor night — a flexible middle.

options.label: Night owl
options.desc: Comes alive later; struggles with early mornings.

options.label: Variable
options.desc: Shifts with schedule, season, or sleep debt.

systems.name: Learning style (VARK)
systems.statusNote: Hugely popular in education, but research finds no benefit to teaching to a person's "style" — treat it as a preference, not a fact about how you learn.
systems.blurb: Neil Fleming's VARK model sorts how people prefer to take in information into four modes. Pick the ones that feel like you.

options.label: Visual
options.desc: Learns best from images, diagrams, charts, and spatial layouts.

options.label: Aural / Auditory
options.desc: Learns best by listening, discussing, and talking things through.

options.label: Read / Write
options.desc: Learns best through written words — reading, notes, and lists.

options.label: Kinesthetic
options.desc: Learns best by doing — movement, practice, and hands-on experience.

systems.name: Holland Codes (RIASEC career interests)
systems.statusNote: A well-validated model of vocational interests, widely used and supported by decades of research in career counselling. Set out in Holland's theory of vocational choice (Holland, 1959; refined 1997).
systems.blurb: The Holland Codes, or RIASEC model, were developed by psychologist John Holland from the 1950s onward to describe vocational interests. It sorts people and work environments into six interest types — Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional — and members typically identify with the few that fit them best. Our free course explains all six, shows how they map to real careers, and helps you use the model to choose a degree or direction.
systems.source: John Holland, psychologist; developed from the 1950s, formalised in the 1970s

options.label: Realistic
options.desc: Hands-on and practical, preferring concrete work with tools, machines, and physical or mechanical tasks.

options.label: Investigative
options.desc: Analytical and curious, drawn to scientific inquiry, research, and solving abstract or technical problems.

options.label: Artistic
options.desc: Creative and expressive, favouring open-ended, unstructured work in the arts, design, and ideas.

options.label: Social
options.desc: Helping and people-focused, motivated by teaching, caring for, and supporting others.

options.label: Enterprising
options.desc: Leading and persuading, energised by influencing people, business, and achieving goals.

options.label: Conventional
options.desc: Organising and detail-oriented, comfortable working systematically with data, records, and structured procedures.

citations.title: A theory of vocational choice
citations.authors: Holland, J. L.

citations.title: Making Vocational Choices: A Theory of Vocational Personalities and Work Environments (3rd ed.)
citations.authors: Holland, J. L.

citations.title: The development, evolution, and status of Holland's theory of vocational personalities: Reflections and future directions for counseling psychology
citations.authors: Nauta, M. M.

systems.name: VIA Character Strengths
systems.statusNote: The VIA Classification is grounded in peer-reviewed psychology research, and its self-report survey shows acceptable reliability, though debate continues about its factor structure and the exact number of underlying virtues. Set out by Peterson & Seligman (2004).
systems.blurb: The VIA Classification of Character Strengths and Virtues, developed by psychologists Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman around 2004, identifies 24 positive character strengths organised under six broad virtues. It sorts people by which strengths they most naturally and authentically express, known as their signature strengths. Our free course traces the idea from positive psychology through the full map of virtues and strengths, and shows how to put your signature strengths to work in daily life.

options.label: Creativity
options.desc: Wisdom virtue: thinking of novel and productive ways to conceptualise and do things.

options.label: Curiosity
options.desc: Wisdom virtue: taking an active interest in ongoing experience and finding subjects fascinating.

options.label: Judgment (Critical Thinking)
options.desc: Wisdom virtue: thinking things through, examining evidence from all sides, and not jumping to conclusions.

options.label: Love of Learning
options.desc: Wisdom virtue: mastering new skills, topics, and bodies of knowledge for their own sake.

options.label: Perspective (Wisdom)
options.desc: Wisdom virtue: being able to provide wise counsel and see the larger picture in life.

options.label: Bravery
options.desc: Courage virtue: not shrinking from threat, challenge, difficulty, or pain, and acting on convictions.

options.label: Perseverance
options.desc: Courage virtue: finishing what one starts and persisting in a course of action despite obstacles.

options.label: Honesty
options.desc: Courage virtue: speaking the truth and presenting oneself in a genuine and sincere way.

options.label: Zest
options.desc: Courage virtue: approaching life with excitement and energy and living it as an adventure.

options.label: Love
options.desc: Humanity virtue: valuing close relationships with others and being capable of giving and receiving care.

options.label: Kindness
options.desc: Humanity virtue: doing favours and good deeds for others and caring about their welfare.

options.label: Social Intelligence
options.desc: Humanity virtue: being aware of the motives and feelings of oneself and others and knowing how to fit in.

options.label: Teamwork
options.desc: Justice virtue: working well as a member of a group and being loyal and committed to the team.

options.label: Fairness
options.desc: Justice virtue: treating all people the same according to notions of fairness and justice.

options.label: Leadership
options.desc: Justice virtue: encouraging a group to get things done while maintaining good relations within it.

options.label: Forgiveness
options.desc: Temperance virtue: forgiving those who have done wrong and giving people a second chance.

options.label: Humility
options.desc: Temperance virtue: letting one's accomplishments speak for themselves and not seeking the spotlight.

options.label: Prudence
options.desc: Temperance virtue: being careful about one's choices and not taking undue risks or saying things one might regret.

options.label: Self-Regulation
options.desc: Temperance virtue: regulating what one feels and does and being disciplined over one's appetites and emotions.

options.label: Appreciation of Beauty & Excellence
options.desc: Transcendence virtue: noticing and appreciating beauty, excellence, and skilled performance in all domains of life.

options.label: Gratitude
options.desc: Transcendence virtue: being aware of and thankful for the good things that happen.

options.label: Hope
options.desc: Transcendence virtue: expecting the best in the future and working to achieve it.

options.label: Humor
options.desc: Transcendence virtue: liking to laugh and tease and bringing smiles to other people.

options.label: Spirituality
options.desc: Transcendence virtue: having coherent beliefs about the higher purpose and meaning of the universe.

systems.name: Gallup CliftonStrengths
systems.statusNote: A proprietary Gallup assessment widely used in workplace and coaching settings; it has internal reliability data but is not an independently validated scientific personality taxonomy on the level of the Big Five.
systems.blurb: CliftonStrengths (formerly StrengthsFinder) is a self-assessment created by psychologist Don Clifton and Gallup, first released in 2001, that sorts people by their dominant talents across 34 themes grouped into four domains: Executing, Influencing, Relationship Building, and Strategic Thinking.
systems.source: Don Clifton & Gallup, 2001 (themes refined from earlier StrengthsFinder work)

options.label: Achiever
options.desc: An Executing theme marked by stamina and a constant drive to accomplish and complete tasks.

options.label: Arranger
options.desc: An Executing theme for those who flexibly organise people and resources to reach maximum productivity.

options.label: Belief
options.desc: An Executing theme defined by core, unchanging values that give life purpose and direction.

options.label: Consistency
options.desc: An Executing theme focused on treating people equally by setting clear rules and fair routines.

options.label: Deliberative
options.desc: An Executing theme marked by careful, vigilant decision-making that anticipates obstacles and risks.

options.label: Discipline
options.desc: An Executing theme for those who thrive on structure, order, and predictable routines.

options.label: Focus
options.desc: An Executing theme that sets a clear direction and follows through, filtering out distractions.

options.label: Responsibility
options.desc: An Executing theme defined by taking psychological ownership of commitments and following through on them.

options.label: Restorative
options.desc: An Executing theme energised by identifying problems and finding ways to solve them.

options.label: Activator
options.desc: An Influencing theme that turns thoughts into action, impatient to get things moving.

options.label: Command
options.desc: An Influencing theme marked by presence and a readiness to take charge and confront.

options.label: Communication
options.desc: An Influencing theme for those who put thoughts into words easily and make ideas vivid.

options.label: Competition
options.desc: An Influencing theme that measures progress against others and strives to win and be first.

options.label: Maximizer
options.desc: An Influencing theme focused on transforming something strong into something superb rather than fixing weaknesses.

options.label: Self-Assurance
options.desc: An Influencing theme marked by inner confidence in one's ability to take risks and manage one's own life.

options.label: Significance
options.desc: An Influencing theme driven by a desire to make a big impact and be recognised for it.

options.label: Woo
options.desc: An Influencing theme (Winning Others Over) energised by meeting new people and breaking the ice.

options.label: Adaptability
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that lives in the moment and responds flexibly to whatever comes.

options.label: Connectedness
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that senses links between all things and finds meaning in them.

options.label: Developer
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that recognises and cultivates the potential in others.

options.label: Empathy
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme attuned to sensing the feelings and perspectives of others.

options.label: Harmony
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that seeks consensus and avoids conflict to keep people aligned.

options.label: Includer
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that works to make others feel part of the group and left out by no one.

options.label: Individualization
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme attuned to the unique qualities of each person and how they can work together.

options.label: Positivity
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that brings enthusiasm and lifts the energy of those nearby.

options.label: Relator
options.desc: A Relationship Building theme that draws strength from deep, close relationships with a few people.

options.label: Analytical
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme that searches for reasons and causes, testing ideas with evidence.

options.label: Context
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme that understands the present by researching its history and origins.

options.label: Futuristic
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme inspired by visions of what could be and energising others with them.

options.label: Ideation
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme fascinated by ideas and finding connections between seemingly unrelated things.

options.label: Input
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme with a craving to collect and archive information, things, and ideas.

options.label: Intellection
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme characterised by introspection and a love of mental activity and thinking.

options.label: Learner
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme driven by a desire to continuously learn and improve.

options.label: Strategic
options.desc: A Strategic Thinking theme that quickly spots patterns and alternative paths toward a goal.

systems.name: Belbin Team Roles
systems.statusNote: A widely used management framework derived from observational studies; it is a practical model of behavioural contributions rather than a validated psychometric trait theory, and its inventory has faced criticism over reliability.
systems.blurb: A model of nine behavioural roles people tend to adopt within a team, developed by British researcher Meredith Belbin and his colleagues from studies at Henley Management College in the 1970s and 1980s. It sorts people by the characteristic ways they contribute to group work, grouped into action-oriented, people-oriented, and thinking-oriented clusters.
systems.source: Meredith Belbin and colleagues, Henley Management College, 1970s-1980s

options.label: Plant
options.desc: A creative, imaginative idea generator who solves difficult problems with original thinking.

options.label: Resource Investigator
options.desc: An outgoing, enthusiastic networker who explores opportunities and develops contacts outside the team.

options.label: Co-ordinator
options.desc: A mature, confident chairperson who clarifies goals, promotes decision-making, and delegates effectively.

options.label: Shaper
options.desc: A driven, challenging member who provides the energy and pressure to keep the team moving and overcome obstacles.

options.label: Monitor Evaluator
options.desc: A sober, strategic, and discerning member who weighs options carefully and judges accurately.

options.label: Teamworker
options.desc: A cooperative, diplomatic, and perceptive member who listens, builds harmony, and averts friction.

options.label: Implementer
options.desc: A practical, reliable, and disciplined member who turns ideas and plans into concrete actions.

options.label: Completer Finisher
options.desc: A conscientious, anxious member who searches out errors and polishes work to deliver it on time and to a high standard.

options.label: Specialist
options.desc: A single-minded, dedicated member who provides rare knowledge and deep expertise in one specific subject.

systems.name: Conflict style (Thomas-Kilmann)
systems.blurb: How you handle conflict — your default mode under disagreement, from the widely-used Thomas-Kilmann model.
systems.statusNote: Based on the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI), a popular workplace framework. A reflective self-ID, not a formal assessment.

options.label: Competing
options.desc: Assertive and uncooperative — stands firm and pushes for your position.

options.label: Collaborating
options.desc: Assertive and cooperative — works for a solution that satisfies everyone.

options.label: Compromising
options.desc: Seeks a practical middle ground both sides can accept.

options.label: Avoiding
options.desc: Unassertive and uncooperative — sidesteps or delays the conflict.

options.label: Accommodating
options.desc: Unassertive and cooperative — yields to keep the peace.

systems.name: Leadership style
systems.blurb: How you lead a team — your default style when you're the one in charge. Drawn from well-known leadership models.
systems.statusNote: Based on widely-taught leadership frameworks (Lewin's styles plus common modern types). A reflective self-ID, not a formal assessment.

options.label: Democratic
options.desc: Involves the team and decides together.

options.label: Autocratic
options.desc: Makes the call and directs clearly from the top.

options.label: Laissez-faire
options.desc: Hands-off — trusts people to run with it.

options.label: Transformational
options.desc: Inspires with vision and lifts people to do their best.

options.label: Transactional
options.desc: Runs on clear goals, structure, and rewards.

options.label: Servant
options.desc: Leads by serving — puts the team's growth and needs first.

options.label: Coaching
options.desc: Develops people, giving feedback and growing their skills.

options.label: Visionary
options.desc: Sets a bold direction and rallies people toward it.

systems.name: How you make decisions
systems.statusNote: A self-description of how you typically make decisions. Most of us flex by situation — pick your default.
systems.blurb: Your default way of reaching a decision.

options.label: Analytical
options.desc: Weigh the data and the evidence.

options.label: Intuitive
options.desc: Go with my gut and instinct.

options.label: Consultative
options.desc: Gather others' input, then decide.

options.label: Decisive
options.desc: Decide quickly and move on.

options.label: Cautious
options.desc: Take time and avoid mistakes.

options.label: By consensus
options.desc: Decide together with the group.

systems.name: Followership style (Kelley)
systems.statusNote: Robert Kelley's followership model (1992) maps how people follow — along two axes: how actively engaged they are, and how independently they think. A reflective self-ID, the counterpart to leadership style.
systems.blurb: How you show up as a follower, not the one in charge.

options.label: Exemplary
options.desc: Independent, critical-thinking and fully engaged.

options.label: Conformist
options.desc: Eager and willing, but rarely questions.

options.label: Pragmatist
options.desc: Cautious middle-of-the-road; does what's needed.

options.label: Passive
options.desc: Waits for direction, with low initiative.

options.label: Alienated
options.desc: Capable and critical, but disengaged or cynical.

systems.name: Motivation to lead
systems.statusNote: The Motivation to Lead (MTL) scale (Chan & Drasgow, 2001) is a validated 27-item measure of three independent reasons people take on leadership — affective-identity, social-normative and non-calculative motivation. A 2020 meta-analysis (Badura et al.) linked these motives to who emerges as, and succeeds as, a leader. You can lean high or low on each.
systems.blurb: Chan and Drasgow's validated model of why — and whether — people step forward to lead, across three independent drives: an affective-identity pull (enjoying leadership and identifying as a leader), a social-normative sense of duty, and a non-calculative willingness to lead whatever the personal cost.

dimensions.name: Affective-identity
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you enjoy leading and see yourself as a leader, often taking charge in a group; leaning low means you feel little pull towards the role and are happy to let someone else take the helm.

dimensions.name: Social-normative
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you step up to lead from a sense of duty and responsibility when someone is needed; leaning low means you feel no special obligation to take the lead.

dimensions.name: Non-calculative
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you take on leadership without weighing the personal cost, effort or reward; leaning low means you prefer to lead only when the benefits to you clearly outweigh the burdens.

systems.name: Career anchor (Schein)
systems.blurb: What you'd least give up in your work — your deepest career value, from Edgar Schein's Career Anchors model.
systems.statusNote: Based on Edgar Schein's Career Anchors, a widely-used career-development framework. A reflective self-ID, not a formal assessment.

options.label: Technical / functional
options.desc: Mastering a craft or specialism and being expert at it.

options.label: General management
options.desc: Leading, integrating, and being responsible for outcomes.

options.label: Autonomy / independence
options.desc: Freedom to work your own way, on your own terms.

options.label: Security / stability
options.desc: Steady, predictable employment and peace of mind.

options.label: Entrepreneurial creativity
options.desc: Building something new and your own.

options.label: Service / dedication to a cause
options.desc: Work in service of values you believe in.

options.label: Pure challenge
options.desc: Solving hard problems and overcoming tough obstacles.

options.label: Lifestyle
options.desc: Balancing work with the rest of life and personal needs.

systems.name: Where you work best
systems.statusNote: A simple self-identification of the setting that suits you — none judged.
systems.blurb: The kind of environment where you do your best work.

options.label: Office
options.desc: A shared workplace with colleagues around you.

options.label: Remote / home
options.desc: Working from home or wherever you choose.

options.label: Hybrid
options.desc: A mix of office and remote.

options.label: On the move
options.desc: Travelling, between sites, rarely at one desk.

options.label: Outdoors / field
options.desc: Out in the field, on site, or in the open air.

systems.name: Multiple Intelligences (Gardner)
systems.statusNote: Howard Gardner’s theory is hugely popular in education; it remains debated and is not well supported as a set of distinct “intelligences”.
systems.blurb: Howard Gardner’s theory that intelligence is not one thing but several relatively independent capacities. Pick the ones that feel like your strengths.

options.label: Linguistic
options.desc: A way with words — reading, writing, speaking, and language.

options.label: Logical–Mathematical
options.desc: Logic, numbers, reasoning, and abstract problems.

options.label: Spatial
options.desc: Images, space, and visualising how things fit together.

options.label: Bodily–Kinesthetic
options.desc: The body, movement, coordination, and physical skill.

options.label: Musical
options.desc: Rhythm, pitch, sound, and music.

options.label: Interpersonal
options.desc: Reading, understanding, and relating to other people.

options.label: Intrapersonal
options.desc: Self-understanding, reflection, and knowing your own mind.

options.label: Naturalistic
options.desc: Nature, living things, and patterns in the natural world.

options.label: Existential (proposed)
options.desc: The big questions of meaning, life, and existence.

systems.name: Field of study
systems.statusNote: Self-identified — the subjects you've studied or love, by university faculty.
systems.blurb: The academic fields you've studied or are drawn to — the university faculties. Pick all that are part of you.

options.label: Natural Sciences
options.desc: Physics, chemistry, biology, and earth sciences.

options.label: Mathematics
options.desc: Pure and applied maths, logic, and statistics.

options.label: Engineering
options.desc: Designing and building — mechanical, civil, electrical, and more.

options.label: Computer Science
options.desc: Computing, software, data, and AI.

options.label: Medicine & Health
options.desc: Medicine, nursing, and the health professions.

options.label: Social Sciences
options.desc: Sociology, economics, politics, and anthropology.

options.label: Psychology
options.desc: The mind, behaviour, and how people work.

options.label: Humanities
options.desc: History, philosophy, literature, and languages.

options.label: Arts & Design
options.desc: Fine art, music, theatre, and design.

options.label: Business & Economics
options.desc: Management, finance, marketing, and economics.

options.label: Law
options.desc: Legal study, justice, and policy.

options.label: Education
options.desc: Teaching, learning, and pedagogy.

options.label: Agriculture & Environment
options.desc: Farming, ecology, and environmental science.

systems.name: Learning style (Honey & Mumford)
systems.blurb: How you prefer to learn — the four styles from Honey and Mumford's popular model, built on Kolb's learning cycle.
systems.statusNote: Based on Honey & Mumford's learning styles. Popular and widely used, though research finds little support for 'matching' teaching to a style. A reflective self-ID, not a prescription.

options.label: Activist
options.desc: Learns by doing — dives in and tries things hands-on.

options.label: Reflector
options.desc: Learns by observing and thinking things over first.

options.label: Theorist
options.desc: Learns by understanding the underlying model or theory.

options.label: Pragmatist
options.desc: Learns by seeing how ideas work in the real world.

systems.name: Learning style (Kolb)
systems.blurb: How you take in and use experience to learn — the four styles from Kolb's experiential learning model.
systems.statusNote: Based on David Kolb's Experiential Learning model. Influential and widely taught, though the 'learning styles' idea has limited research support. A reflective self-ID.

options.label: Diverging
options.desc: Feels and watches — imaginative, sees many angles, good with people.

options.label: Assimilating
options.desc: Thinks and watches — logical, drawn to ideas and concepts.

options.label: Converging
options.desc: Thinks and does — practical problem-solving and applying ideas.

options.label: Accommodating
options.desc: Feels and does — hands-on, intuitive, learns by trying.

systems.name: How you study best
systems.blurb: The way you actually get things to stick — your go-to study method.
systems.statusNote: A plain description of how you prefer to study; nothing more is read into it.

options.label: Solo & quiet
options.desc: Focus best alone, in silence.

options.label: Group study
options.desc: Learn best discussing with others.

options.label: Visual notes / mind-maps

systems.name: Achievement goal orientation
systems.statusNote: The 2 × 2 achievement goal framework (Elliot & McGregor, 2001), operationalised by the Achievement Goal Questionnaire and its revision (Elliot & Murayama, 2008), is a validated model in educational and motivation psychology. It crosses how you define competence — by mastery (your own standard) or by performance (relative to others) — with valence — approach (pursuing success) or avoidance (preventing failure) — to give four goal orientations. It develops the earlier mastery-versus-performance goal distinction of Dweck, Nicholls and Ames, and is conceptually separate from implicit theories of ability (the fixed-vs-growth mindset).
systems.blurb: Achievement goal orientation is about what you are really chasing when you take on a challenge — the kind of success that drives you. Andrew Elliot and Holly McGregor's validated 2 × 2 framework crosses two questions: do you define doing well by mastering the material and improving on your own past (a mastery goal) or by outperforming other people (a performance goal); and are you drawn toward attaining success (approach) or toward avoiding failure (avoidance)? The four combinations — mastery-approach, performance-approach, mastery-avoidance and performance-avoidance — describe distinct ways learners and achievers orient themselves, and they predict how people study, respond to setbacks and feel about their work. Achievement goals are about the goals you pursue, separate from your underlying mindset about whether ability is fixed or can grow.

options.label: Mastery-approach
options.desc: You learn to genuinely understand and improve. Success means deepening your grasp and getting better than you were before — your own progress is the measure, whether or not anyone else notices.

options.label: Performance-approach
options.desc: You're driven to excel relative to others. Success means showing what you can do and coming out ahead — performing visibly well compared with the people around you.

options.label: Mastery-avoidance
options.desc: You aim never to fall short of your own standard. Success means avoiding gaps, misunderstanding or forgetting — not leaving anything half-learned or slipping below what you know you're capable of.

options.label: Performance-avoidance
options.desc: You aim not to look less able than others. Success means staying clear of mistakes that would seem incompetent and not falling behind the people around you.

systems.name: Adult attachment style
systems.statusNote: A well-researched framework in relationship psychology, grounded in attachment theory and supported by decades of empirical study of close relationships. Adult attachment styles were introduced by Hazan & Shaver (1987), extending Bowlby and Ainsworth's earlier work.
systems.blurb: Adult attachment theory describes characteristic patterns in how people seek, experience, and regulate closeness in intimate relationships. Rooted in John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth's work on infant attachment (1960s-70s) and extended to adults, the four-category model of Kim Bartholomew and Leonard Horowitz (1991) sorts people by their underlying models of self and others into four styles. Our free course traces attachment from its childhood roots through how the styles play out in love, and ends on the most hopeful finding — that attachment can change, and how people move toward security.

systems.statusNote: The Experiences in Close Relationships measure (Brennan, Clark & Shaver, 1998; revised by Fraley, Waller & Brennan, 2000) is the research standard for adult attachment. systems.blurb: The Experiences in Close Relationships scale (ECR) maps adult attachment not as a single type but on two independent, research-validated dimensions: attachment anxiety (fear of rejection and abandonment) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness and dependence). Your standing is continuous rather than a fixed category — and the four familiar styles (secure, anxious-preoccupied, dismissing, and fearful) emerge as the quadrants of this two-dimensional space.

systems.name: Parent & peer attachment (IPPA)
systems.statusNote: The Inventory of Parent and Peer Attachment (IPPA; Armsden & Greenberg, 1987, Journal of Youth and Adolescence) is a widely used, validated self-report measure of the security of one's attachment to parents and to close friends, scored on three subscales — Trust, Communication, and Alienation.
systems.blurb: How close do you feel to the people who raised you, and to your closest friends? The Inventory of Parent and Peer Attachment (IPPA) measures exactly that — the felt security of your bonds with parents and peers, kept distinct from romantic attachment. Developed by Gay Armsden and Mark Greenberg in 1987 and used in hundreds of studies since, it rates these relationships on three dimensions: Trust (do they understand and respect you?), Communication (can you talk openly about what troubles you?), and Alienation (do you feel angry, isolated, or let down?). High trust and open communication with low alienation mark a secure base; the reverse signals a strained one.

systems.name: The fate of the universe
systems.statusNote: These are genuine cosmological scenarios from physics rather than folklore, but choosing one is a personal pick among open hypotheses — not a settled fact — so this is marked a popular self-identification, not a measured trait. The long-term fates of stars, galaxies and the universe were set out by Adams and Laughlin (1997, Reviews of Modern Physics); the Big Rip was modelled by Caldwell, Kamionkowski and Weinberg (2003, Physical Review Letters). Under the standard cosmological model the Big Freeze is the mainstream expectation, but the outcome depends on the nature of dark energy, which is not yet precisely measured.
systems.blurb: How will the cosmos end? Modern cosmology maps several possible long-term futures for the universe, and which one comes to pass depends mostly on the still-mysterious nature of dark energy. This is a self-identification over genuine scientific scenarios — a cold and endless Big Freeze, a structure-shredding Big Rip, a collapsing Big Crunch, an endlessly cycling Big Bounce, or a sudden rewrite of physics through vacuum decay — rather than a claim about which is true. Current measurements lean toward the Big Freeze, but the question is genuinely open.
systems.source: Adams & Laughlin, A Dying Universe (Reviews of Modern Physics, 1997)

options.label: Big Crunch
options.desc: Expansion eventually reverses and gravity pulls all matter back into a hot, dense state — a mirror image of the Big Bang.

options.label: Big Bounce
options.desc: A collapse or other transition seeds a fresh expanding universe, so the cosmos cycles through endless births and deaths.

options.label: Vacuum decay
options.desc: Our vacuum is only metastable, and a bubble of true vacuum could nucleate and spread at light speed, rewriting the laws of physics.

options.label: Still an open question
options.desc: The outcome hinges on the nature of dark energy, which we have not yet measured — so the honest scientific position is that it remains undecided.

systems.statusNote: Numerology has no scientific basis; the meanings assigned to numbers are not empirically validated and reflect esoteric tradition rather than measurable traits.
systems.blurb: The Life Path number is the central figure in modern Western (Pythagorean) numerology, a divinatory practice popularised in the early 20th century by writers such as L. Dow Balliett and Juno Jordan that draws on much older number symbolism attributed to Pythagoras. It is calculated from a full date of birth: the month, day, and year are each reduced by summing their digits down to a single digit, those three results are added together, and the total is reduced once more to a single digit. The single number it yields is said to indicate one's core nature and life direction. Master numbers 11, 22, and 33 are kept unreduced when they appear as the final total. Our free course shows how to calculate your number and walks through the folk meaning of each Life Path — an esoteric cultural practice, not a scientifically grounded one.

systems.blurb: Human Design, created by Ra Uru Hu in 1987, blends astrology, the I Ching, the chakra system and Kabbalah. From your birth date, time and place it assigns one of five energy types — Manifestor, Generator, Manifesting Generator, Projector or Reflector — each with its own decision-making strategy. Our free course explains the basics, the five types, and how to read your chart — a contemporary New Age synthesis, not a scientific system.

options.label: Manifestor
options.desc: Initiating and independent — here to start things and act on impulse.

options.label: Generator
options.desc: A sustainable life-force that thrives by responding to what lights them up.

options.label: Manifesting Generator
options.desc: A fast, multi-passionate hybrid of Manifestor and Generator energy.

options.label: Projector
options.desc: A guide who sees others clearly and works best when invited and recognised.

options.label: Reflector
options.desc: Rare and lunar — mirrors the health of the community around them.

systems.name: Blood-type personality (ketsueki-gata)
systems.statusNote: A popular belief in Japan and Korea with no scientific support; controlled studies find no reliable link between ABO blood type and personality.
systems.blurb: Ketsueki-gata is the popular East Asian belief that a person's ABO blood type shapes their temperament. Popularised in 1970s Japan by Masahiko Nomi, it sorts people into four personality profiles corresponding to blood types A, B, AB, and O.
systems.source: Masahiko Nomi, Japan, 1970s (building on earlier 1920s ideas by Takeji Furukawa)

options.label: Type A
options.desc: Stereotyped as earnest, organised, and reserved, yet prone to anxiety and a strong sense of responsibility.

options.label: Type B
options.desc: Stereotyped as creative, individualistic, and passionate, with an unconventional and free-spirited streak.

options.label: Type AB
options.desc: Stereotyped as rational, adaptable, and complex, while remaining private and somewhat hard to read.

options.label: Type O
options.desc: Stereotyped as confident, sociable, and ambitious, with a resilient and goal-driven outlook.

systems.name: Ayurvedic dosha (Prakriti)
systems.statusNote: A concept from traditional Ayurvedic medicine, not established or validated by modern science.
systems.blurb: Prakriti is the mind-body constitution described in Ayurveda, the traditional medical system of the Indian subcontinent rooted in classical Sanskrit texts of the early centuries CE. It sorts people by the balance of three doshas (Vata, Pitta, and Kapha), each tied to elemental qualities and characteristic physical and temperamental traits. Our free course explains the three doshas, helps you find your own with a body-type test, and shows how Ayurveda suggests balancing them — a traditional knowledge system, not one validated by modern science.
systems.source: Traditional Ayurvedic medicine; classical texts such as the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita (early centuries CE)

options.label: Vata
options.desc: Air and ether: described as light, quick, creative, and variable.

options.label: Pitta
options.desc: Fire and water: described as sharp, driven, and intense.

options.label: Kapha
options.desc: Earth and water: described as steady, calm, and grounded.

options.label: Vata-Pitta
options.desc: A dual constitution blending the quick, variable qualities of Vata with the sharp, driven intensity of Pitta.

options.label: Pitta-Kapha
options.desc: A dual constitution blending the sharp, driven intensity of Pitta with the steady, grounded calm of Kapha.

options.label: Vata-Kapha
options.desc: A dual constitution blending the quick, variable qualities of Vata with the steady, grounded calm of Kapha.

options.label: Tridoshic
options.desc: A constitution in which Vata, Pitta, and Kapha are present in roughly equal, balanced measure.

systems.name: Five-Element constitution (TCM)
systems.statusNote: Drawn from traditional Chinese medicine; it is a classical philosophical framework, not a system validated by modern science.
systems.blurb: The Five-Element (Wu Xing) constitutional types come from traditional Chinese medicine, a system whose written foundations trace to the Han dynasty (roughly 2nd century BCE). It sorts people into temperament and body-type categories aligned with the five elements: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water.
systems.source: Traditional Chinese medicine, Wu Xing theory; classical foundations from the Han dynasty (c. 2nd century BCE)

systems.name: D&D moral alignment
systems.statusNote: A playful framework from tabletop gaming, not a scientifically validated personality model.
systems.blurb: The Dungeons & Dragons moral alignment grid plots characters on two axes, law versus chaos and good versus evil, yielding nine combined alignments. The good-evil axis was added by Gary Gygax in a 1976 article, incorporated into the 1977 Basic Set, and the full nine-alignment grid was canonized in the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Player's Handbook (1978); it sorts people by their stance on order versus freedom and altruism versus self-interest.
systems.source: Gary Gygax / TSR, Dungeons & Dragons; good-evil axis introduced 1976, nine-alignment grid canonized in the AD&D Player's Handbook (1978)

options.label: Neutral Good
options.desc: Pursues doing good as a goal in itself, working with or around law and chaos as needed to help others.

options.label: Chaotic Good
options.desc: Values personal freedom and conscience over rules, doing good by following one's own heart rather than imposed order.

options.label: Lawful Neutral
options.desc: Acts in accordance with order, tradition, or a personal code, valuing consistency and structure above questions of good or evil.

options.label: True Neutral
options.desc: Holds no strong allegiance to order or freedom nor to altruism or self-interest, often seeking balance or simply acting on practical need.

options.label: Chaotic Neutral
options.desc: Prizes individual freedom and self-direction above all, resisting both rules and obligations to good or evil.

options.label: Lawful Evil
options.desc: Pursues self-interest through order, hierarchy, and rules, exploiting structure and codes to dominate or control others.

options.label: Neutral Evil

systems.name: Gaming motives (MOGQ)
systems.statusNote: The Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ) is a validated instrument developed by Demetrovics, Urbán, Nagygyörgy and colleagues (2011) from a factor analysis of 3,818 online gamers. It identifies seven motives for play — social, escape, competition, coping, skill development, fantasy and recreation. A reflective self-report of motivation, not a clinical test or a measure of problem gaming.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of why people play games. Developed in 2011 by Zsolt Demetrovics and colleagues, the Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ) grew out of a survey of more than 3,800 players whose answers, under factor analysis, sorted the pull of play into seven distinct motives: socialising with others, escaping from reality, competing to win, coping with stress and difficult feelings, developing skills and concentration, living out a fantasy as someone else, and simple recreation and fun. Rather than naming a single type, it captures the mix of reasons that draw you to the screen — most players feel several at once. This asks which motives pull at you the hardest.
systems.source: Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (Demetrovics, Urbán, Nagygyörgy et al., 2011)

options.label: Social
options.desc: I play to be with others — making friends, teaming up, and meeting new people through the game.

options.label: Escape
options.desc: I play to get away from reality — to forget unpleasant things and leave everyday problems behind for a while.

options.label: Competition
options.desc: I play to compete — to test myself against others, win, and prove how good I am.

options.label: Coping

systems.name: Empathy (Interpersonal Reactivity Index)
systems.statusNote: The Interpersonal Reactivity Index (Davis, 1980, 1983) is the most widely used self-report measure of empathy. It treats empathy not as one trait but as four independent dimensions — two that are more cognitive (perspective taking and fantasy) and two that are more affective (empathic concern and personal distress) — each scored on its own continuous scale.
systems.blurb: The Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) maps empathy as four separate, research-validated dimensions rather than a single trait. Two are more cognitive — perspective taking (spontaneously seeing a situation from another person's point of view) and fantasy (becoming imaginatively absorbed in the feelings of characters in books, films and stories) — and two are more affective — empathic concern (other-oriented warmth and sympathy for people in difficulty) and personal distress (the self-oriented unease you feel in tense or emotional situations involving others). You can stand high or low on each one independently, so this describes the shape of your empathy rather than how empathic you are overall.

dimensions.name: Perspective taking
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you spontaneously imagine how a situation looks from another person's point of view before you react; leaning low means you tend to stay anchored in your own perspective.

dimensions.name: Fantasy
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you easily transpose yourself into the feelings and actions of characters in books, films and stories; leaning low means fiction moves you less and you stay at arm's length from it.

dimensions.name: Empathic concern
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you often feel warmth, sympathy and concern for people who are worse off than you; leaning low means others' misfortune moves you less and you keep a cooler distance.

dimensions.name: Personal distress
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means tense or distressing situations involving other people leave you feeling anxious and unsettled yourself; leaning low means you stay calm and self-possessed when those around you are in distress.

systems.name: Perfectionism
systems.statusNote: Perfectionism is one of the most-studied traits in personality and clinical psychology, and is well established as multidimensional rather than a single quality. This follows Hewitt and Flett's Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (1991), which separates perfectionism by its direction — toward the self, toward other people, and the perfection a person believes others demand of them — each scored on its own continuous scale. Research also distinguishes adaptive perfectionistic strivings (high personal standards) from maladaptive perfectionistic concerns (fear of mistakes and harsh self-criticism); see Stoeber and Otto (2006).
systems.blurb: Perfectionism is the tendency to hold exacting standards and to measure yourself or others against them — and psychologists find it is not one thing but several, which is why two perfectionists can look quite different. This maps it along the three directions described by Hewitt and Flett: self-oriented perfectionism (the demanding standards you set for yourself), other-oriented perfectionism (the standards you expect other people to meet) and socially-prescribed perfectionism (the sense that others expect you to be perfect). You can stand high or low on each one independently. A further distinction separates healthy perfectionistic strivings — high standards held alongside self-acceptance — from the more painful perfectionistic concerns, where mistakes feel intolerable and a never-good-enough self-criticism takes hold. This describes the shape of your perfectionism, not whether having high standards is good or bad.

dimensions.name: Self-oriented perfectionism
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you set demanding standards for yourself and push hard to meet them; leaning low means you hold yourself to gentler, more forgiving standards.

dimensions.name: Other-oriented perfectionism
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you expect the people around you to meet very high standards; leaning low means you accept other people's imperfections more readily.

dimensions.name: Socially-prescribed perfectionism
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel that other people — family, peers or society — expect you to be perfect; leaning low means you feel little outside pressure to meet others' standards.

systems.name: Hope (agency & pathways)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. Hope theory and the Adult Hope Scale were developed and validated by C. R. Snyder and colleagues (1991), who defined hope as the combination of agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (the perceived ability to plan routes to goals). The scale's two-factor structure, reliability and validity are well established, and hope shows discriminant validity from optimism and self-efficacy.
systems.blurb: Hope theory, developed by psychologist C. R. Snyder, treats hope not as a passing wish but as a goal-directed way of thinking with two measurable parts: agency — the motivation and willpower to pursue your goals — and pathways — the knack for mapping routes to reach them, and for finding a new way when the obvious one is blocked. The Adult Hope Scale places you on these two dimensions rather than sorting you into a type. Research sets hope apart from optimism, a general expectation that things will turn out well: hope is specifically about whether you feel both the drive and the means to get where you want to go.

dimensions.name: Agency (willpower)
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means feeling energised and determined in pursuing your goals — confident you can get yourself going and keep going. Leaning low means that drive comes and goes, and starting or sustaining momentum toward a goal can feel harder.

dimensions.name: Pathways (waypower)
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you can usually picture several ways to reach a goal and improvise a new one when the obvious path closes. Leaning low means you tend to see fewer options and can feel blocked when a plan falls through.

systems.name: Gratitude (abundance, simple things & others)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. Gratitude as a stable disposition has been captured by two well-validated self-report instruments: the six-item Gratitude Questionnaire (GQ-6) of McCullough, Emmons and Tsang (2002), which measures the tendency to recognise and respond to the good one receives, and the Gratitude, Resentment and Appreciation Test (GRAT) of Watkins, Woodward, Stone and Kolts (2003), whose three-factor structure — a sense of abundance (the absence of feeling deprived), simple appreciation of everyday pleasures, and appreciation of others' contributions — is the basis for the three dimensions here. Both scales show good reliability and validity and correlate with greater wellbeing. A higher score is one tendency among many, not a measure of worth.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of how readily you notice and feel thankful for the good in your life. Psychologists treat gratitude not as a passing mood but as a lasting disposition, and two validated measures anchor that view: the Gratitude Questionnaire (GQ-6), developed by Michael McCullough, Robert Emmons and Jo-Ann Tsang in 2002, and the Gratitude, Resentment and Appreciation Test (GRAT) of Philip Watkins and colleagues in 2003, which maps the grateful disposition across three separate fronts. The first is a sense of abundance — feeling that life has treated you well, rather than that it owes you or has left you short. The second is simple appreciation — savouring small everyday pleasures, a warm drink, good weather, a quiet moment, instead of letting them pass unnoticed. The third is appreciation of others — recognising how much other people add to your life and feeling moved to thank them. You can sit high on one front and low on another, so this describes the texture of your gratitude rather than a single score.
systems.source: Gratitude, Resentment and Appreciation Test (Watkins et al., 2003)

dimensions.name: Sense of abundance
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel life has given you plenty and rarely dwell on what you lack or feel the world owes you. Leaning low means you more often feel short-changed, noticing what is missing or unfair before what is already there.

dimensions.name: Simple appreciation
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you notice and relish small everyday pleasures — a warm drink, good weather, a quiet moment — and they genuinely lift you. Leaning low means ordinary good things tend to pass unremarked, and it takes something bigger to move you.

dimensions.name: Appreciation of others
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you readily recognise how much other people add to your life and feel moved to thank them. Leaning low means you more often see your circumstances as self-made and notice the help of others less.
