systems.name: Authenticity
systems.statusNote: Empirical. The Authenticity Scale was developed and validated by Alex Wood and colleagues (2008), drawing on Carl Rogers's person-centred account of the fully functioning person and on Kernis and Goldman's (2006) multicomponent model of authenticity. Its twelve items load on three reliable factors — authentic living, self-alienation and accepting external influence — that together index how closely a person's outward life matches their inner experience. Higher authentic living together with lower self-alienation and lower acceptance of external influence is what the instrument scores as greater dispositional authenticity, a pattern that tends to go with higher well-being and self-esteem. The three strands describe how you relate to your true self, not your worth, and any profile across them is one honest way of living.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of how closely the life you live matches the person you feel you really are. Drawing on humanistic psychology, Alex Wood and colleagues' Authenticity Scale (2008) breaks authenticity into three measurable strands: authentic living — how far you act in line with your own values and beliefs; self-alienation — how in or out of touch you feel with the 'real you'; and accepting external influence — how readily you shape yourself around what others expect. The three vary independently, so you might live boldly by your values yet still feel only half in touch with yourself, or know yourself deeply while bending easily to others. This places you along each strand rather than judging you authentic or not — there is no wrong way to sit.
systems.source: Authenticity Scale (Wood, Linley, Maltby, Baliousis & Joseph, 2008)

dimensions.name: Authentic living
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you mostly act in line with your own values and beliefs, and stand by them even when it is awkward or unpopular. Leaning low means you more often set them aside to suit the moment, the room or what is expected of you.

dimensions.name: Self-alienation
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you often feel distant from the 'real me' — unsure what you genuinely feel or who you are underneath. Leaning low means you feel you know yourself well and recognise your own feelings as they arise. On the original scale, lower self-alienation is the more authentic pole.

dimensions.name: Accepting external influence
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you readily take on what other people think you should do or be, and are strongly swayed by their expectations. Leaning low means you steer by your own sense of yourself — taking others in, but not handing them the wheel.

systems.name: Passion (harmonious & obsessive)
systems.statusNote: The Passion Scale (Vallerand et al., 2003) is the research-standard measure of the Dualistic Model of Passion, distinguishing two ways a self-defining love for an activity can be carried: harmonious passion — freely chosen and integrated alongside the rest of life — and obsessive passion — an internal compulsion that can crowd other things out. The two are independent dimensions, so a person can lean high or low on each, and the two-factor structure has been validated across many activities, languages and samples (Marsh, Vallerand et al., 2013).
systems.blurb: Passion here is a strong, lasting love for an activity you value and pour yourself into — a sport, a craft, a cause, your work. The Dualistic Model of Passion, developed by Robert Vallerand and colleagues, finds it takes two forms that can each run strong or weak in the same person. Harmonious passion is freely chosen and sits in balance with the rest of life: you love the activity, yet remain in charge of it. Obsessive passion carries an inner pressure to keep going — the pursuit can take you over, grow hard to switch off, and crowd out other things that matter. Measured as two independent dimensions rather than a single type, this maps the shape of your passion: the same deep love can enrich a life or come to rule it.

dimensions.name: Harmonious passion
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means the pursuits you love sit in harmony with the rest of your life — you take them up because you want to, and can step away when you need to; leaning low means that easy, freely chosen kind of love for an activity is less a part of how you live.

dimensions.name: Obsessive passion
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means a pursuit can take you over — an inner pressure keeps you at it, it is hard to switch off, and it can crowd out other things you care about; leaning low means your involvements stay in their place and rarely pull at you against your will.

systems.name: Temperament type (Thomas & Chess)
systems.blurb: Your basic, inborn temperament — the classic types from Thomas and Chess's landmark study of how we're wired from the start.
systems.statusNote: Based on the Thomas & Chess temperament types from the New York Longitudinal Study, a foundational developmental-psychology framework. A reflective self-ID, not a clinical assessment.

options.label: Easy
options.desc: Generally calm, adaptable, and even in mood.

options.label: Difficult / spirited
options.desc: Intense, reactive, and slower to settle into routines.

options.label: Slow to warm up
options.desc: Cautious at first, warming gradually to new people and situations.

options.label: Mixed
options.desc: A blend that doesn't fit neatly into one type — as is true for many.

systems.name: Sensitivity type (Highly Sensitive Person)
systems.statusNote: Sensory-processing sensitivity (SPS) is a temperament trait measured by Aron & Aron's Highly Sensitive Person Scale (1997). The trait shows up as Aron's DOES profile — depth of processing, overstimulation, emotional reactivity and sensitivity to subtle stimuli. The three sensitivity groups — dandelions, tulips and orchids — were empirically identified by Lionetti, Aron, Aron, Burns, Jagiellowicz & Pluess (2018), building on the differential-susceptibility 'orchid and dandelion' metaphor (Boyce & Ellis, 2005). A reflective self-ID, not a clinical assessment, and distinct from introversion — roughly a third of highly sensitive people are extroverts.
systems.blurb: How deeply your nervous system registers and responds to your surroundings — from subtle beauty to stress and other people's moods.
systems.source: Sensory-processing sensitivity / Highly Sensitive Person Scale (Aron & Aron)

options.label: Dandelion (low sensitivity)
options.desc: You take most environments in your stride — resilient and steady, rarely thrown by noise, change or other people's moods, and not greatly swayed by very good or very harsh surroundings alike.

options.label: Tulip (medium sensitivity)
options.desc: You sit between the two — you notice and respond to your surroundings, but are seldom overwhelmed by them. This is where most people fall.

options.label: Orchid (high sensitivity)
options.desc: You process experience deeply and pick up on fine detail and subtlety. Rich surroundings and kindness nourish you, while noise, time pressure and conflict can overwhelm — you feel both the lows and the highs more keenly.

systems.name: Sensation seeking
systems.statusNote: Sensation seeking is a well-established trait in personality psychology, introduced by Marvin Zuckerman (1971) and measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale, Form V (Zuckerman, Eysenck & Eysenck, 1978), with a widely used brief version (BSSS) developed by Hoyle and colleagues (2002). Decades of research connect it to biological and genetic markers. A reflective self-ID, not a diagnosis.
systems.blurb: Sensation seeking is a personality trait, identified by psychologist Marvin Zuckerman, describing how strongly a person craves varied, novel, complex, and intense experiences — and how willing they are to take physical, social, or financial risks to have them. The Sensation Seeking Scale maps it across four facets: thrill & adventure seeking, experience seeking, disinhibition, and boredom susceptibility. With roots in biology and brain chemistry, it helps explain why some people chase the new and intense while others find contentment in the calm and familiar.

dimensions.name: Thrill & adventure seeking
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means craving risky, exciting physical activity — speed, heights, extreme sports; leaning low means preferring safer, calmer pursuits and steady ground.

dimensions.name: Experience seeking
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means seeking novelty through the mind and senses — travel, art, music, and unconventional people and ideas; leaning low means finding comfort in the familiar and the routine.

dimensions.name: Disinhibition
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means seeking release and stimulation through social abandon — lively parties, spontaneity, and variety; leaning low means preferring restraint, calm, and a quieter social pace.

dimensions.name: Boredom susceptibility
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means quickly tiring of repetition, routine, and predictability and craving change; leaning low means feeling at ease with steadiness, repetition, and familiar company.

systems.name: Reinforcement Sensitivity (BIS/BAS Scales)
systems.statusNote: An empirically validated self-report measure of Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory. The BIS/BAS Scales were developed and validated by Carver & White (1994); the underlying neuropsychology originated with Jeffrey Gray (1970) and was revised by Gray & McNaughton (2000).
systems.blurb: Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory, first proposed by Jeffrey Gray, explains temperament through two brain systems that react to the world in opposite ways: a Behavioural Inhibition System (BIS) that responds to threat, punishment, and uncertainty with caution and anxiety, and a Behavioural Activation System (BAS) that responds to reward with approach, energy, and pursuit. Carver and White's BIS/BAS Scales (1994) place you on the inhibition pole and on three facets of activation — Drive, Fun Seeking, and Reward Responsiveness — showing whether you are wired more to avoid what could go wrong or to chase what could go right. It is a cornerstone of personality neuroscience, distinct from descriptive trait models because it grounds temperament in approach-and-avoidance motivation rather than in clusters of adjectives.
systems.source: Jeffrey A. Gray (theory); Charles Carver & Teri White, BIS/BAS Scales, 1994

dimensions.name: Behavioural Inhibition (BIS)
dimensions.desc: The Behavioural Inhibition System governs sensitivity to possible punishment, threat, and things going wrong. Scoring high means you notice danger quickly, feel anxiety readily, and pause or hold back to stay safe; scoring low means threats rarely rattle you and you press on where others would hesitate.

dimensions.name: Drive (BAS)
dimensions.desc: Drive captures how persistently you pursue the goals you want. Scoring high means you go after what you desire with determination and don't give up easily; scoring low means you take desired outcomes more casually and feel less pull to chase them.

dimensions.name: Fun Seeking (BAS)
dimensions.desc: Fun Seeking is the appetite for new rewards and the readiness to act on impulse to find them. Scoring high means you crave novelty and will jump at a good opportunity on the spur of the moment; scoring low means you prefer to weigh things up first and feel less pull toward the new.

dimensions.name: Reward Responsiveness (BAS)
dimensions.desc: Reward Responsiveness is how strongly good things move you. Scoring high means the prospect or arrival of a reward gives you a clear lift of excitement and energy; scoring low means you respond to rewards more calmly and evenly.

systems.name: Gender identity
systems.statusNote: Self-identified; this is how the member describes their own gender, which is distinct from sex assigned at birth and from sexual orientation.
systems.blurb: Gender identity is a person's deeply felt internal sense of their own gender, which may or may not match the sex they were assigned at birth. It is distinct both from sex assigned at birth and from sexual orientation (who a person is attracted to). This system sorts people by how they internally experience and name their own gender.
systems.source: Self-identified; reflects contemporary understanding of gender identity developed across the 20th and 21st centuries.

options.label: Woman
options.desc: A person whose internal sense of gender is female.

options.label: Man
options.desc: A person whose internal sense of gender is male.

options.label: Transgender woman
options.desc: A woman who was assigned male at birth.

options.label: Transgender man
options.desc: A man who was assigned female at birth.

options.label: Non-binary
options.desc: A person whose gender is not exclusively that of a man or a woman.

options.label: Genderqueer
options.desc: A person whose gender identity falls outside or challenges conventional binary categories of man and woman.

options.label: Genderfluid
options.desc: A person whose gender identity shifts or varies over time rather than remaining fixed.

options.label: Agender
options.desc: A person who identifies as having no particular gender or as being without gender.

options.label: Bigender
options.desc: A person who identifies with two genders, either simultaneously or shifting between them.

options.label: Demigender
options.desc: A person who feels a partial, rather than full, connection to a particular gender.

options.label: Two-Spirit
options.desc: An identity specific to some Indigenous North American cultures, encompassing varied gender and social roles within those cultural traditions.

options.label: Questioning
options.desc: A person who is currently exploring or uncertain about their gender identity.

systems.name: Sex assigned at birth
systems.statusNote: This is a demographic record of the sex noted at birth, typically based on observed anatomy; it is a factual administrative category and is distinct from a person's gender identity.
systems.blurb: Sex assigned at birth is the classification recorded on a person's birth certificate, usually determined by a clinician's observation of external anatomy at delivery. It sorts people into female, male, or intersex, and is separate from gender identity, which is a person's own internal sense of their gender.
systems.source: Standard medical and civil-registration practice; formalised in birth-certificate systems over the 19th and 20th centuries.

options.label: Female
options.desc: Assigned female at birth, typically based on the observation of anatomy associated with the female sex.

options.label: Male
options.desc: Assigned male at birth, typically based on the observation of anatomy associated with the male sex.

options.label: Intersex
options.desc: Born with sex characteristics — chromosomes, gonads, or anatomy — that do not fit typical binary definitions of female or male.

systems.name: Personal pronouns
systems.statusNote: This is a self-reported identity field, not a scientific classification; pronouns describe how a person refers to and wishes to be referred to by others.
systems.blurb: A personal pronoun is the word set others use to refer to a member in the third person. The practice of routinely sharing one's pronouns spread widely in the 2010s, building on long-standing English usage and on neopronoun sets proposed since the 19th and 20th centuries. It sorts members by the pronoun set they use and ask others to use.
systems.source: Established English usage with neopronoun coinages from the 1800s-1900s; routine pronoun-sharing popularised in the 2010s

options.label: she/her
options.desc: Feminine third-person pronouns, declined as she/her/hers.

options.label: he/him
options.desc: Masculine third-person pronouns, declined as he/him/his.

options.label: they/them
options.desc: Gender-neutral pronouns used in the singular, declined as they/them/theirs.

options.label: she/they
options.desc: Indicates that both she/her and they/them are welcome.

options.label: he/they
options.desc: Indicates that both he/him and they/them are welcome.

options.label: ze/hir
options.desc: A gender-neutral neopronoun set, declined as ze/hir/hir/hirs (ze rhymes with 'zee'; hir pronounced like 'here').

options.label: xe/xem
options.desc: A gender-neutral neopronoun set, declined as xe/xem/xyr/xyrs (xe pronounced like 'zee'; xyr like 'zeer').

options.label: it/its
options.desc: Pronouns some people use for themselves by choice, declined as it/its.

options.label: name only (please use my name)
options.desc: Prefers to be referred to by name rather than by any pronoun.

options.label: any pronouns
options.desc: Comfortable with any pronoun set being used.

options.label: ask me
options.desc: Prefers to be asked directly which pronouns to use.

systems.name: Gender expression
systems.statusNote: Gender expression is how you outwardly present — through style, grooming and manner — which is distinct from gender identity. A self-description, shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: How you outwardly present, regardless of identity.

options.label: Masculine
options.desc: Predominantly masculine presentation.

options.label: Feminine
options.desc: Predominantly feminine presentation.

options.label: Androgynous
options.desc: A blend of masculine and feminine.

options.label: Gender-neutral
options.desc: A neutral, understated presentation.

options.label: Fluid
options.desc: Your expression shifts over time.

options.label: Beyond the binary
options.desc: Outside the masculine–feminine frame.

systems.name: How central gender is to you
systems.statusNote: A self-description of how central your gender is to your overall sense of identity. Entirely valid however you answer.
systems.blurb: How much gender figures in your sense of self.

options.label: Central to who I am
options.desc: A defining part of my identity.

options.label: An important part
options.desc: It matters, among other things.

options.label: One part among many
options.desc: Just one facet of me.

options.label: Rarely front of mind
options.desc: I don't think about it much.

options.label: Still exploring
options.desc: I'm figuring out what it means to me.

options.label: It varies
options.desc: Its importance shifts over time.

systems.name: Gender-role traits (BSRI)
systems.statusNote: The Bem Sex Role Inventory (Sandra Bem, 1974) rates 'instrumental' traits (assertive, independent, decisive) and 'expressive' traits (warm, compassionate, gentle) as two independent scales; the familiar four-way classification — masculine-typed, feminine-typed, androgynous, undifferentiated — followed in Spence, Helmreich & Stapp (1975) and Bem (1977). One of the most-used instruments in the psychology of gender; Bem's own thesis was that androgyny is common and adaptive. Honest caveats: the trait lists reflect what 1970s American samples rated as desirable 'for a man' or 'for a woman', average scores have shifted across the decades since, and many researchers now read the two scales simply as instrumentality and expressiveness. A self-description of where you sit, not a test.
systems.blurb: Which of the classic trait clusters describes you, whatever your gender — the 'instrumental' (assertive, independent), the 'expressive' (warm, attuned), both at once, or neither.

options.label: Masculine-typed (instrumental)
options.desc: The instrumental cluster leads — independent, assertive, decisive — whatever your gender.

options.label: Feminine-typed (expressive)
options.desc: The expressive cluster leads — warm, compassionate, attuned to others — whatever your gender.

options.label: Androgynous
options.desc: High on both clusters — as comfortable being assertive as being tender, depending on what the moment asks.

options.label: Undifferentiated
options.desc: Neither cluster stands out — in Bem's scheme that simply means these two trait lists aren't what define you.

systems.name: Sexual orientation
systems.statusNote: Sexual orientation is a widely studied aspect of human identity rather than a single proprietary test; it describes self-reported patterns of attraction and is treated by major health bodies as a normal dimension of human diversity.
systems.blurb: Sexual orientation describes the enduring pattern of a person's romantic and sexual attraction to others. The modern vocabulary developed across the late 19th and 20th centuries and continues to expand, and people are described by the gender or genders to whom they are attracted, or by the absence of such attraction.
systems.source: Modern usage developed from late-19th-century sexology through 20th- and 21st-century LGBTQ+ communities

options.label: Heterosexual (Straight)
options.desc: Attraction primarily to people of a different gender, typically men attracted to women or women attracted to men.

options.label: Gay
options.desc: Attraction to people of the same gender, often referring to men but also used broadly for same-gender attraction.

options.label: Lesbian
options.desc: A woman who is primarily attracted to other women.

options.label: Bisexual
options.desc: Attraction to more than one gender.

options.label: Pansexual
options.desc: Attraction to people regardless of their gender.

options.label: Asexual
options.desc: Experiencing little or no sexual attraction to others.

options.label: Demisexual
options.desc: Experiencing sexual attraction only after forming a strong emotional bond.

options.label: Queer
options.desc: A flexible umbrella term embracing a range of sexual orientations and gender identities outside heterosexual and cisgender norms, often chosen as a personal self-identifier.

options.label: Questioning
options.desc: Currently exploring one's sexual orientation and not yet settled on a label.

systems.name: Kinsey scale
systems.statusNote: A self-identification: Alfred Kinsey’s 0–6 scale (plus X) placing sexual orientation on a continuum rather than a binary.
systems.blurb: The Kinsey scale, introduced by Alfred Kinsey in 1948, rates sexual orientation from 0 (exclusively heterosexual) to 6 (exclusively homosexual), with X for no socio-sexual response.

options.label: 0 — Exclusively heterosexual
options.desc: Attraction and experience exclusively with the other sex.

options.label: 1 — Predominantly heterosexual
options.desc: Mostly heterosexual, only incidentally homosexual.

options.label: 2 — Mostly heterosexual
options.desc: Predominantly heterosexual, but more than incidentally homosexual.

options.label: 3 — Equally bisexual
options.desc: Equally heterosexual and homosexual.

options.label: 4 — Mostly homosexual
options.desc: Predominantly homosexual, but more than incidentally heterosexual.

options.label: 5 — Predominantly homosexual
options.desc: Mostly homosexual, only incidentally heterosexual.

options.label: 6 — Exclusively homosexual
options.desc: Attraction and experience exclusively with the same sex.

options.label: X — Asexual
options.desc: No socio-sexual contacts or reactions.

systems.name: Romantic orientation
systems.statusNote: Romantic orientation is a self-reported identity framework that distinguishes romantic from sexual attraction; it is descriptive rather than a validated scientific taxonomy.
systems.blurb: Romantic orientation describes the gender or genders toward which a person feels romantic attraction, which can differ from their sexual orientation. The split between romantic and sexual attraction was articulated within asexual and aromantic communities in the early 2000s and is widely used in LGBTQ+ discourse to sort people by the pattern of their romantic attractions.
systems.source: Asexual and aromantic communities, early 2000s (popularised via AVEN and related online spaces)

options.label: Heteroromantic
options.desc: Romantic attraction directed toward people of a gender different from one's own.

options.label: Homoromantic
options.desc: Romantic attraction directed toward people of the same gender as one's own.

options.label: Biromantic
options.desc: Romantic attraction toward people of two or more genders.

options.label: Panromantic
options.desc: Romantic attraction toward people regardless of their gender or gender identity.

options.label: Aromantic
options.desc: Experiencing little or no romantic attraction toward anyone.

options.label: Demiromantic
options.desc: Romantic attraction that develops only after forming a strong emotional bond with someone.

options.label: Grayromantic
options.desc: Experiencing romantic attraction rarely, weakly, or only under specific circumstances, falling between aromantic and romantic.

systems.name: How your orientation feels
systems.statusNote: Sexual and romantic orientation can feel fixed for some and fluid for others — both are normal. A respectful self-description of how stable or fluid yours feels over time. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: How stable or fluid your orientation feels over time.

options.label: Fixed
options.desc: Stable and consistent over time.

options.label: Mostly fixed
options.desc: Largely stable, with a little movement.

options.label: Fluid
options.desc: It shifts over time.

options.label: Very fluid
options.desc: Highly changeable and free-flowing.

options.label: Questioning
options.desc: Still exploring and figuring it out.

systems.name: How open you are about it
systems.statusNote: A self-description of how openly you share your sexual or romantic orientation. Entirely personal — there's no right level, and safety and context matter.
systems.blurb: How openly you share your orientation with others.

options.label: Open with everyone
options.desc: I share it freely and openly.

options.label: Out to most
options.desc: Open with most people in my life.

options.label: Close circle only
options.desc: Out to those I trust.

options.label: Keep it private
options.desc: I keep it largely to myself.

options.label: Depends on the setting
options.desc: Open in some places, not others.

options.label: Still figuring it out
options.desc: I'm working it out for myself.

systems.name: Klein Sexual Orientation Grid
systems.statusNote: The Klein Sexual Orientation Grid (KSOG) was devised by sex researcher Fritz Klein in The Bisexual Option (1978) and formalised and validated by Klein, Sepekoff & Wolf (1985), who rated seven dimensions of orientation across past, present and ideal time frames. It is a widely used research instrument that maps orientation as a continuum on each dimension rather than a single label. Here you record your present-day standing on each of the seven variables — a reflective self-ID, not a diagnosis.
systems.blurb: The Klein Sexual Orientation Grid (KSOG) is a multidimensional measure of sexual orientation, devised by sex researcher Fritz Klein in 1978 to answer a limitation of the single-axis Kinsey scale — that orientation is not one thing. Instead of one number, it rates seven separate dimensions — sexual attraction, behaviour, fantasies, emotional preference, social preference, self-identification, and lifestyle — each on a 1-7 continuum running from exclusively other-sex to exclusively same-sex, with a balanced middle for bisexuality. Klein also asked how each dimension shifts across a person's past, present, and ideal, treating orientation as a dynamic process rather than a fixed category.
systems.source: Klein Sexual Orientation Grid (Klein, Sepekoff & Wolf, 1985)

dimensions.name: Sexual attraction
dimensions.desc: Who you feel sexually attracted to. Leaning high means attraction to the same sex; leaning low means the other sex; the centre means drawn to both.

dimensions.name: Sexual behaviour
dimensions.desc: Who you have actually had sexual contact with. Leaning high means partners of the same sex; leaning low means the other sex; the centre means both.

dimensions.name: Sexual fantasies
dimensions.desc: Who appears in your sexual fantasies and daydreams. Leaning high means the same sex; leaning low means the other sex; the centre means both.

dimensions.name: Emotional preference
dimensions.desc: Who you form your closest, most loving emotional bonds with. Leaning high means the same sex; leaning low means the other sex; the centre means both equally.

dimensions.name: Social preference
dimensions.desc: Who you most enjoy spending social time with. Leaning high means mostly the same sex; leaning low means mostly the other sex; the centre means both equally.

dimensions.name: Self-identification
dimensions.desc: How you label your own orientation. Leaning high means gay or lesbian; leaning low means heterosexual; the centre means bisexual.

dimensions.name: Lifestyle
dimensions.desc: Whether the social world you live in is mostly heterosexual, mostly LGBTQ+, or a mix of both. Leaning high means a largely LGBTQ+ community; leaning low means a largely heterosexual one.

citations.authors: Klein, F., Sepekoff, B., & Wolf, T. J.

citations.title: The Bisexual Option
citations.authors: Klein, F.

systems.name: Race & ethnicity (U.S. federal categories)
systems.statusNote: These are official U.S. self-identification categories set by federal policy for data collection, not a scientific taxonomy of human biology.
systems.blurb: The minimum race and ethnicity categories defined by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget in Statistical Policy Directive No. 15, used across federal statistics and surveys. As revised in March 2024, it combines race and ethnicity into a single question and adds a Middle Eastern or North African category, sorting people by self-identified geographic and cultural origins. Respondents may select more than one category.

options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the original peoples of North, Central, and South America, including, for example, Navajo Nation, Blackfeet Tribe, Maya, Aztec, Native Village of Barrow Inupiat Traditional Government, and Nome Eskimo Community.

options.label: Asian
options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the original peoples of Central or East Asia, Southeast Asia, or South Asia, including, for example, Chinese, Asian Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, and Japanese.

options.label: Black or African American
options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the Black racial groups of Africa, including, for example, African American, Jamaican, Haitian, Nigerian, Ethiopian, and Somali.

options.label: Hispanic or Latino
options.desc: Includes individuals of Mexican, Puerto Rican, Salvadoran, Cuban, Dominican, Guatemalan, and other Central or South American or Spanish culture or origin.

options.label: Middle Eastern or North African (MENA)
options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the original peoples of the Middle East or North Africa, including, for example, Lebanese, Iranian, Egyptian, Syrian, Iraqi, and Israeli.

options.label: Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander
options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, or other Pacific Islands, including, for example, Native Hawaiian, Samoan, Chamorro, Tongan, Fijian, and Marshallese.

options.label: White
options.desc: Includes individuals with origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, including, for example, English, German, Irish, Italian, Polish, and French.

systems.name: Ethnic group (UK ONS census)
systems.statusNote: These are official administrative and statistical categories used for population monitoring, not biological or scientific classifications of human variation.
systems.blurb: A self-identified ethnic group classification used by the UK Office for National Statistics in the 2021 Census of England and Wales. It sorts respondents into five high-level groups, each with named subgroups, primarily reflecting ethnic and national origin and heritage.
systems.source: UK Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census of England and Wales

options.label: Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh
options.desc: A UK census high-level group whose subgroups are Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Chinese, and Any other Asian background.

options.label: Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African
options.desc: A UK census high-level group whose subgroups are Caribbean, African, and Any other Black, Black British, or Caribbean background.

options.label: Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups
options.desc: A UK census high-level group for people identifying with more than one ethnic group, whose subgroups are White and Black Caribbean, White and Black African, White and Asian, and Any other Mixed or Multiple ethnic background.

options.label: White
options.desc: A UK census high-level group whose subgroups are English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British, Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, Roma, and Any other White background.

options.label: Other ethnic group
options.desc: A UK census high-level group whose subgroups are Arab and Any other ethnic group.

systems.name: Ancestry & regional heritage
systems.statusNote: This is a broad self-identified grouping of geographic ancestry, not a precise genetic or scientific taxonomy; human populations vary continuously and these regions have fuzzy, overlapping boundaries.
systems.blurb: A coarse classification of the world region or regions a person's ancestors came from, framed independently of any single country's census categories. It sorts people by broad continental and sub-continental origin rather than by nationality, language, or ethnicity.
systems.source: Composite of common geographic-ancestry groupings used in demography and population studies; modern usage, mid-20th century onward

systems.name: Connection to your heritage
systems.statusNote: A self-description of how connected you feel to your cultural and ancestral heritage — about felt closeness, not which heritage. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: How close you feel to your cultural and ancestral roots.

options.label: Reconnecting
options.desc: Rediscovering roots you'd drifted from.

systems.name: Ethnic identity status (MEIM)
systems.statusNote: Phinney's Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure (1992; revised with Ong, 2007) is the most widely used research measure of ethnic identity, designed to work across all ethnic groups. It assesses two dimensions — exploration and commitment — which, following Marcia's identity-status model, combine into four statuses. The statuses are developmental, not fixed: people commonly move between them across a lifetime.
systems.blurb: How far you have explored — and settled — what your ethnic and cultural heritage means to you.

options.label: Diffuse
options.desc: Your heritage isn't something you've much explored, and it doesn't carry strong meaning for you right now.

options.label: Foreclosed
options.desc: You hold the sense of heritage you grew up with — taken on from family and community more than from your own searching.

options.label: In search
options.desc: You're actively exploring your background — its history, customs and meaning — but haven't settled what it means to you yet.

options.label: Achieved
options.desc: You've explored your heritage and come to a clear, secure sense of what it means in your life.

systems.name: Nationality / citizenship
systems.statusNote: Nationality is a legal and administrative status, not a scientific taxonomy; it reflects state membership and is recorded by governments rather than empirically derived.
systems.blurb: A classification of people by the sovereign state of which they are a national or citizen. The modern framework of nation-states crystallised in Europe after the Peace of Westphalia (1648) and spread worldwide through the 19th and 20th centuries; it sorts people by the country whose legal membership they hold.
systems.source: Sovereign-state framework, codified by the United Nations (founded 1945); list reflects UN member and observer states.

systems.name: Acculturation strategy (Berry)
systems.statusNote: John Berry's acculturation model (1997) is a validated framework in cross-cultural psychology. For people living between two cultures, it identifies four strategies from two questions: do you maintain your heritage culture, and do you take part in the wider society?
systems.blurb: John Berry's acculturation model describes the strategies people use when they live between two cultures. From two questions — do you maintain your heritage culture, and do you take part in the wider society? — it maps four strategies: integration (keep both), assimilation (take up the new), separation (hold to heritage), and marginalisation (at home in neither). Developed in cross-cultural psychology from the 1980s and most cited in Berry's 1997 synthesis, it sorts people by stance rather than ranking cultures or scoring how 'adapted' anyone is.

options.label: Integration
options.desc: Keep my heritage and take full part in the wider society.

options.label: Assimilation
options.desc: Embrace the wider society and let my heritage fade.

options.label: Separation
options.desc: Hold to my heritage and keep apart from the wider society.

options.label: On the margins
options.desc: Feel fully at home in neither culture.

systems.name: Bicultural Identity Integration (BII)
systems.statusNote: Bicultural Identity Integration (BII) is a validated individual-difference construct in acculturation and cultural-identity research, introduced by Benet-Martínez & Haritatos (2005) and measured by the BIIS-2 (Huynh, Benet-Martínez & Nguyen, 2018). It captures how a person living between two cultures experiences the relationship between them on two independent dimensions.
systems.blurb: Bicultural Identity Integration describes how a person who belongs to two cultures — through migration, mixed heritage, or growing up between worlds — experiences the fit between them. Research by Verónica Benet-Martínez and colleagues shows this is not one scale but two independent ones: cultural harmony (do your two cultures feel compatible, or in tension?) and cultural blendedness (do they feel fused into one self, or kept separate and switched between?). The two vary on their own — you can feel high harmony yet keep the cultures distinct, or blend them fully yet still feel conflict.
systems.source: Bicultural Identity Integration (BII) — Benet-Martínez & Haritatos (2005); BIIS-2 (Huynh, Benet-Martínez & Nguyen, 2018)

dimensions.name: Cultural harmony
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means your two cultures feel compatible and at ease together; leaning low means you sense a clash or tension between them, as if pulled in two directions.

dimensions.name: Cultural blendedness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means your two cultures feel fused into a single, blended sense of self; leaning low means you keep them separate and shift between them depending on the setting.

systems.name: Image of God (Four Gods)
systems.statusNote: Based on the Baylor Religion Survey (thousands of respondents) and set out in Froese and Bader's 2010 book America's Four Gods. The two dimensions — engagement and judgement — are measured from survey items, which is why this is marked empirical. If you don't picture a God or higher power, this one may simply not apply.
systems.blurb: Froese and Bader's 'Four Gods' typology, from the Baylor Religion Survey, describes how people who picture a God tend to see it. Two measurable dimensions — how engaged God is in the world, and how judging — cross to give four images: authoritative (engaged and judging), benevolent (engaged and loving), critical (distant but judging) and distant (a cosmic force that set things in motion and stepped back). It maps a believer's image of the divine rather than ranking faiths or saying which God is real.

systems.name: How you read religious ideas (Post-Critical Belief)
systems.statusNote: David Wulff (1991) crossed two dimensions of religious attitude — inclusion versus exclusion of transcendence, and a literal versus symbolic reading of religious content — to map four quadrants. Dirk Hutsebaut and colleagues built this into the Post-Critical Belief Scale and validated it on large samples; the shortened 18-item form (Duriez, Soenens & Hutsebaut, 2005) is widely used in the psychology of religion, which is why this is marked empirical. The four stances describe an interpretive style even-handedly — there is no 'right' answer, and they cover both believers and non-believers.
systems.blurb: A way of describing how a person handles religious ideas, set on two measured axes: whether they read scripture and doctrine literally or symbolically, and whether they affirm or set aside a transcendent reality. Crossing the two yields four even-handed stances — literal belief, symbolic faith, literal rejection, and a symbolic reading that keeps the meaning but not the supernatural. It captures an interpretive style, not which religion is right or whether God exists.

options.label: Literal belief
options.desc: You take your tradition's teachings literally and hold them to be true.

options.label: Symbolic faith
options.desc: You read scripture and ritual as symbol and metaphor, while still affirming a transcendent reality behind them — a 'second naivete'.

options.label: Literal rejection
options.desc: You read religious claims literally too — and conclude they are not true.

options.label: Symbolic, no supernatural
options.desc: You value religious stories as human-made symbol and myth, without a literal or transcendent reality behind them.

systems.name: Triguna — your mode of nature
systems.statusNote: The three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) come from Samkhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17-18). Modern psychologists have operationalised the model into validated self-report instruments — the Vedic Personality Inventory (Wolf, 1998; reported Cronbach's alpha approx .85-.92) and the Mysore Triguna Scale (Shilpa & Venkatesha Murthy, 2012). This is a reflective self-ID of which mode tends to lead in you, not a clinical or fixed measure: classically all three are present in everyone and shift over time.
systems.blurb: The three gunas — the 'modes of nature' at the heart of Samkhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita. Indian thought holds that everything in nature, including each person's temperament, is woven from three strands: sattva (clarity, calm and harmony), rajas (drive, passion and restless motion) and tamas (stability, rest and inertia). All three live in everyone, but one tends to lead — colouring how you think, act, eat and feel. Modern psychology has turned this ancient map into validated questionnaires such as the Vedic Personality Inventory and the Mysore Triguna Scale; this asks which mode is strongest in you.
systems.source: The three gunas of Samkhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita; operationalised as the Vedic Personality Inventory (Wolf, 1998) and the Mysore Triguna Scale (Shilpa & Venkatesha Murthy, 2012)

options.label: Sattva (clarity & harmony)
options.desc: Calm, clear and balanced. When sattva leads you tend to think before you act and seek truth, kindness and harmony — feeling light, lucid and content, drawn to knowledge and peace of mind.

options.label: Rajas (drive & passion)
options.desc: Active, driven and restless. When rajas leads you are full of energy, ambition and desire — quick to act and to feel, chasing goals and excitement and happiest in motion, though sometimes pulled along by craving and unrest.

options.label: Tamas (stillness & stability)
options.desc: Steady, grounded and slow to change. When tamas leads you value rest, routine and stability and hold firm under pressure — the mode of sleep, endurance and inertia, which can settle into deep calm or into resistance to change.

systems.name: Where you place religious authority
systems.statusNote: In the Abrahamic faiths the question of where final authority rests — in the sacred text, in tradition and its teachers, in reason, in personal experience, in conscience, or in the community — lies behind most reforms and divisions, from the Reformation's appeal to 'scripture alone' to the place of the Oral Torah in Judaism and the sources of law (usul al-fiqh) in Islam. The four classic Christian sources — scripture, tradition, reason and experience — were named the 'Wesleyan Quadrilateral' by Albert Outler (1964); the Islamic sources are set out by Kamali (2003). This is an even-handed self-description of where you lean, not a measured trait, and no answer is treated as the correct one. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: Across Christianity, Islam and Judaism, where does the last word lie when belief or practice is in question — in the sacred text itself, in tradition and its teachers, in reason, in personal experience, in conscience, or in the gathered community? This long-running question sits behind most of the reforms and splits in Abrahamic history, and it cuts across denominations: two people in the same church, mosque or synagogue can place authority quite differently. This asks where you lean, with each source described even-handedly and none held up as the right one.
systems.source: Sources of religious authority: the 'Wesleyan Quadrilateral' (Outler, 1964) and the sources of Islamic law, usul al-fiqh (Kamali, 2003)

systems.name: Your dominant language
systems.statusNote: Language dominance is measured by validated self-report instruments — the Bilingual Language Profile (Birdsong, Gertken & Amengual, 2012) and the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q; Marian, Blumenfeld & Kaushanskaya, 2007) — which combine language history, use, proficiency, and attitudes into a single dominance profile. The categories here are an accessible reading of that continuous profile, not a clinical assessment.
systems.blurb: Language dominance is which of your languages is strongest — the one that comes fastest, feels most automatic, and that you tend to think, count, and dream in. It isn't fixed: a first language can stay dominant for life, two languages can sit in balance, or a language learned later can quietly overtake the one you grew up with. Linguists gauge it with self-report instruments such as the Bilingual Language Profile (Birdsong, Gertken & Amengual, 2012) and the LEAP-Q (Marian, Blumenfeld & Kaushanskaya, 2007), which weigh how, when, and how much you use each language rather than treating 'native speaker' as all-or-nothing. This is your dominant-language profile — from living in a single language, through balanced bilingualism, to a heritage tongue you understand more than you can speak.

options.label: One language
options.desc: You live almost entirely in a single language — it's the only one you use day to day, so it is your dominant language by default.

options.label: Mother-tongue dominant
options.desc: You use more than one language, but the first you learned is clearly strongest — where you're most fluent and feel most yourself.

options.label: Balanced bilingual
options.desc: Two or more languages are roughly equal — which one leads depends on the topic, person, or setting rather than one always winning.

options.label: Second-language dominant
options.desc: A language you picked up later has overtaken your first — through immersion, schooling, or where you live — and is now the one you reach for most.

options.label: Heritage / receptive
options.desc: You grew up hearing a family or heritage language and understand it, but you're more fluent in your community's main language — often grasping more than you can comfortably say.

systems.name: Humour styles (HSQ)
systems.statusNote: The Humor Styles Questionnaire (Martin, Puhlik-Doris, Larsen, Gray & Weir, 2003) is a validated, widely used measure of how people use humour in everyday life. It distinguishes four independent styles along two axes — whether the humour is benign or potentially harmful, and whether it is aimed at the self or at others: affiliative and self-enhancing (the benign styles) and aggressive and self-defeating (the potentially harmful ones). You are scored on all four at once rather than sorted into one type, and researchers tend to link the benign styles to greater wellbeing. This is a descriptive self-report of habits, not a diagnosis or a verdict on your character.
systems.blurb: The four ways you use humour — to connect, to cope, to tease, or at your own expense — from the research-validated Humor Styles Questionnaire.
systems.source: Humor Styles Questionnaire (HSQ; Martin, Puhlik-Doris, Larsen, Gray & Weir, 2003)

citations.title: Individual differences in uses of humor and their relation to psychological well-being: Development of the Humor Styles Questionnaire
citations.authors: Martin, R. A., Puhlik-Doris, P., Larsen, G., Gray, J., & Weir, K.

citations.title: "A joke a day keeps the doctor away?" Meta-analytical evidence of differential associations of habitual humor styles with mental health
citations.authors: Schneider, M., Voracek, M., & Tran, U. S.

dimensions.name: Affiliative humour
dimensions.low: I rarely use humour to connect
dimensions.high: I often joke to bring people together
dimensions.desc: Affiliative humour is the easy, good-natured wit you use to amuse others, ease tension and strengthen bonds — bantering, telling jokes, laughing along. Leaning high means humour is one of your main ways of connecting with people; leaning low means you bond in other ways. This is the benign, other-directed style, and researchers tie it to social ease and wellbeing.

dimensions.name: Self-enhancing humour
dimensions.low: I rarely find the funny side under stress
dimensions.high: I use humour to keep perspective
dimensions.desc: Self-enhancing humour is the knack for keeping a humorous outlook on life and using it to cope — finding the funny side of your own troubles and staying amused when things go wrong. Leaning high means humour helps you regulate stress and keep perspective; leaning low means you lean on other coping tools. This is the benign, self-directed style, which researchers associate with resilience.

dimensions.name: Aggressive humour
dimensions.low: My jokes are rarely at others' expense
dimensions.high: I often tease, mock or use sarcasm
dimensions.desc: Aggressive humour is wit used to criticise, tease or put others down — sarcasm, ridicule, mockery and jokes at someone's expense. Leaning high means a sharper, more pointed edge to your humour; leaning low means you steer clear of laughs that land on other people. Researchers note this style can strain relationships — describing a habit, not judging the person.

dimensions.name: Self-defeating humour
dimensions.low: I rarely put myself down for laughs
dimensions.high: I often make myself the butt of the joke
dimensions.desc: Self-defeating humour is amusing others by excessively disparaging yourself — going along with being the butt of the joke and using self-mockery to win approval or deflect. Leaning high means a habit of getting laughs at your own expense; leaning low means your humour rarely runs yourself down. Researchers link heavy use to lower wellbeing — a descriptive pattern, not a verdict.

systems.name: Individualist or collectivist
systems.statusNote: Individualism–collectivism is a validated cross-cultural dimension (Hofstede, 1980), measurable at the individual level (Triandis & Gelfand, 1998). It describes how much you prioritise personal goals versus group belonging — neither end is better.
systems.blurb: A core dimension of cross-cultural psychology: whether you define yourself mainly as an independent individual — prizing personal freedom, choice and self-reliance — or through your groups, prizing belonging, loyalty and harmony. Most people sit somewhere along the scale rather than at either extreme.

options.label: Strongly individualist
options.desc: You prize personal freedom, self-reliance, and your own goals.

options.label: Individualist-leaning
options.desc: You lean toward independence but value belonging too.

options.label: Balanced
options.desc: You weigh personal and group needs about equally.

options.label: Collectivist-leaning
options.desc: You lean toward the group but keep your own space too.

options.label: Strongly collectivist
options.desc: You prize loyalty, harmony, and the good of the group.

citations.title: Culture's Consequences: International Differences in Work-Related Values
citations.authors: Hofstede, G.

citations.title: Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation
citations.authors: Markus, H. R., & Kitayama, S.

citations.authors: Triandis, H. C., & Gelfand, M. J.

citations.title: Rethinking individualism and collectivism: Evaluation of theoretical assumptions and meta-analyses
citations.authors: Oyserman, D., Coon, H. M., & Kemmelmeier, M.

systems.name: Tradition or progress
systems.statusNote: A self-identification of how you relate to tradition versus change — a cultural-temporal outlook, framed even-handedly and separate from party politics.
systems.blurb: How you weigh keeping heritage against embracing change.

options.label: Traditionalist
options.desc: You value heritage, custom, and continuity.

options.label: Balanced
options.desc: Respect the past, but stay open to change.

options.label: Pragmatic
options.desc: Whatever works best, old or new.

options.label: Progressive
options.desc: You favour reform and moving things forward.

options.label: Radical
options.desc: You'd rebuild things from the ground up.

systems.name: How you see history
systems.statusNote: Long-standing ways of understanding how history unfolds — drawn from the philosophy of history. A self-description of which view fits you; historians genuinely disagree.
systems.blurb: How you think history actually moves and what drives it.

options.label: Progress
options.desc: History broadly advances — things improve over the long run.

options.label: Cyclical
options.desc: History moves in repeating cycles of rise and fall.

options.label: Contingent
options.desc: History turns on chance, accidents and contingency.

options.label: Material forces
options.desc: Driven by economics, technology and material conditions.

options.label: Great figures
options.desc: Shaped mainly by influential individuals and leaders.

options.label: Ideas & culture
options.desc: Driven by ideas, beliefs, religion and culture.

options.label: Decline
options.desc: Things broadly decline from an earlier high point.

systems.name: How you explore history
systems.statusNote: A self-description of how you most love to engage with history and heritage. Pick any that fit — many of us enjoy several.
systems.blurb: The ways you like to explore the past.

options.label: Museums & sites
options.desc: Visiting museums and historic places.

options.label: Documentaries
options.desc: History on screen and in audio.

options.label: History books
options.desc: Reading and deep dives into the past.

options.label: Family history
options.desc: Tracing genealogy and ancestry.

options.label: Heritage travel
options.desc: Travelling to historic places and roots.

options.label: Living history
options.desc: Reenactment and hands-on history.

systems.name: Honour, Face & Dignity
systems.statusNote: Leung & Cohen (2011, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) describe three 'cultural logics' of self-worth — honour (worth is reputation, earned and defended), face (worth is granted by your place in the community) and dignity (worth is inherent and unconditional) — which individuals endorse to differing degrees. A reflective self-description, not a ranking; no orientation is better than another.
systems.blurb: Three cultural logics of self-worth from cross-cultural psychology: honour (a good name, earned and defended), face (the standing your community grants you) and dignity (worth that is inherent and unconditional).

options.label: Honour
options.desc: Your worth is bound up with your good name and reputation — something to be earned, lived up to, and defended. Loyalty, courage and keeping your word matter deeply, and a slight to your honour is taken seriously.

options.label: Face
options.desc: Your worth flows from your standing in the community and the respect others extend to you. You protect it through humility, fulfilling your role, and keeping harmony rather than asserting yourself.

options.label: Dignity
options.desc: Your worth is inherent and unconditional — no insult or outside opinion can take it away. You answer to your own conscience and see every person as having equal, built-in worth.

options.label: A blend
options.desc: You draw on more than one of these — perhaps the inner certainty of dignity alongside the loyalty of honour, or a sense of face shaped by your community. Many people, especially those raised across cultures, weave all three together.
