systems.name: Disability status
systems.statusNote: This is a self-identification field for inclusion and accessibility purposes, not a clinical diagnosis or medical record, and people may identify with more than one category or none.
systems.blurb: A self-identification framework that lets members describe whether and how they experience disability, drawing on contemporary disability-rights and accessibility conventions. It groups people by broad, self-reported categories of physical, sensory, cognitive, mental-health, and chronic conditions rather than by medical diagnosis.
systems.source: Modern accessibility and disability-rights self-identification practice (late 20th–21st century), informed by the social model of disability

options.label: No disability
options.desc: The member does not currently identify as having a disability.

options.label: Mobility or physical disability
options.desc: The member identifies with a condition affecting movement, dexterity, or physical functioning, which may involve mobility aids or physical accommodations.

options.label: Blind or low vision
options.desc: The member is blind or has low vision and may use screen readers, magnification, braille, or other visual accommodations.

options.label: Deaf or hard of hearing
options.desc: The member is Deaf or hard of hearing and may use sign language, captions, or other communication accommodations.

options.label: Cognitive or learning disability
options.desc: The member identifies with a condition that affects learning, memory, attention, or information processing, such as dyslexia or a related difference.

options.label: Mental health condition
options.desc: The member identifies with a mental health condition, such as an anxiety, mood, or other psychological condition that affects daily life.

options.label: Chronic illness or chronic pain
options.desc: The member lives with a long-term illness or persistent pain that may affect energy, stamina, or daily functioning.

options.label: Speech or communication disability
options.desc: The member identifies with a condition affecting speech or communication and may use augmentative or alternative communication methods.

options.label: Neurological condition
options.desc: The member identifies with a neurological condition, such as epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, or a related condition affecting the nervous system.

options.label: Multiple disabilities
options.desc: The member identifies with two or more disabilities that together shape their experience and accessibility needs.

options.label: Prefer to self-describe
options.desc: The member prefers to describe their disability status in their own terms rather than selecting a listed category.

systems.name: Accessibility that matters to you
systems.statusNote: A neutral, opt-in self-identification of the accessibility features that help you take part fully — shared only if you choose, in a supportive space. Useful for everyone, not only disabled people.
systems.blurb: The accessibility features that make spaces, content, and tools work well for you.

options.label: Step-free access
options.desc: Ramps, lifts, and wheelchair-friendly spaces.

options.label: Captions & subtitles
options.desc: Captioned video and transcribed audio.

options.label: Screen-reader friendly
options.desc: Content that works well with screen readers.

options.label: Clear, plain language
options.desc: Simple, well-structured wording.

options.label: Low-sensory spaces
options.desc: Calm spaces with less noise and softer light.

options.label: Flexible timing
options.desc: Self-paced, with extra time when needed.

options.label: Sign language
options.desc: Sign-language interpretation or content.

options.label: High contrast & large text
options.desc: Readable colours and adjustable text size.

systems.name: Visible or invisible
systems.statusNote: A neutral, opt-in self-identification of whether a disability or condition is apparent to others — invisible disabilities are widely recognised. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: Whether a disability or condition you live with is visible to others.

options.label: Visible
options.desc: Apparent to others.

options.label: Invisible / hidden
options.desc: Not apparent to others.

options.label: A mix
options.desc: Some aspects visible, some not.

options.label: Fluctuating
options.desc: Varies from day to day.

systems.name: How you understand disability
systems.statusNote: There are several recognised ways of understanding disability — most notably the social and medical models. A respectful self-description of the lens that fits you. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: The lens through which you understand disability.

options.label: Social model
options.desc: Disability comes mainly from barriers in society, not the person.

options.label: Medical model
options.desc: A condition to understand, treat or manage.

options.label: A bit of both
options.desc: Both the body and society's barriers matter.

options.label: Identity & diversity
options.desc: A valued part of who you are and human diversity.

options.label: Practical differences
options.desc: Just practical differences to work around day to day.

systems.name: Language you prefer for disability
systems.statusNote: A self-description of the wording you prefer. Person-first and identity-first are both widely used and valid; preference is personal and varies by community.
systems.blurb: How you prefer disability to be talked about.

options.label: Identity-first
options.desc: I say 'disabled person'.

options.label: Person-first
options.desc: I say 'person with a disability'.

options.label: Either feels fine
options.desc: I'm comfortable with both.

options.label: Depends on context
options.desc: It varies by setting and audience.

options.label: By the specific condition
options.desc: I name the condition itself.

options.label: My own words
options.desc: I describe it in my own way.

systems.name: Functional domains (Washington Group)
systems.statusNote: The Washington Group Short Set on Functioning (WG-SS), developed and field-tested by the UN-affiliated Washington Group on Disability Statistics and adopted for national censuses and surveys worldwide (Madans, Loeb & Altman, 2011); grounded in the WHO International Classification of Functioning (ICF).
systems.blurb: The international standard for measuring functioning. The Washington Group Short Set asks about difficulty in six everyday domains — seeing, hearing, walking, remembering or concentrating, self-care, and communicating. Rather than labelling a diagnosis, it maps where, if anywhere, everyday activities are harder — the culturally neutral, functional approach the UN Washington Group designed for censuses and surveys worldwide, and the basis for making services accessible. Share only the domains you choose.
systems.source: Washington Group on Disability Statistics — Short Set on Functioning (WG-SS)

options.label: Seeing
options.desc: Difficulty seeing, even when wearing glasses.

options.label: Hearing
options.desc: Difficulty hearing, even when using a hearing aid.

options.label: Walking & mobility
options.desc: Difficulty walking or climbing steps.

options.label: Remembering & concentrating
options.desc: Difficulty remembering or concentrating.

options.label: Self-care
options.desc: Difficulty with self-care, such as washing all over or dressing.

options.label: Communicating
options.desc: Difficulty communicating in your usual language — understanding others, or being understood.

citations.title: Measuring disability and monitoring the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: the work of the Washington Group on Disability Statistics
citations.authors: Madans, J. H., Loeb, M. E., & Altman, B. M.

systems.name: Neurodivergence
systems.statusNote: Neurodiversity is a real and widely accepted descriptive framework for natural brain variation, but these are self-identifications honestly labelled, not clinical diagnoses.
systems.blurb: Neurodivergence describes naturally occurring variation in how a brain processes, learns, and experiences the world. The term grew from the neurodiversity movement of the late 1990s, and here it sorts members by how they self-identify rather than by any formal assessment.
systems.source: Neurodiversity movement, coined by sociologist Judy Singer, late 1990s

options.label: Neurotypical
options.desc: A person whose neurological development and cognition fall within the range commonly regarded as typical.

options.label: ADHD
options.desc: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, a variation marked by differences in attention regulation, impulse control, and activity level.

options.label: Autistic (Autism spectrum)
options.desc: Being on the autism spectrum, a lifelong variation in social communication, sensory experience, and patterns of interest.

options.label: Dyslexia
options.desc: A learning difference affecting the accurate and fluent reading, spelling, and decoding of written words.

options.label: Dyscalculia
options.desc: A learning difference affecting the understanding of numbers, quantities, and arithmetic.

options.label: Dyspraxia (DCD)
options.desc: Developmental coordination disorder, a variation affecting motor planning, coordination, and fine or gross movement.

options.label: Tourette syndrome / tic disorder
options.desc: A neurological condition characterised by involuntary, repeated movements or vocalisations known as tics.

options.label: OCD
options.desc: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, involving recurring intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviours done to ease the resulting distress.

options.label: Highly Sensitive Person
options.desc: A self-identified trait of heightened sensory processing sensitivity, with deeper response to stimuli and emotion.

options.label: Twice-exceptional / Gifted
options.desc: Being intellectually gifted, where twice-exceptional means giftedness alongside a co-occurring learning or neurodevelopmental difference.

systems.name: Generational cohort
systems.statusNote: Generational labels are widely used demographic and marketing shorthand; the specific birth-year cutoffs are approximate, vary by source, and are largely Western-centric rather than the product of a single validated framework.
systems.blurb: A way of grouping people into named cohorts by birth-year range, on the premise that those who come of age in a shared historical and technological era hold some common formative experiences. The modern framing was popularised by writers and researchers through the 20th century and refined by polling organisations such as Pew Research Center.
systems.source: Popularised through 20th-century social commentary; ranges commonly follow Pew Research Center definitions.

options.label: The Silent Generation
options.desc: Born 1928-1945, a cohort shaped by the Great Depression and the Second World War, often associated with caution and conformity.

options.label: Baby Boomers
options.desc: Born 1946-1964, named for the post-war surge in births and associated with the cultural and economic shifts of the 1960s and 1970s.

options.label: Generation X
options.desc: Born 1965-1980, raised during the rise of personal computing and cable television and often characterised as independent and self-reliant.

options.label: Millennials / Gen Y
options.desc: Born 1981-1996, the first cohort to come of age around the turn of the millennium and the early spread of the internet and mobile phones.

options.label: Generation Z
options.desc: Born 1997-2012, the first generation to grow up with smartphones and social media as an everyday part of childhood.

options.label: Generation Alpha
options.desc: Born 2013-2025, growing up amid widespread tablets, voice assistants, and online learning from their earliest years.

systems.name: Decade you identify with
systems.statusNote: A light, for-fun self-identification of the cultural era whose music, style, and mood feels most like you — which may differ from when you were born.
systems.blurb: The decade whose culture, music, and style feels most like home to you.

options.label: 1950s & earlier
options.desc: Classic, vintage, mid-century charm.

options.label: The 1960s
options.desc: Counterculture, soul, and optimism.

options.label: The 1970s
options.desc: Disco, rock, and bold style.

options.label: The 1980s
options.desc: Synths, neon, and big energy.

options.label: The 1990s
options.desc: Grunge, hip-hop, and the early internet.

options.label: The 2000s
options.desc: Pop, flip phones, and Y2K.

options.label: The 2010s
options.desc: Streaming, social media, and indie.

options.label: The 2020s
options.desc: The present moment.

systems.name: Event that shaped your generation
systems.statusNote: A reflective self-identification of the major world event that most shaped your outlook growing up — varies by age and place.
systems.blurb: The big world event that most shaped your generation's outlook.

options.label: The Cold War
options.desc: Growing up under its shadow.

options.label: Fall of the Berlin Wall
options.desc: The end of the Cold War era.

options.label: 9/11 & its aftermath
options.desc: The post-2001 world.

options.label: The 2008 financial crisis
options.desc: Recession and its long tail.

options.label: The rise of social media
options.desc: Coming of age online.

options.label: The COVID-19 pandemic
options.desc: Lockdowns and a changed world.

options.label: The AI era
options.desc: Growing up as AI arrives.

systems.name: The age you feel
systems.statusNote: A light self-description of how old you feel inside, regardless of your actual age. Just for fun and self-reflection. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: How old you feel inside, whatever your birth year says.

options.label: Old soul
options.desc: Wiser and more reflective than your years.

options.label: A little older
options.desc: You feel a touch older than your age.

options.label: Right on time
options.desc: You feel about your actual age.

options.label: Young at heart
options.desc: Playful and youthful, whatever the number.

options.label: Ageless
options.desc: Age doesn't really define how you feel.

options.label: It shifts
options.desc: Your felt age changes with the day and mood.

systems.name: Your sense of time
systems.statusNote: A self-description of where your mind naturally dwells in time. Loosely inspired by research on time perspective — most of us blend these.
systems.blurb: How you relate to the past, present and future.

options.label: Nostalgic
options.desc: Drawn to the past and fond memories.

options.label: Present-focused
options.desc: Grounded in the here and now.

options.label: Seize the day
options.desc: Live for the moment as it comes.

options.label: Future-focused
options.desc: Always planning and looking ahead.

options.label: Legacy-minded
options.desc: Thinking in the long term.

options.label: Balanced
options.desc: Spread evenly across past, present and future.

systems.name: Time perspective (Zimbardo, ZTPI)
systems.statusNote: The Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory (Zimbardo & Boyd, 1999) is a validated 56-item measure whose five factors were established by exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis with good reliability; it is among the most widely used individual-differences measures of time orientation. Each factor is a continuous dimension, not a fixed category.
systems.blurb: The Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory (ZTPI) measures the habitual, often unconscious way you sort the flow of experience into past, present and future — a bias Zimbardo argued steers everyday decisions as powerfully as a personality trait. Instead of one type, it places you on five independent dimensions: a negative and a positive relationship with the past, a hedonistic and a fatalistic stance toward the present, and a future, planning orientation. Zimbardo and Boyd held that the healthiest profile is not maxing any single one but a 'balanced time perspective' — high past-positive, fairly high future, moderate present-hedonism, and low past-negative and present-fatalism.

dimensions.name: Past-negative
dimensions.desc: How much a bleak, regretful view of the past colours your outlook. Leaning high means dwelling on hurt, failure and bad memories; leaning low means recalling the past without lingering bitterness. Of the five, this factor is the one most consistently linked to lower well-being.

dimensions.name: Past-positive
dimensions.desc: How fondly and sentimentally you hold the past. Leaning high means treasuring happy memories, family and tradition; leaning low means feeling little nostalgic pull toward what has gone.

dimensions.name: Present-hedonistic
dimensions.desc: How much you seek pleasure, novelty and excitement in the present. Leaning high means spontaneity, sensation and enjoying now with little thought of consequences; leaning low means a more measured, deferred approach to enjoyment.

dimensions.name: Present-fatalistic
dimensions.desc: How much you feel the present is governed by fate rather than your own choices. Leaning high means believing that effort changes little and that what will be will be; leaning low means feeling that your decisions shape what happens.

dimensions.name: Future
dimensions.desc: How much you orient toward goals, planning and future rewards. Leaning high means working now for later payoff and weighing consequences; leaning low means giving tomorrow little weight in today's choices.

citations.title: Putting time in perspective: A valid, reliable individual-differences metric
citations.authors: Zimbardo, P. G., & Boyd, J. N.
citations.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1271–1288

citations.title: The Time Paradox: The New Psychology of Time That Will Change Your Life
citations.authors: Zimbardo, P. G., & Boyd, J. N.

systems.name: Political orientation
systems.statusNote: Political orientation is a self-reported social and demographic category, not an empirically validated psychometric instrument; labels carry different meanings across countries and eras.
systems.blurb: A self-identified label describing a person's broad political and economic values and their preferred role for the state, markets, and social change. The categories below draw on modern political-science taxonomies of ideology that took shape across the 19th and 20th centuries, and sort people by where they place themselves on overlapping economic and social dimensions.
systems.source: Modern comparative political science and the left-right spectrum, originating in the French Revolution era (late 18th century) and refined through the 19th-20th centuries

options.label: Progressive
options.desc: Favours active reform to expand social and economic equality and to advance civil rights, often through government action and structural change.

options.label: Liberal
options.desc: Emphasises individual rights, civil liberties, and a regulated market economy, typically supporting a moderate welfare state and incremental reform.

options.label: Social democrat
options.desc: Seeks to combine a market economy with strong public services, labour protections, and redistribution achieved through democratic, reformist means.

options.label: Democratic socialist
options.desc: Advocates social ownership or strong public control of major sectors of the economy, pursued through democratic and electoral processes.

options.label: Socialist
options.desc: Holds that the means of production should be socially or collectively owned to reduce class inequality and curb private capital.

options.label: Communist
options.desc: Aims for a classless, stateless society with common ownership of the means of production, in the tradition of Marx and later theorists.

options.label: Centrist
options.desc: Positions itself between the political left and right, favouring moderation, pragmatism, and compromise over strongly ideological programmes.

options.label: Conservative
options.desc: Values tradition, social stability, and gradual change, often favouring established institutions and a limited pace of reform.

options.label: Classical liberal
options.desc: Emphasises individual liberty, free markets, private property, and limited government in the tradition of early liberal thinkers such as Locke and Smith.

options.label: Libertarian
options.desc: Prioritises maximising individual freedom and minimising state power in both economic and personal matters.

options.label: Green / Ecologist
options.desc: Places environmental sustainability and ecological limits at the centre of politics, often alongside social justice and participatory democracy.

options.label: Nationalist
options.desc: Centres the interests, identity, and sovereignty of a particular nation, often emphasising shared culture, borders, and self-determination.

options.label: Anarchist
options.desc: Rejects compulsory state authority and hierarchy in favour of voluntary, self-organised, and cooperative social arrangements.

options.label: Populist
options.desc: Frames politics as a contest between ordinary people and a self-serving elite, claiming to represent the will of the common people; it appears on both the left and the right.

options.label: Apolitical
options.desc: Does not identify with a particular political ideology and generally takes little interest in partisan or political affairs.

systems.name: Political compass
systems.statusNote: A popular self-placement model for political views, not a scientifically validated measure of personality or ideology.
systems.blurb: The political compass is a two-axis model that maps political views on an economic dimension (left to right) and a social dimension (libertarian to authoritarian). Two-axis variants were developed through the 20th century and the term was popularised by the Political Compass website in the early 2000s. It sorts people by their economic and social-authority preferences rather than placing them on a single left-right line.
systems.source: Two-axis political models, 20th century; term popularised by the Political Compass website, c. 2001

dimensions.name: Economic axis
dimensions.desc: Low favours collective ownership and economic equality organised through the state, while high favours free markets and private property.

dimensions.name: Social axis
dimensions.desc: Low favours maximal personal and civil freedom, while high favours strong state authority and social order.

systems.name: Left or right
systems.blurb: Where you place yourself on the classic left–right spectrum. Each position is described plainly and even-handedly — this is your label to claim, not ours to judge.
systems.statusNote: A self-placement on the left–right spectrum. Described neutrally; no position is presented as better or worse.

options.label: Far-left
options.desc: Favours sweeping economic equality and major structural change.

options.label: Left
options.desc: Favours stronger public services, redistribution, and social reform.

options.label: Centre-left
options.desc: Leans progressive but works within existing institutions.

options.label: Centre
options.desc: Mixes ideas from both sides and prefers moderate, pragmatic policy.

options.label: Centre-right
options.desc: Leans toward free markets and tradition within existing institutions.

options.label: Right
options.desc: Favours free markets, limited government, and established values.

options.label: Far-right
options.desc: Favours strong national identity and a sharp break from the current order.

options.label: Apolitical / unsure
options.desc: Doesn't place themselves on the spectrum, or prefers not to.

systems.name: Preferred form of government
systems.blurb: How you think a society is best governed. Each form is described plainly and even-handedly — your view to claim, not ours to judge.
systems.statusNote: A self-identification with a form of government, described neutrally; no form is presented as correct.

options.label: Representative democracy
options.desc: Citizens elect representatives to govern on their behalf.

options.label: Direct democracy
options.desc: Citizens vote directly on laws and major decisions.

options.label: Constitutional monarchy
options.desc: An elected government alongside a ceremonial or limited monarch.

options.label: Federal / decentralised
options.desc: Power shared between national and strong regional or local governments.

options.label: Technocracy
options.desc: Decisions led by experts and specialists in each field.

options.label: Anarchism
options.desc: A society organised without a coercive state.

options.label: One-party / strong state

systems.name: Political efficacy
systems.statusNote: Political efficacy is one of the most-studied attitudes in political science, introduced in Campbell, Gurin and Miller's The Voter Decides (1954) and later separated into two validated dimensions — internal efficacy (belief in your own political competence) and external efficacy (belief that the system is responsive) — by Craig, Niemi and Silver (1990) and Niemi, Craig and Mattei (1991). Their survey items are carried in national election studies worldwide. You can lean high or low on each dimension independently.
systems.blurb: A long-established measure from political science of how a person relates to politics, across two independent dimensions. Internal efficacy is your confidence that you can understand political matters and take part effectively; external efficacy is your sense that government and the political system actually respond to people like you. The two vary independently — you can feel capable yet unheard, or heard yet unsure — and both ends are described even-handedly, with neither better nor worse.

dimensions.name: Internal efficacy
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel confident that you can understand political issues and take part effectively — that you have what it takes to follow politics and make your voice count; leaning low means political matters often feel too complicated or remote for you to engage with confidently.

dimensions.name: External efficacy
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you believe that government and officials are responsive to people like you, and that ordinary views genuinely shape what those in power do; leaning low means you feel that decision-makers pay little heed to people like you, however much they take part.

systems.name: Investment model of commitment (Rusbult)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. The Investment Model was introduced by Caryl Rusbult in 1980 and operationalised in the widely used Investment Model Scale of Rusbult, Martz and Agnew (1998), which measures four facets — satisfaction level, quality of alternatives, investment size and commitment level — with good reliability. It is one of the most validated accounts of relationship commitment in social psychology, replicated across friendships and partnerships and many cultures. The dimensions describe the footing a relationship rests on, not its worth; a higher or lower score on any one is one pattern among many.
systems.blurb: Caryl Rusbult's validated account of what actually holds a relationship together — and why people stay. The Investment Model proposes that commitment grows from three measurable forces: satisfaction (how rewarding the relationship feels), quality of alternatives (how appealing your options outside it seem), and investment size (how much you have put in that leaving would cost — shared years, memories, mutual friends, plans). High satisfaction, poor alternatives and heavy investment together produce a strong intention to stay. The Investment Model Scale of Rusbult, Martz and Agnew (1998) measures all four facets, and the model has held up across hundreds of studies of friendships and partnerships alike. You can sit high on one force and low on another, so this maps the footing your commitment rests on rather than a single verdict.

dimensions.name: Satisfaction
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means the relationship feels rewarding and meets your needs for closeness, support and companionship. Leaning low means it more often leaves you wanting, falling short of what you hope for.

dimensions.name: Quality of alternatives
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means the options outside the relationship look appealing — another partner, life on your own, or leaning on friends and family. Leaning low means you see little elsewhere that would draw you away.

dimensions.name: Investment size
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means a great deal is tied to the relationship that leaving would cost you — shared years, memories, mutual friends, plans and things built together. Leaning low means little would be lost if it ended.

dimensions.name: Commitment
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you intend to stay, feel attached, and picture the relationship lasting. Leaning low means you hold it more lightly, with less sense of a shared long-term future. In the model this is what the other three forces combine to produce.

systems.name: Communal or exchange orientation
systems.statusNote: Communal and exchange relationships were distinguished by Clark and Mills (1979); the Communal Orientation Scale (Clark, Ouellette, Powell & Milberg, 1987) measures the disposition at the individual level. The two are relationship norms rather than better-or-worse types — close ties usually run on communal rules, market and work ties on exchange rules.
systems.blurb: Communal and exchange orientation describes two ways of running a relationship, first drawn out by social psychologists Margaret Clark and Judson Mills. In a communal relationship you give and respond to the other person's needs out of care, without keeping track of who owes what; in an exchange relationship benefits are recorded and expected to be repaid in kind, like a fair trade. This self-identification places you along that continuum in your close relationships — from strongly communal, giving freely, to strongly exchange, valuing clear reciprocity. Most people are communal with loved ones and exchange-minded with colleagues or strangers, so where you sit by default reveals how you give care and weigh fairness.
systems.source: Clark & Mills — communal vs exchange relationships

options.desc: You like relationships to feel fair and reciprocal, and keep a loose sense of give and take.

options.label: Strongly exchange
options.desc: You prefer clear reciprocity — a benefit given is meant to be returned in kind, keeping things even.

systems.name: Friendship functions (McGill Friendship Questionnaire)
systems.statusNote: The McGill Friendship Questionnaire — Friendship Functions (Mendelson & Aboud, 1999) is a validated 30-item measure of how fully a friendship fulfils six functions: stimulating companionship, help, intimacy, reliable alliance, self-validation and emotional security. The three 'doing' functions (companionship, help, reliable alliance) and three 'feeling' functions (intimacy, self-validation, emotional security) build on Robert Weiss's social-provisions theory. Here those functions are a reflective self-report of what you most value in friendship — not a test, and not a ranking of your friends.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of what close friendships actually give us. Drawing on the McGill Friendship Questionnaire, developed by the psychologists Morton Mendelson and Frances Aboud in 1999, it sorts the good a friend brings into six functions — the fun of shared company, practical help and guidance, the closeness of honest sharing, a loyal alliance you can count on, the quiet reassurance that you matter, and a felt sense of security when life turns uncertain. Rather than naming a single type or ranking your friends, it asks what your friendships mean to you. Most of us lean on several of these at once, and the balance shifts with the friend and the season of life. Pick the functions that ring truest for the friendships you treasure.

systems.name: Caregiving style
systems.statusNote: The caregiving behavioural system is a well-researched counterpart to the attachment system, governing how we give care rather than seek it. Kunce and Shaver (1994) and Collins and Feeney (2000) measured individual differences in caregiving along proximity, sensitivity and cooperation; insecure caregiving is commonly described as either over-involved (hyperactivating) or distant (deactivating). These named styles summarise those research dimensions.
systems.blurb: Your caregiving style is how you respond when someone you love is suffering — the giving side of close relationships. Attachment theory pairs the familiar attachment system (seeking comfort) with a caregiving behavioural system (providing it). Research on couples (Kunce & Shaver, 1994; Collins & Feeney, 2000) maps the support people give along proximity, sensitivity and cooperation, finding that a secure, responsive style can give way to over-giving, keeping distance, or taking control. Where your attachment style asks how you reach for care, this asks how you offer it.
systems.source: Caregiving behavioural system in attachment theory (Kunce & Shaver, 1994; Collins & Feeney, 2000)

options.label: Secure / responsive
options.desc: You read what someone actually needs and offer well-timed, sensitive support — a safe haven when they hurt and a secure base when they're ready to cope again. You help without taking over or losing yourself.

options.label: Anxious / overinvolved
options.desc: You give a great deal of care — sometimes more than is asked — and find it hard to step back. Driven partly by your own worry, you can become over-involved in a loved one's problems (a hyperactivating, compulsive pattern).

options.label: Avoidant / distant
options.desc: Other people's distress feels uncomfortable, so you keep some distance. You tend to offer practical fixes over emotional closeness and provide less support when leaned on (a deactivating pattern).

options.label: Controlling / directive
options.desc: Your care is well-meant but directive: you take charge and apply your own solution rather than asking what the other person wants, sometimes overriding their wishes (low on cooperation, high on control).

systems.name: Where you are with changing a habit
systems.statusNote: The Transtheoretical Model's Stages of Change (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983; Prochaska, DiClemente & Norcross, 1992) is a widely studied, validated model of how people change health behaviours such as smoking and drinking, developed from research on how smokers quit on their own.
systems.blurb: The Transtheoretical Model describes personal change not as one decision but as movement through stages — and people usually loop through them more than once before a new pattern sticks. Developed by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente from studies of smokers who quit without treatment, it maps where you are with a habit you might be changing — drinking, smoking, or other substance use — from not yet considering it, through weighing it up and preparing, to acting and maintaining the change. Naming your stage is the starting point of motivational, non-judgemental approaches to change: there is no 'behind', only where you are now.

systems.name: Self-compassion
systems.statusNote: The Self-Compassion Scale (Neff, 2003) is a widely validated measure of how kindly people treat themselves in moments of failure, struggle or suffering. It captures three components, each running between a compassionate and an uncompassionate pole: self-kindness rather than self-criticism, a sense of common humanity rather than isolation, and balanced mindful awareness rather than being swept up by distress. Research treats it as distinct from self-esteem — a steady, non-evaluative way of relating to yourself that does not depend on success or social comparison.
systems.blurb: Self-compassion is how warmly you treat yourself when you struggle, fail or suffer — not how highly you rate yourself. Kristin Neff's model maps it on three independent dimensions, each running between a kind and an unkind pole: meeting your own setbacks with warmth rather than harsh self-criticism, seeing your hardships as part of the shared human experience rather than feeling alone in them, and holding painful feelings in balanced awareness rather than being carried away by them. Unlike self-esteem, it asks not 'how good am I?' but 'how do I relate to myself when things go wrong?' — and it can be cultivated.

dimensions.name: Self-kindness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means meeting your own mistakes and shortcomings with warmth, patience and understanding; leaning low means responding to them with harsh self-criticism and disapproval.

dimensions.name: Common humanity
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means seeing your failures and hard times as part of the human experience that everyone shares; leaning low means feeling alone and cut off in them, as though only you struggle this way.

dimensions.name: Mindful balance
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means holding painful thoughts and feelings in clear, balanced awareness; leaning low means being swept up in them and over-identifying with the distress.

systems.name: Emotion regulation (reappraisal & suppression)
systems.statusNote: The Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (Gross & John, 2003) is the research-standard measure of two everyday strategies for managing feelings — cognitive reappraisal (rethinking a situation to change the emotion it brings) and expressive suppression (holding back the outward show of emotion). The two are independent dimensions, so you can lean high or low on each.
systems.blurb: The Emotion Regulation Questionnaire describes how you manage your feelings through two independent strategies: cognitive reappraisal — reinterpreting a situation to change the emotion it produces — and expressive suppression — keeping the outward signs of emotion in check. The two are separate dimensions rather than opposite ends of one scale, so you can lean high or low on each. Research links habitual reappraisal with more positive emotion and closer relationships, while the effects of suppression vary with the person and cultural setting — so this maps a style, not a verdict.

dimensions.name: Cognitive reappraisal
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you often rethink what a situation means to soften or shift the emotion it brings; leaning low means you tend to take events as you first read them rather than reframing them.

dimensions.name: Expressive suppression
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you keep emotions from showing on the outside even when you feel them strongly; leaning low means your feelings are usually visible and freely expressed.

systems.name: Mindfulness (Five Facets)
systems.statusNote: Mindfulness is a well-studied psychological construct with roots in contemplative traditions, brought into modern clinical and wellbeing research by Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based programmes. Brown and Ryan (2003) introduced the widely used Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, framing dispositional mindfulness as present-moment attention and awareness. Baer, Smith, Hopkins, Krietemeyer and Toney (2006) factor-analysed several existing mindfulness questionnaires and identified five facets — observing, describing, acting with awareness, non-judging of inner experience and non-reactivity to inner experience — now measured by the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ); Baer and colleagues (2008) confirmed this structure in meditating and non-meditating samples. The facets are measured independently and describe tendencies rather than a diagnosis, and mindfulness is generally regarded as a skill that practice can strengthen.
systems.blurb: Mindfulness is the quality of paying attention to the present moment with openness and acceptance, instead of running on autopilot or being swept up in judgement and reaction. Rather than a single on-or-off trait, research treats it as a profile of five distinct, separately measured facets, captured by the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (Baer and colleagues, 2006): observing the stream of sensations, thoughts and feelings; describing inner experience in words; acting with awareness rather than on autopilot; holding your thoughts and feelings without judging them; and staying non-reactive, letting difficult experiences come and go. This maps where you sit on each facet, every one rated on its own continuum, so two people who both feel 'mindful' can have very different shapes — keenly tuned to the senses, say, yet quick to judge their own reactions. The facets describe tendencies, not a verdict, and mindfulness is widely held to be a skill that practice and training can develop.
systems.source: Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (Baer et al., 2006)

dimensions.name: Observing
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you readily notice sensations, sounds, smells and passing thoughts and feelings as they arise; leaning low means such inner and outer details tend to slip by unattended.

dimensions.name: Describing
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you can find words for what you are feeling or thinking and put inner experience into language; leaning low means your experiences are harder to name or articulate.

dimensions.name: Acting with awareness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you stay attentive to what you are doing in the moment; leaning low means you often act automatically with your mind elsewhere, then notice you have been on autopilot.

dimensions.name: Non-judging of inner experience
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you take an accepting, non-evaluative stance toward your own thoughts and feelings; leaning low means you tend to criticise yourself for having certain thoughts or emotions, labelling them good or bad.

dimensions.name: Non-reactivity to inner experience
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you can let difficult thoughts and feelings come and go without being carried away by them; leaning low means strong reactions tend to grab you and pull you along.

systems.name: Resilience
systems.statusNote: Resilience — dealing well with stress and adversity — is studied through several validated self-report scales rather than one. The Brief Resilience Scale (Smith et al., 2008) was built to capture its most basic meaning: bouncing back, or how quickly you recover after hard times. The Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (Connor & Davidson, 2003), and earlier work on psychological hardiness (Kobasa, 1979), capture a second strand — the qualities that help you stay steady and adapt while adversity lasts, such as a sense of control, commitment, and treating change as a challenge. Bonanno (2004) found that resilience is the most common response to loss, not a rare gift. Offered as a reflective self-rating, not a clinical measure: resilience draws on your supports and circumstances as much as your temperament, and it can be strengthened with practice.
systems.blurb: The capacity to recover from stress and adversity — and to keep your footing while it lasts. This lens draws on the psychology of resilience to look at two strands researchers measure separately: how quickly you bounce back after a setback, and how steady and adaptable you stay under ongoing strain. Resilience isn't a fixed gift — it leans on your supports and circumstances as much as your temperament, and it can be built with practice.
systems.source: Brief Resilience Scale (Smith et al., 2008) + Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (Connor & Davidson, 2003)

dimensions.name: Bouncing back
dimensions.desc: How quickly you recover and return to your usual self after a setback or stressful event — the core of the Brief Resilience Scale. Taking longer to bounce back is common and says nothing about your worth; recovery often depends on how heavy the blow was and what support you have around you.

dimensions.name: Staying steady
dimensions.desc: How well you keep your footing and adapt while a hardship is still going on — the hardy, adaptable strand of resilience research. It draws on a sense of control, commitment to what matters to you, and meeting change as a challenge rather than only a threat.

systems.statusNote: The MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status (Adler et al., 2000) is a validated single-item measure: people place themselves on a ten-rung ladder for where they stand relative to others in their society. It predicts health and wellbeing even after accounting for objective measures like income and education.
systems.blurb: Where you place yourself on a ladder of standing relative to others in your society.
systems.source: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status (Adler et al.)

dimensions.name: Social-status ladder
dimensions.desc: The ladder represents where people stand in your society. Leaning high means you see yourself near the top — those best off in money, education and jobs; leaning low means nearer the bottom. It captures your perceived standing relative to others, which can differ from any objective measure.

systems.name: Social comparison orientation
systems.statusNote: Social comparison orientation is the dispositional tendency to size yourself up against other people — a trait first framed by Leon Festinger's social comparison theory (1954) and measured by the Iowa–Netherlands Comparison Orientation Measure (INCOM), a validated scale developed by Frederick Gibbons and Bram Buunk (1999). It has two strands: comparing your abilities and circumstances (how you're doing) and comparing your opinions and feelings (what you think). High comparers attend closely to where they stand relative to others; low comparers take their bearings more from within. Neither end is better, and this says nothing about confidence or worth — it is a descriptive self-report of a habit of attention, not a judgement of it.
systems.blurb: How much you tend to measure yourself against other people — in how you're doing, and in what you think.
systems.source: Iowa–Netherlands Comparison Orientation Measure (INCOM; Gibbons & Buunk, 1999)

dimensions.name: Comparing where you stand
dimensions.low: I rarely measure myself against others
dimensions.high: I often check how I'm doing against others
dimensions.desc: This is the ability strand of the INCOM: how much you gauge your own performance, achievements and circumstances by looking at other people. Leaning high means you frequently notice how you stack up — at work, in looks, in success — and use others as a yardstick; leaning low means you judge your progress mostly by your own standards. Neither is better: a stronger pull to compare can spur improvement but also feed envy, while a weaker one brings independence but less outside feedback.

dimensions.name: Comparing what you think
dimensions.low: I trust my own views without checking
dimensions.high: I look to others to gauge my views
dimensions.desc: This is the opinion strand of the INCOM: how much you turn to other people to work out what to think or feel. Leaning high means you like to know others' reactions before settling your own view and find it useful to compare where you stand on an issue; leaning low means you form opinions from within and rarely feel the need to check them against the crowd. Neither is better — comparing opinions aids learning and belonging, while relying on your own lends conviction and independence.

systems.name: Sense of community (BSCS)
systems.statusNote: The Brief Sense of Community Scale (Peterson, Speer & McMillan, 2008) is a validated eight-item measure of psychological sense of community, built directly on McMillan & Chavis's (1986) four-element theory of community — membership, influence, integration and fulfilment of needs, and shared emotional connection. First validated with a community sample of US city residents, the sense-of-community family of measures has since been adapted for schools, workplaces and online communities, and research links a stronger sense of community to wellbeing and civic participation. 'Community' here is whichever one matters most to you — your street, town, club, congregation or online world. Where you lean on each dimension is a self-description, not a test score.
systems.blurb: How strongly your community feels like yours — a place where you belong, are heard, find what you need and feel bound to the people in it.
systems.source: Brief Sense of Community Scale (Peterson, Speer & McMillan, 2008)

dimensions.name: Needs fulfilment
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means your community feels like a place where what you need — help, connection, opportunity — can actually be found; leaning low means you mostly meet those needs somewhere else.

dimensions.name: Group membership
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means feeling like a true member — this is your community and you belong in it; leaning low means feeling more like a guest, or an outsider looking in.

dimensions.name: Influence
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means feeling that you matter here and can help shape what happens; leaning low means feeling that decisions are made around you, without you.

dimensions.name: Shared emotional connection
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means a felt bond with the people here — shared history, shared places, time spent together; leaning low means the ties still feel thin and the history short.

systems.name: Volunteer motivations (Volunteer Functions Inventory)
systems.statusNote: The Volunteer Functions Inventory (Clary et al., 1998) is a validated 30-item instrument that measures six motivational functions giving your time can serve: values, understanding, enhancement, career, social and protective. It grew from functional theories of motivation — the idea that the same act meets different psychological needs in different people. Here those functions are offered as a reflective self-report of what giving means to you, not a test or a ranking.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of why people give their time to others. Drawing on the Volunteer Functions Inventory, developed by the psychologists E. Gil Clary, Mark Snyder and their colleagues in 1998, it sorts the motivations behind volunteering and helping into six functions — acting on deeply held values, learning and understanding the world, growing in confidence and self-worth, gaining skills and career experience, belonging among people you value, and easing difficult feelings. The idea comes from functional psychology: the same act of giving can serve very different purposes for different people, and knowing which functions matter to you helps explain why some causes feel rewarding and others fall flat. Rather than naming a single type, it asks what giving does for you. Most of us are moved by several of these at once, and the balance shifts with the cause and the chapter of life. Pick the functions that ring truest for you.

options.label: Acting on your values
options.desc: You give because it expresses what you believe — humanitarian concern and a wish to help people who have less.

options.label: Learning & understanding
options.desc: You give to learn — to understand the world and other people, and to put your knowledge and skills to use.

options.label: Growth & self-worth
options.desc: Giving lifts you — it builds confidence and self-worth, and the rewarding sense of being needed and growing as a person.

options.label: Skills & career
options.desc: You give partly to gain experience, skills and connections that support your studies or career.

options.label: Belonging & connection
options.desc: You give to be among others — strengthening friendships and sharing in something valued by people who matter to you.

options.label: Easing difficult feelings
options.desc: Giving helps you cope — easing guilt or worry and offering some relief from your own troubles.

citations.authors: Clary, E. G., Snyder, M., Ridge, R. D., Copeland, J., Stukas, A. A., Haugen, J., & Miene, P.
citations.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(6), 1516–1530

systems.name: Need for uniqueness
systems.statusNote: Consumers' Need for Uniqueness (Tian, Bearden & Hunter, 2001) — building on Snyder and Fromkin's (1977) need-for-uniqueness theory — is a validated trait measure of how much a person pursues differentness from others through the things they choose, wear and own. Its three research-derived facets are offered here as gentle self-ratings, not a test score.
systems.blurb: Need for uniqueness is the drive to set yourself apart from other people through what you choose, wear and surround yourself with — a validated personality trait that runs from blending comfortably with the crowd to actively cultivating a one-of-a-kind look. Researchers find it shows up in three ways: seeking original, tasteful choices; being willing to make bold or unconventional ones even when others raise an eyebrow; and losing interest in a favourite once everyone has it. It is the mirror image of the need to belong, and most people feel some pull from both.
systems.source: Consumers' Need for Uniqueness (CNFU; Tian, Bearden & Hunter)

dimensions.name: Bold choices

dimensions.name: Avoiding the common
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means a favourite loses some of its appeal once everyone has it, nudging you toward something less common; leaning low means you enjoy what you love just as much when it is widely shared.

systems.name: Dance Motivation Inventory (DMI)
systems.statusNote: The Dance Motivation Inventory (DMI) is a validated instrument developed by Maraz, Király, Urbán, Griffiths & Demetrovics (2015) through an exploratory factor analysis of 447 salsa and ballroom dancers. It identifies eight distinct motives for dancing; this asks which ones drive you. A self-report measure of motivation, not a clinical test.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of why people dance. Developed in 2015 by Aniko Maraz and colleagues from a factor analysis of hundreds of salsa and ballroom dancers, the Dance Motivation Inventory found that the pull of the dance floor breaks into eight distinct motives — keeping fit, lifting the mood, intimacy, socialising, the trance of losing yourself in movement, mastering your own body, the confidence it brings, and escaping everyday life. It sorts you by the motives that drive you most, going past a single answer to the full mix behind why you move.
systems.source: Dance Motivation Inventory (Maraz, Király, Urbán, Griffiths & Demetrovics, 2015)

systems.name: Aesthetic centrality (CVPA)
systems.statusNote: The Centrality of Visual Product Aesthetics scale (Bloch, Brunel & Arnold, 2003) is a validated measure of how significant visual aesthetics are in a person's relationship with the products and objects around them. Developed and validated across eight studies, it captures three facets — value (good design adds benefit to life), acumen (the ability to recognise and judge design quality), and response (the strength of one's reaction to design).
systems.blurb: The Centrality of Visual Product Aesthetics (CVPA) scale measures how much the look and design of everyday things matter to you — not which styles you prefer, but how central visual beauty is to the way you choose, use and live with objects. It maps three validated facets: the value you place on good design, your acumen for telling good design from bad, and the intensity of your response to beautiful or ugly things. People high in CVPA are moved by design and will go out of their way for it; people low in CVPA weigh function and price first.

dimensions.name: Value of beauty
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means believing good design and aesthetics genuinely add value and enjoyment to life; leaning low means treating how something looks as a minor extra beside its function and price.

dimensions.name: Design acumen
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means readily recognising and judging design quality — noticing craft, proportion and detail others miss; leaning low means good and bad design tend to look much the same to you.

dimensions.name: Response intensity
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means a beautiful object can genuinely delight you while an ugly one can bother you; leaning low means how a thing looks rarely stirs much feeling either way.

citations.title: Individual Differences in the Centrality of Visual Product Aesthetics: Concept and Measurement
citations.authors: Bloch, P. H., Brunel, F. F., & Arnold, T. J.

systems.name: Science curiosity
systems.statusNote: Based on the Science Curiosity Scale (Kahan, Landrum, Carpenter, Helft & Hall Jamieson, 2017), a behaviourally validated measure of the disposition to seek out science for pleasure — built from self-report combined with people's actual information-seeking choices. It is treated as a single dimension and is distinct from both science literacy (what you know) and general curiosity. A reflective self-ID, not a test score.
systems.blurb: Science curiosity is the disposition to seek out and savour science for its own sake — the pull toward a documentary, a why-does-that-happen question, or a fresh discovery when no exam or job requires it. Researchers measure it as a single trait running from low to high, distinct from how much science you already know. Its most striking finding: people high in science curiosity tend to engage open-mindedly with surprising evidence rather than dismiss what cuts against their existing beliefs.

dimensions.name: Science curiosity

systems.name: Self-control & self-discipline
systems.statusNote: The Brief Self-Control Scale (Tangney, Baumeister & Boone, 2004) is a widely validated measure of trait self-control — the everyday capacity to regulate impulses, emotions and habits. Designed as a single overall score, it predicts outcomes from grades and health to relationships (de Ridder et al., 2012); later work (de Ridder et al., 2011) distinguishes two sides — inhibiting unwanted impulses and initiating wanted action. Offered as a reflective self-rating, not a clinical measure: self-control can be strengthened with practice, and the once-popular idea of willpower as a quickly depletable resource (ego depletion) has not replicated reliably in large studies.
systems.blurb: Trait self-control is the everyday ability to steer your own behaviour — to hold back impulses and temptations, and to make yourself do what matters even when you don't feel like it. The Brief Self-Control Scale captures it across two sides: restraint (stopping unwanted urges) and follow-through (getting yourself to act on your intentions). Higher self-control tracks with steadier habits, better health and study, and calmer relationships — and rather than a fixed trait, it can be strengthened with practice.

dimensions.name: Restraint
dimensions.desc: Holding back urges and impulses — resisting temptation, keeping your cool under pressure, and not letting a craving or a passing mood decide what you do.

dimensions.name: Follow-through
dimensions.desc: Making yourself do what you mean to — starting the dull-but-needed task, keeping to good routines, and seeing things through even when motivation runs low.

systems.name: Maximiser or satisficer
systems.statusNote: Maximising versus satisficing was introduced by Schwartz, Ward, Monterosso, Lyubomirsky, White and Lehman (2002), who built the first Maximisation Scale and linked a strong maximising tendency to more regret, more social comparison and lower life satisfaction. Nenkov, Morrin, Ward, Schwartz and Hulland (2008) refined it into a validated short form with three facets — alternative search, decision difficulty and high standards — of which the first two track with dissatisfaction while high standards is the more adaptive, growth-oriented side. Offered here as a reflective self-rating, not a clinical measure: neither style is better, and most people sit somewhere in between and shift with how much the choice matters.
systems.blurb: Faced with a choice — a job, a phone, a place to eat — do you hunt for the very best option, or take the first one that is good enough? Psychologist Barry Schwartz named the first tendency maximising and the second satisficing. The short Maximisation Scale maps it across three sides: how widely you search for alternatives, how hard you find the act of deciding, and how high you set your standards. Maximisers often end up with objectively better outcomes yet feel more regret and less satisfaction with them — the heart of what Schwartz called the paradox of choice.
systems.source: Maximisation Scale (Schwartz et al. 2002; short form Nenkov et al. 2008)

dimensions.name: Alternative search
dimensions.desc: How widely you cast about before choosing. At the high end you keep looking for more options — more listings, more reviews, more of what else is out there — even once a good one is already in hand; at the low end you commit to the first option that clears the bar and move on.

dimensions.name: Decision difficulty
dimensions.desc: How hard the act of deciding itself feels. At the high end a wide menu is daunting — picking a gift, a film or a dish can mean second-guessing and delay; at the low end choices come easily and you rarely look back once they are made.

dimensions.name: High standards
dimensions.desc: How high you set the bar for yourself and your choices. At the high end you want the very best and rarely settle for second-rate; at the low end good enough genuinely satisfies. Of the three sides this is the most adaptive — it pairs with curiosity and drive more than with regret.

citations.title: Maximizing versus satisficing: Happiness is a matter of choice

systems.name: Travel motives (Travel Career Pattern)
systems.statusNote: The Travel Career Pattern (TCP) was developed by Philip L. Pearce and Uk-Il Lee (2005) through interview and large-scale survey studies that refined the earlier Travel Career Ladder. Factor analysis identified 14 travel-motivation factors arranged in three layers: a common core (escape/relax, novelty, strengthening relationships), a middle layer that shifts with how experienced a traveller is (e.g. experiencing other cultures, being close to nature, personal development, self-actualisation, stimulation, autonomy), and a less-central outer layer (e.g. isolation, nostalgia, romance, recognition). This presents the model's principal motives as a reflective self-report — not a clinical test or a measure of how much you travel.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of why people travel. Developed by the tourism scholars Philip Pearce and Uk-Il Lee in 2005, the Travel Career Pattern grew out of large surveys of travellers whose answers, under factor analysis, sorted the pull of travel into distinct motives arranged in layers. At the common core sit escape and relaxation, the draw of novelty, and the wish to strengthen relationships; gathered around them are motives that shift with how seasoned a traveller you are — soaking up other cultures, getting close to nature, growing as a person, chasing stimulation, and craving freedom and solitude. Rather than naming a single type, it captures the mix of reasons that get you out of the door — most of us feel several at once, and the blend changes over a lifetime of travelling. This asks which motives pull at you the hardest.

options.desc: I travel to get away and recharge — to leave routine, stress and everyday pressures behind and simply rest.

options.label: Novelty & discovery
options.desc: I travel for the new and unfamiliar — fresh places, different ways of life, and experiences I've never had before.

options.desc: I travel to share the journey with people I care about — strengthening bonds, making memories together, and leaving room for romance.

options.label: Freedom & solitude

systems.name: Proactive personality
systems.statusNote: Proactive personality, measured by the Proactive Personality Scale (Bateman & Crant, 1993), is a validated trait describing how strongly a person identifies opportunities, takes the initiative, and acts to change their environment rather than adapt to it. It is scored as a single continuum, and a meta-analysis (Fuller & Marler, 2009) links higher scores to job performance, career success, leadership and entrepreneurship. The positions below mark roughly where you sit on that continuum — both initiating and adapting are workable styles, not better-or-worse scores.
systems.blurb: Proactive personality is a research-validated trait describing how readily you take the initiative to shape your own circumstances. People high in it scan their surroundings for opportunities, act on them, and persevere until they have brought about a change, rather than waiting for events to unfold or simply adapting to conditions as they find them. Introduced by Bateman and Crant in 1993, it is one of the most studied dispositions in the psychology of work and careers, where higher scores predict job performance, career success and entrepreneurship. This self-ID places you along that continuum — from the initiator, who sets out to change things, through the selective initiator, who pushes on chosen priorities and adapts elsewhere, to the adapter, who reads conditions and responds to them as they arise. It describes a style of engaging with the world, not how capable or ambitious you are.

options.label: Initiator
options.desc: You scan for opportunities and act on them, setting out to reshape your situation rather than wait for it to change — and you tend to persevere until you have made a difference.

options.label: Selective initiator
options.desc: You take the lead on the things that matter most to you and work within the flow of events on the rest — proactive about your priorities, adaptive elsewhere.

options.label: Adapter
options.desc: You tend to take situations as they come, reading conditions and responding as they unfold rather than setting out to change your environment — letting circumstances guide your next move.

systems.name: Money attitudes (MAS)
systems.statusNote: The Money Attitude Scale (Yamauchi & Templer, 1982) is a validated 29-item psychometric measure of the meaning money holds for a person, with four factors — Power-Prestige, Retention-Time, Distrust and Anxiety. A reflective self-ID, not a financial or clinical assessment.
systems.blurb: The Money Attitude Scale (MAS) maps how you relate to money on four research-validated dimensions rather than sorting you into a single type: Power-Prestige (money as status and influence), Retention-Time (careful, future-focused saving and planning), Distrust (suspicion and hesitation in money decisions) and Anxiety (money as a source of worry and of security). Developed by Yamauchi and Templer in 1982, it captures the emotional and motivational side of money — not how much you have, but what it means to you. The linked course teaches this through the closely related money scripts framework (Klontz), which keeps finding the same four-way pattern in how people relate to money.

dimensions.name: Power-Prestige
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means treating money as a sign of success and a tool for status, recognition and influence — spending to impress and measuring yourself against others by it; leaning low means money has little to do with status or your sense of worth.

dimensions.name: Retention-Time
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means managing money carefully and for the future — budgeting, tracking spending, saving and planning ahead; leaning low means living more in the present and watching your finances less closely.

dimensions.name: Distrust
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means feeling hesitant, suspicious and doubtful in money matters — second-guessing purchases and worrying you're being overcharged or not getting fair value; leaning low means feeling confident and at ease with money decisions.

dimensions.name: Anxiety
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means money is a source of worry — feeling anxious about spending and about not having enough, while also looking to money for protection and peace of mind; leaning low means money rarely stirs anxiety for you.

systems.name: Material values (MVS)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. The Material Values Scale was developed and validated by Marsha Richins and Scott Dawson (1992), with a refined short form by Richins (2004). It treats materialism not as a character flaw but as a value orientation — the importance a person places on acquiring and owning possessions — measured along three reliable factors: success (judging your own and others' success by what they own), centrality (placing acquisition near the heart of your life) and happiness (seeing possessions as a route to satisfaction and well-being). It is one of the most widely used measures in consumer and well-being research. The three strands describe what possessions mean to you, not your worth; any profile across them is one honest way of relating to the material world.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of how central acquiring and owning possessions is to your sense of success, identity and happiness — a value orientation, not a verdict on character. Marsha Richins and Scott Dawson's Material Values Scale (1992), later refined into a short form (2004), breaks materialism into three measurable strands: success — how far you read your own and others' achievement from what they own; centrality — how much acquiring things sits at the heart of your goals and daily life; and happiness — how strongly you feel that having more would make you more content. The three vary independently, so you might love beautiful things at the centre of your life yet never measure people by them, or chase little yet quietly believe more would help. This places you along each strand rather than labelling you materialistic or not — and unlike money attitudes, which is about your relationship with money itself, it is about what the things money buys come to mean.

dimensions.name: Success
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you tend to read success — your own and other people's — from what someone owns, treating fine possessions as a sign of achievement and of a life going well. Leaning low means you judge success by other things entirely, and what a person owns tells you little about them.

dimensions.name: Centrality
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means acquiring and owning things sits near the heart of your life — you take real pleasure in getting them and organise time and effort around them. Leaning low means possessions stay at the edge of what matters to you, useful but rarely the point.

dimensions.name: Happiness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel your life would be better and more satisfying with more and finer things, and that what you own is closely tied to how content you feel. Leaning low means you look for contentment away from possessions, and having more would change little about how happy you are.

systems.name: Ethical ideology (EPQ)
systems.blurb: How you decide what is right — your ethical ideology, from Forsyth's research-validated taxonomy that crosses two dimensions: how strongly you hold that the right action must always avoid harming others (idealism), and how far you reject universal moral rules in favour of judging each situation on its own (relativism).
systems.statusNote: Forsyth's taxonomy of ethical ideologies (1980), measured by the Ethics Position Questionnaire, is a validated and widely used model in moral psychology. It scores two independent dimensions — idealism (the belief that the right action can always avoid harm to others) and relativism (the rejection of universal moral absolutes in favour of weighing each situation) — and crossing high and low on each yields four positions: situationism, absolutism, subjectivism and exceptionism. A reflective self-ID describing how you reason about right and wrong, not a measure of how moral you are.

options.label: Situationist
options.desc: High idealism, high relativism — you reject fixed moral rules and judge each act in its own context, but still aim for the choice that best protects everyone involved.

options.label: Absolutist
options.desc: High idealism, low relativism — you believe acting on universal moral rules is what produces the best, least harmful outcome, so the right principle should hold in every case.

options.label: Subjectivist
options.desc: Low idealism, high relativism — you base right and wrong on your own values and read of the situation rather than on universal principles, accepting that some harm may be unavoidable.

options.label: Exceptionist
options.desc: Low idealism, low relativism — you treat moral rules as a guide but stay pragmatic, weighing costs and benefits and allowing exceptions when breaking a rule leads to a better result.

systems.blurb: How you decide what's right — the moral framework you reason from. Each described plainly and even-handedly.

options.label: Care ethics

options.label: Contractarianism
options.desc: Morality is the set of rules rational people would agree to.

options.label: Moral relativism

options.label: Religious ethics

options.label: Intuitionism
options.desc: We grasp right and wrong directly through moral intuition.

systems.name: Moral foundations that matter most to you
systems.blurb: Which moral instincts weigh heaviest for you — from Moral Foundations Theory, Jonathan Haidt and colleagues' researched model of how people's values differ. It proposes six foundations — care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and liberty — that we each weight differently, which is part of why good people disagree. Our free course walks through all six and why moral intuition tends to come before reasoning. Pick all that resonate.

systems.name: Social value orientation (SVO)
systems.statusNote: Social value orientation (Messick & McClintock, 1968; Van Lange et al., 1997) is a validated measure of how people weigh their own outcomes against others' when interests are interdependent. It reliably predicts cooperation in real situations.
systems.blurb: How you weigh your own gain against other people's.
systems.source: Social Value Orientation (Van Lange et al.)

options.label: Altruistic
options.desc: Put others' gain ahead of your own.

options.label: Prosocial

options.label: Competitive
options.desc: Aim to come out ahead of others.

systems.name: Forgiveness (self, others & situations)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. The Heartland Forgiveness Scale was developed and validated by Laura Yamhure Thompson, C. R. Snyder and colleagues (2005), who defined dispositional forgiveness as the freeing of oneself from negative feelings toward the source of a transgression, and measured it across three independent domains — forgiveness of oneself, of other people, and of situations beyond anyone's control. Forgiving here means releasing your own resentment and ill will; it is not the same as condoning, excusing, forgetting, or necessarily reconciling. The scale's three-factor structure, reliability and validity are well established.
systems.blurb: A research-backed map of how readily you let go of resentment. Developed by the psychologists Laura Yamhure Thompson, C. R. Snyder and colleagues in 2005, the Heartland Forgiveness Scale treats forgiveness not as a single act but as a lasting disposition, and measures it across three separate fronts. The first is forgiveness of yourself, easing the self-blame that can linger after your own mistakes. The second is forgiveness of other people, releasing the grudges and the wish for payback that a wrong can leave behind. The third is forgiveness of situations, making peace with hard circumstances no one chose — illness, loss, bad luck, the way things simply turned out. Forgiving here means freeing yourself of bitterness, not condoning, excusing or forgetting what happened, and not necessarily reconciling. You can sit high on one front and low on another, so this describes the shape of your forgiveness rather than a single score.

dimensions.name: Forgiveness of self
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you treat yourself with understanding after a mistake — you can own the fault, learn from it, and let the self-blame go. Leaning low means you tend to be hard on yourself, replaying your missteps and carrying guilt or regret long after the moment has passed.

dimensions.name: Forgiveness of others
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means that when someone wrongs you, you can release the resentment and the urge to get even, even if the relationship itself changes. Leaning low means hurt and grudges tend to stay with you, and letting go of a wrong can take a long time.

dimensions.name: Forgiveness of situations
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you can come to terms with circumstances no one could control — illness, loss, bad luck, the way things turned out — without staying bitter at life. Leaning low means such situations can leave a lasting sense of grievance that is hard to shake.

systems.name: Free will vs determinism
systems.blurb: Where you stand on one of philosophy's oldest questions: do we truly choose, or is everything determined? Each view described plainly and even-handedly.
systems.statusNote: A self-identification with a position in the free-will debate, described neutrally; none is presented as the correct answer.

options.label: Libertarian free will
options.desc: We have genuine free will; our choices are truly our own.

options.label: Hard determinism
options.desc: Everything is caused by prior events, so free will is an illusion.

options.label: Compatibilism
options.desc: Free will and determinism can both be true — freedom is acting on your own reasons.

options.label: Hard incompatibilism
options.desc: Free will is impossible whether or not the world is determined.

options.label: Undecided

systems.name: Do you believe in fate?

options.desc: Events unfold according to a plan or destiny.
