options.label: We make our own path
options.desc: We shape our lives mainly through our choices.

options.label: Mostly chance
options.desc: Life is largely random; we find our own meaning.

systems.name: Locus of control
systems.statusNote: A well-studied psychological measure (Rotter, 1966) of how much you feel you control what happens in your life, versus outside forces. Distinct from the metaphysics of free will — it's about your felt sense of agency.
systems.blurb: How much you feel you steer your own life, versus outside forces and circumstance.

dimensions.name: Locus of control
dimensions.desc: Leaning internal means feeling that your own choices and effort mainly shape your outcomes, while leaning external means feeling that luck, fate, powerful others or circumstance largely decide what happens to you.

systems.name: Do you believe in karma?
systems.statusNote: Whether you feel the universe keeps a moral balance — that what goes around comes around. A self-description of your view; it's a belief, not a proven law. Shared only if you choose.
systems.blurb: Where you land on cosmic justice and 'what goes around comes around'.

options.label: Karma is real
options.desc: What goes around truly comes around.

options.label: Loosely true
options.desc: Kindness tends to come back, in a soft way.

options.label: The world is fair
options.desc: Things broadly even out in the end.

options.label: We make justice
options.desc: Fairness is something people must create.

options.label: Indifferent universe
options.desc: No cosmic scorekeeping — outcomes are chance and effort.

systems.name: Belief in luck
systems.statusNote: The Belief in Good Luck Scale (Darke & Freedman, 1997) is a validated measure of whether people see luck as a stable personal force that consistently favours them, versus random chance no one can influence. Distinct from fate (predetermination) and karma (moral justice).
systems.blurb: Whether you see luck as a force that favours you, or just randomness.
systems.source: Belief in Good Luck Scale (Darke & Freedman)

dimensions.name: Belief in luck
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel luck is a stable force that tends to favour you (or not) and can be courted; leaning low means you see luck as random chance no one can influence or rely on.

systems.name: Belief in a just world
systems.statusNote: Belief in a just world — the sense that people generally get what they deserve and deserve what they get — was identified by Melvin Lerner (1980) and is among social psychology's most-studied beliefs (Rubin & Peplau, 1975; Lipkus, 1991). Claudia Dalbert (1999) distinguished two strands: a general belief that the world at large is fair, and a personal belief that your own life is fair. A stronger personal belief tends to go with wellbeing and resilience; a stronger general belief is also linked to more readily assuming that victims brought misfortune on themselves. Neither end is right or wrong — this is a descriptive self-report of a worldview, not a claim about how just the world actually is. Distinct from karma (cosmic moral balance) and locus of control (felt personal agency).
systems.blurb: How strongly you feel the world is fundamentally fair — that people, including you, tend to get what they deserve.
systems.source: Belief in a Just World scale (Lerner; Dalbert)

dimensions.name: General just-world belief

This is Dalbert's general belief in a just world.

dimensions.name: Personal just-world belief
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel your own life is basically fair — that your efforts are rewarded and what happens to you is broadly deserved; leaning low means you feel life often treats you unfairly, whatever you do. This is Dalbert's personal belief in a just world, the strand most closely tied to wellbeing.

systems.name: Free will & determinism beliefs (FAD-Plus)
systems.statusNote: A validated psychometric scale of lay beliefs about free will and determinism (the FAD-Plus), developed and validated by Paulhus & Carey (2011) and applied by Carey & Paulhus (2013).
systems.blurb: The FAD-Plus (Free Will And Determinism scale) is a validated psychological measure of the everyday beliefs people hold about whether we truly choose and what shapes a human life. Rather than forcing one philosophical position, it scores you separately on four independent beliefs: that people freely author their own choices (Free Will), that behaviour follows lawful natural causes such as genes, upbringing and the brain (Scientific Determinism), that a destiny or higher plan governs what happens (Fatalistic Determinism), and that life is largely chance and cannot be foreseen (Unpredictability). Its central finding is that these are not simple opposites — many people endorse free will and determinism at the same time — so your profile captures the mix you actually carry rather than the single label you might pick in a debate. Developed by Delroy Paulhus and Jasmine Carey, it is a standard instrument for studying how these lay beliefs relate to morality, politics and how we judge responsibility.
systems.source: Delroy Paulhus & Jasmine Carey, The FAD-Plus, Journal of Personality Assessment, 2011

dimensions.name: Free Will
dimensions.desc: This belief holds that people are the genuine authors of their own decisions and can be held responsible for them. Scoring high means you see choices as truly free and within a person's control; scoring low means you doubt that real freedom of choice exists.

dimensions.name: Scientific Determinism
dimensions.desc: This belief holds that human behaviour follows lawful natural causes — genetics, upbringing, brain chemistry and circumstance. Scoring high means you see actions as the predictable product of prior causes; scoring low means you think science cannot fully account for what people do.

dimensions.name: Fatalistic Determinism
dimensions.desc: This belief holds that a destiny, fate or higher plan already governs how a life will unfold. Scoring high means you feel events are meant to be and laid out in advance; scoring low means you see the future as open rather than preordained.

dimensions.name: Unpredictability
dimensions.desc: This belief holds that life is largely a matter of chance and cannot be reliably predicted or controlled. Scoring high means you see much of what happens as random and unforeseeable; scoring low means you see life as more orderly and knowable.

dimensions.name: Need for cognition

systems.statusNote: Based on the Epistemic Curiosity model (Litman & Spielberger, 2003; Litman, 2008), a validated measure that tells apart Interest-type curiosity — exploring for the pleasure of learning — from Deprivation-type curiosity — the drive to close a gap in what you don't yet know. A reflective self-ID, not a test score.
systems.blurb: Two sides of curiosity that research tells apart: the joy of exploring new ideas, and the itch to resolve what you don't yet know. You might run high on one, both, or neither.

dimensions.name: Joy of discovery
dimensions.desc: How much your curiosity is driven by the pleasure of finding out new things; leaning high means you explore and learn for the sheer enjoyment of it, leaning low means you are content with what you know and feel little pull toward novelty.

dimensions.name: Need to know
dimensions.desc: How strongly an unanswered question nags at you; leaning high means not-knowing feels like an itch you must scratch until it's resolved, leaning low means you can happily leave a question open.

systems.name: Need for Cognitive Closure
systems.statusNote: Need for cognitive closure is a well-established motivational construct in social and cognitive psychology, measured by the Need for Closure Scale of Webster and Kruglanski (1994). Kruglanski and Webster (1996) describe the underlying process as 'seizing' on early information and then 'freezing' on a conclusion, which makes a firm answer feel preferable to continued open enquiry. The original scale captures five facets — preference for order, preference for predictability, decisiveness, discomfort with ambiguity and closed-mindedness; Roets and Van Hiel (2011) introduced a brief 15-item version that treats the overall need for closure as a single dimension and sets the decisiveness facet aside. This is a neutral disposition: neither a high nor a low need for closure is better, and most people sit somewhere in between.
systems.blurb: Need for cognitive closure is the desire for a firm, definite answer to a question and a matching dislike of ambiguity, confusion and loose ends — the psychological pull to settle a matter rather than leave it open. Arie Kruglanski's research frames it as 'seizing and freezing': under a strong need for closure people grasp early information quickly and then hold to their conclusion, while those with a low need for closure stay comfortable suspending judgement and weighing alternatives for longer. This maps your standing along the five facets of the classic Need for Closure Scale — a preference for order, a preference for predictability, decisiveness, discomfort with ambiguity and closed-mindedness — each rated on its own continuum. It describes how readily you reach for certainty, not whether your conclusions are correct, and a high score is neither better nor worse than a low one.

dimensions.name: Preference for order
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you like structure, routine and things kept in their place, and find disorder unsettling; leaning low means you are relaxed about mess and happy to improvise.

dimensions.name: Preference for predictability
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you prefer a stable, knowable future and would rather avoid surprises; leaning low means you are comfortable when things are uncertain or could turn out many ways.

dimensions.name: Decisiveness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you reach decisions quickly and commit to them; leaning low means you take your time and keep weighing the options. Later research treats this facet as somewhat separate from the rest.

dimensions.name: Discomfort with ambiguity
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means unclear or open-ended situations make you uneasy and you want them resolved; leaning low means you can sit with not-knowing and hold a question open.

dimensions.name: Closed-mindedness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means that once you have reached a view you are reluctant to reopen it or take on conflicting evidence; leaning low means you readily revisit a conclusion when new information arrives.

systems.name: Meaning in Life (MLQ)
systems.statusNote: The Meaning in Life Questionnaire (Steger, Frazier, Oishi & Kaler, 2006) is a validated psychological scale with two subscales: Presence of meaning (how much you feel your life has meaning) and Search for meaning (how actively you seek it). The two are measured separately and can be high or low independently.

systems.name: How you feel about death
systems.statusNote: The Death Attitude Profile–Revised (Wong, Reker & Gesser, 1994) is a validated measure in death and end-of-life psychology. It separates fear of death and death avoidance from three kinds of acceptance — neutral, approach (rooted in an afterlife) and escape (release from suffering). Described neutrally; pick the stance closest to how you feel.
systems.blurb: Your emotional stance toward your own mortality — from dread to calm acceptance. This is about how death feels to you, not what you believe comes after (that's View of death).

options.label: Fear of death
options.desc: The prospect of death frightens or unsettles you — it feels like something to dread.

options.desc: You see death as a natural, inevitable part of life — neither feared nor welcomed — and focus on living well.

options.label: Escape acceptance

systems.name: Sense of coherence (SOC)
systems.statusNote: Empirical. Sense of coherence (SOC) is the central concept of the salutogenic model developed by medical sociologist Aaron Antonovsky (1987), and is measured by his Orientation to Life Questionnaire (the 29-item SOC-29 and short 13-item SOC-13). It asks not what makes people ill but what keeps them well, and is one of the most widely studied resources in health and well-being research. It is defined by three components — comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness — that together describe how confidently a person meets the stresses of life; the structure and reliability of the scale were set out by Antonovsky (1993). A strong or weak standing on any thread is one honest way of relating to life, not a measure of worth.
systems.blurb: Sense of coherence is the heart of Aaron Antonovsky's salutogenic model — his answer to why some people stay well under heavy stress while others fall ill. Rather than asking what makes us sick, he asked what keeps us healthy, and located it in a global, enduring way of meeting life. People with a strong sense of coherence experience the world along three threads: comprehensibility — life feels ordered, predictable and explicable rather than chaotic; manageability — you feel you have the resources, your own or others', to meet what life asks of you; and meaningfulness — life's demands feel like challenges worth engaging with, not just burdens to endure. The three act together as a coping resource that shapes how you appraise stress. This places you along each thread. Unlike the Meaning in Life Questionnaire, which is about how much meaning you feel and how actively you seek it, sense of coherence is the wider orientation to living — whether the world makes sense, feels manageable, and is worth the effort.
systems.source: Orientation to Life Questionnaire (Sense of Coherence Scale; Antonovsky, 1987)

dimensions.name: Comprehensibility
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means the world tends to feel ordered, predictable and explicable — events hang together and you can make sense of what happens to you; leaning low means life can feel chaotic, random and hard to read, with events arriving as noise rather than as pattern.

dimensions.name: Manageability
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means you feel you have the resources — your own, or those of people and supports you can call on — to cope with the demands life makes of you; leaning low means demands can feel like more than you can meet, and setbacks like things done to you that you cannot influence.

dimensions.name: Meaningfulness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means life's demands feel like challenges worth investing in — things worth caring about and committing to; leaning low means more of what you face feels like a burden to be endured rather than something that asks for, and rewards, your engagement.

systems.name: Mathematical thinking style
systems.statusNote: Mathematical thinking styles (Borromeo Ferri, 2010) is a validated framework in mathematics-education research describing how a person prefers to imagine, represent and reason through mathematical ideas. It distinguishes an analytic style (formal, symbolic, step-by-step reasoning), a visual style (pictorial, holistic, spatial imagery), and an integrated style that draws on both. It develops Vadim Krutetskii's classic study of the mathematical mind, which identified analytic, geometric and harmonic types (1976). This is a preference, not a test of ability, and no style is better than another.
systems.blurb: Mathematical thinking style is about how your mind prefers to work when you do mathematics — not how good you are at it, but the form your reasoning naturally takes. Drawing on Rita Borromeo Ferri's research and Vadim Krutetskii's classic study of mathematical minds, it describes three styles: analytic thinkers reason in symbols, formulae and logical steps and feel at home with the abstract; visual thinkers reach for pictures, diagrams and spatial relationships and grasp ideas as holistic images; and integrated thinkers move fluidly between the two, using whichever serves the problem. The styles describe a preference, not an aptitude — each is a complete and capable way of doing mathematics, and strong mathematicians are found at every pole.

options.label: Analytic
options.desc: You think in symbols, formulae and logical steps. You're at home with abstract, formal reasoning and work a problem through methodically — you rarely need a picture to understand it, and you trust the algebra to lead the way.

options.label: Visual
options.desc: You think in pictures, diagrams and spatial relationships. You understand mathematics best through holistic, visual representations — a sketch, a graph or a shape makes an idea click, and you often see the answer before you formalise it.

options.label: Integrated
options.desc: You move fluidly between the formal and the visual, drawing on symbols and images as the problem calls for it. Neither pole pulls you strongly — you switch between calculating and picturing, using whichever gets you there.

systems.name: Family cohesion & flexibility (Circumplex Model)
systems.statusNote: Olson's Circumplex Model of Marital and Family Systems (Olson, Sprenkle & Russell, 1979; Olson, 2000) places families on two central dimensions — cohesion and flexibility — measured by the FACES self-report scales, with FACES IV validated by Olson (2011). It is a widely used framework in family-systems research and therapy.
systems.blurb: Developed by David Olson, the Circumplex Model maps any family on two core dimensions: cohesion — the emotional closeness between members, from disengaged independence to enmeshed togetherness — and flexibility — how readily its roles, rules and leadership adapt, from rigid to chaotic. A third factor, communication, helps a family shift along them. Balanced, mid-range levels of both tend to support healthy functioning while the extremes can bring strain, and the FACES questionnaires make it one of the most widely used maps of how families relate.
systems.source: FACES IV (Family Adaptability and Cohesion Evaluation Scales)

dimensions.name: Cohesion (togetherness)
dimensions.desc: How emotionally close your family is — the balance between separateness and togetherness. At the low end families are independent and disengaged, with members largely living parallel lives; at the high end they are very close-knit, even enmeshed, leaving little room apart. Olson's model finds the connected middle ground, where members are bonded yet free, tends to work best.

dimensions.name: Flexibility (adaptability)
dimensions.desc: How readily your family reshapes its roles, rules and leadership when life shifts. At the low end it is highly structured, even rigid, with fixed roles and firm rules; at the high end it is free-flowing, even chaotic, with leadership and routines in constant flux. As with cohesion, a balanced middle — structured yet adaptable — tends to serve families best.

systems.name: Spiritual transcendence (STS)
systems.statusNote: The Spiritual Transcendence Scale (Piedmont, 1999) is a validated measure that treats spiritual transcendence as a stable personality trait — one found to be statistically independent of the Big Five. Its three facets, prayer fulfilment, universality, and connectedness, are offered here as gentle self-ratings that fit religious and secular outlooks alike, not a test score or a measure of how 'spiritual' anyone should be.
systems.blurb: Spiritual transcendence is the capacity to step back from the immediate moment and sense a larger, sacred meaning to life. Psychologist Ralph Piedmont introduced it as a possible sixth dimension of personality — one that sits apart from the Big Five — and measured it across three facets: prayer fulfilment (the joy and peace found in prayer, meditation, or contemplation), universality (a belief that all life is interconnected), and connectedness (a felt bond and responsibility toward humanity across generations and groups). It describes how strongly a transcendent outlook colours your life, in religious or secular terms alike — not whether any belief is right.

dimensions.name: Prayer fulfilment
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means prayer, meditation, or quiet contemplation brings you joy, peace, and a felt connection to something greater; leaning low means such practices play little part in how you find contentment.

dimensions.name: Universality
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means sensing that all people, nature, and existence are deeply interconnected and share one common bond; leaning low means experiencing life's parts as more separate and distinct.

dimensions.name: Connectedness
dimensions.desc: Leaning high means feeling a personal bond with — and responsibility to — humanity across all groups and generations; leaning low means feeling your ties and obligations rest mainly with yourself and those closest to you.

systems.name: What draws you to your scenes
systems.statusNote: Based on the Leisure Motivation Scale (Beard & Ragheb, 1983), a validated 48-item instrument that measures four research-derived reasons people pursue leisure — intellectual, social, competence-mastery and stimulus-avoidance (escape). Its four subscales draw on Maslow's account of human needs and each showed internal-consistency reliability around 0.90 across 1,205 respondents. The full scale scores all four motives at once; here you simply pick the one that pulls you in most.
systems.blurb: We throw ourselves into scenes, hobbies and communities for all sorts of reasons — and the reason itself is a kind of self-portrait. Drawing on the Leisure Motivation Scale (Beard & Ragheb, 1983), this sorts what pulls you towards your pursuits into four research-backed motives: the intellectual draw of learning and discovery, the social draw of friendship and belonging, the competence-mastery draw of challenge and skill, and the stimulus-avoidance draw of escape and rest. Most of us feel all four — this asks which one pulls hardest.

options.label: Intellectual
options.desc: You're here for the ideas — learning, exploring, discovering and imagining. A scene is somewhere to think, create and feed your curiosity.

options.label: Social
options.desc: You're here for the people — friendship, belonging and the esteem of others. A scene is, above all, the company it keeps.

options.label: Competence & mastery
options.desc: You're here for the challenge — achieving, improving and mastering the craft. A scene is a place to test yourself and get genuinely good.

options.label: Escape & unwinding
options.desc: You're here for the relief — resting, unwinding and escaping everyday pressure and over-stimulation. A scene is a refuge that lets you recharge.

systems.name: Seasonal sensitivity (SPAQ)
systems.blurb: How strongly the turning seasons swing your mood, energy, sleep and appetite — and whether you feel at your lowest in the dark days of winter, in the bright heat of summer, or scarcely change at all. Psychologists call this trait 'seasonality'; a pronounced winter pattern is the basis of seasonal affective disorder (SAD).
systems.statusNote: Seasonality is measured by the Seasonal Pattern Assessment Questionnaire (SPAQ; Rosenthal, Bradt & Wehr, 1987), whose six-item Global Seasonality Score gauges how much mood, sleep, appetite, weight, energy and socialising shift across the year. It is a validated research and screening tool — not a diagnosis; only a clinician can diagnose seasonal affective disorder. A reflective self-ID.
systems.source: Seasonal Pattern Assessment Questionnaire (SPAQ) — Rosenthal, Bradt & Wehr (1987)

options.label: Non-seasonal
options.desc: Your mood, sleep, energy and appetite stay much the same whatever the season — a low Global Seasonality Score.

options.label: Subtly seasonal
options.desc: You feel real but mild seasonal shifts — a little winter sluggishness or a summer slump — without it disrupting your life. Researchers call this subsyndromal seasonality (S-SAD).

options.label: Winter pattern
options.desc: You reliably slow down in the short, dark months — lower mood, oversleeping and craving carbohydrates — then lift as the light returns. The most common strong pattern, and the basis of winter SAD.

options.label: Summer pattern
options.desc: The rarer reverse pattern: you struggle more in the long, hot, bright days — restless, sleeping poorly and off your food — and feel steadier in the cooler, darker months.

systems.name: Food neophobia (FNS)
systems.statusNote: The Food Neophobia Scale (Pliner & Hobden, 1992) is a validated ten-item measure of how willing someone is to try unfamiliar foods, used in food research worldwide and translated into many languages. People fall along a continuum from food neophilia (eager for the new) to food neophobia (preferring the familiar). Research finds the trait peaks in early childhood and usually softens with age and with repeated exposure to varied foods, and twin studies suggest a substantial inherited component. Caution toward unknown foods is generally read as an old protective instinct, not a character flaw. Where you place yourself here is a self-description, not a test score.
systems.blurb: How you meet a dish you've never tried — do you chase the unfamiliar, or trust the foods you know? Both are old, human strategies.

options.label: Eager explorer (neophilic)
options.desc: You actively seek out foods you've never tried — an unfamiliar menu is an invitation, and the unknown dish is the one you order.

options.label: Happily open
options.desc: You'll gladly try something new when it comes your way, even if you don't go hunting for it.

options.label: Cautious taster
options.desc: You'll try the unfamiliar now and then, but with some hesitation — you like to know what's in it, and a trusted recommendation helps.

options.label: Faithful to the familiar (neophobic)
options.desc: You stay with foods you know and trust — a common pattern, and the older human default: caution toward unknown foods once kept people safe.

systems.name: Identification with all humanity
systems.statusNote: Identification With All Humanity (IWAH) is a validated individual-difference measure developed by McFarland, Webb and Brown (2012). It assesses how strongly a person identifies with three widening circles — their community, their country, and all humanity. A substantial body of research links the all-humanity bond to support for human rights, global humanitarian concern, and valuing the lives of people in other nations (McFarland et al., 2019).
systems.blurb: Identification with all humanity is how far your sense of 'us' reaches — whether you feel a genuine bond not only with your community and your country, but with all people everywhere as one human family. Introduced by Sam McFarland and colleagues (2012), the scale places you on three widening circles of belonging: your local community, your nation, and humanity as a whole. The outermost circle is the one that matters most — people high in it care about human rights, are moved by the suffering of distant strangers, and support humanitarian help across borders, while those lower in it draw the circle of kinship closer to home. It is the psychology beneath global citizenship and the shared-humanity premise of international law, and it is distinct from how widely you extend moral concern: this measures felt kinship and belonging, not who counts morally.
systems.source: Identification With All Humanity Scale (McFarland, Webb & Brown, 2012)

dimensions.name: Bond with your community
dimensions.desc: How close and connected you feel to the people in your local community and the groups around you. Leaning high, you feel a real sense of belonging with the people nearby and take their joys and troubles partly as your own; leaning low, your sense of 'us' stays close to yourself and a few near ties.

dimensions.name: Bond with your country
dimensions.desc: How much you identify with your fellow citizens and feel part of your nation. Leaning high, you feel genuine kinship with people across your country, even strangers, as fellow members of one people; leaning low, national belonging is not a strong part of how you see yourself.

dimensions.name: Bond with all humanity
dimensions.desc: The heart of the scale: how much you identify with people everywhere as one human family, beyond nation, background, or border. Leaning high, you feel real kinship with and responsibility toward all people, wherever they live, and their suffering moves you as your own would; leaning low, your sense of 'us' stops nearer to home. McFarland and colleagues find this outermost bond predicts concern for human rights and for the welfare of people in distant countries.

systems.name: Patriotism, nationalism and internationalism
systems.statusNote: Patriotism, nationalism and internationalism were established as separate, measurable attitudes by Rick Kosterman and Seymour Feshbach (1989), whose scales remain a standard instrument in political psychology. Later representative-sample studies confirmed that patriotism and nationalism are empirically distinct and predict different attitudes towards other groups (Blank & Schmidt, 2003; De Figueiredo & Elkins, 2003).
systems.blurb: Patriotism, nationalism and internationalism are three separate attitudes a person can hold towards their own country and the rest of the world, distinguished by the political psychologists Rick Kosterman and Seymour Feshbach in 1989. Patriotism is a warm attachment to your country — love for it and pride in belonging — without any claim that it stands above others. Nationalism goes further, holding that your nation is superior and ought to be dominant, placing its standing ahead of other countries. Internationalism looks outward: empathy for people in other nations and support for cooperation, sharing and helping across borders. Crucially these are not a single line running from 'loves country' to 'loves world' — research finds you can score high on more than one at once, so a person may feel deep pride in their country while also caring about the wider world, or feel attached without any sense of superiority. The distinction matters because patriotism and nationalism, though often confused, predict markedly different attitudes towards outsiders. This places you on all three as a spectrum, each presented neutrally, with no pole treated as the right one.
systems.source: Kosterman & Feshbach's patriotism, nationalism and internationalism scales (Kosterman & Feshbach, 1989)

dimensions.name: Patriotism
dimensions.desc: A warm, affective attachment to your country — love for it and pride in belonging. A high score feels a strong personal bond with your nation; a low score feels little emotional attachment to it. This is pride in your own country, with no claim that it is better than anyone else's.

dimensions.name: Nationalism
dimensions.desc: The belief that your nation is superior to others and should be dominant. A high score holds your country above the rest and wants it to lead and prevail; a low score sees nations as equals and rejects the idea that yours should dominate. This goes beyond pride to comparison and standing.

dimensions.name: Internationalism
dimensions.desc: Concern for the welfare of people in other nations and support for cooperation across borders — foreign aid, sharing resources and working through international bodies. A high score cares about the wider world and favours helping and cooperating with other countries; a low score keeps attention and resources on your own nation.

systems.name: Why crime happens
systems.statusNote: The major theoretical schools of criminology — classical / rational-choice, strain, social learning, control, labelling and conflict theory. Each is a long-running explanatory tradition with its own body of empirical research; this asks which one best fits your own view, not which is 'correct'.
systems.blurb: Criminologists have spent two centuries arguing over what really drives someone to break the law — cold cost-benefit calculation, the strain of blocked opportunity, the company we keep, weak bonds to society, the way being labelled a criminal can deepen offending, or the workings of power and inequality. Each answer is a school of thought with its own evidence behind it. Which one comes closest to how you explain crime?

options.label: Rational choice
options.desc: People weigh the likely rewards against the risks and turn to crime when it seems to pay. Make the consequences swift, certain and sure, and most would be deterred. This is the classical tradition running from Beccaria to modern rational-choice theory.

options.label: Strain & blocked opportunity
options.desc: Society urges everyone to chase success but leaves many without legitimate means to reach it. That gap — and the pressure, frustration and inequality behind it — pushes people toward crime.

options.label: Social learning
options.desc: Crime is learned like any other behaviour: from the attitudes, techniques and rewards of the people and groups we spend time with. Surround someone with offending and it starts to look normal.

options.label: Weak bonds & self-control
options.desc: Almost everyone is tempted; what holds us back is strong attachment to family, school and community, and the self-control to resist. Crime appears where those bonds or that restraint are weak.

options.label: Labelling & social reaction
options.desc: What counts as crime depends on how society reacts. Being caught, stigmatised and labelled a criminal can trap someone in that identity and deepen the very behaviour it condemns.

options.label: Power & inequality
options.desc: Look at who writes the laws and who gets punished. Crime and justice reflect power: the rules tend to protect the interests of the powerful, while the poor and marginalised are policed most heavily.

systems.name: Why you obey the law
systems.statusNote: Tom R. Tyler's process-based model of why people obey the law is one of the most replicated findings in legal and criminal-justice psychology. Across surveys and field studies (Tyler, 1990/2006; Sunshine & Tyler, 2003; Jackson et al., 2012), people comply with everyday law far more because they regard legal authorities as legitimate, and because the law aligns with their own morals, than because they fear being caught and punished — the normative bases (legitimacy and morality) consistently outweigh the instrumental one (deterrence). This places you on whichever basis runs strongest for you; it is a self-report of motive, not a measure of how law-abiding you are.
systems.blurb: Why does anyone keep to the law? The legal psychologist Tom Tyler spent decades testing two answers. The instrumental answer is deterrence: people obey because breaking the law is risky — they weigh the odds of being caught against the gain. The normative answer is that people obey because they feel they should — either because they see the police, courts and legislature as legitimate and trust them to act fairly, or because the law matches their own conscience. Tyler's much-replicated finding is that these normative reasons predict everyday compliance far better than fear of punishment does, which is why a system seen as fair and legitimate is obeyed more willingly than one that rules by threat alone. This asks which basis runs strongest for you: a felt duty to legitimate authority, your personal sense of right and wrong, or a clear-eyed reckoning of the consequences. It is about the source of your law-abidingness, not how strictly you follow rules — most people draw on all three, but one tends to lead.
systems.source: Tom R. Tyler's process-based model of legitimacy and compliance — Why People Obey the Law (1990/2006)

options.label: Duty and trust
options.desc: You obey because you see legal authority as legitimate. The law and the institutions behind it — police, courts, the legislature — have, in your eyes, the right to be obeyed, and you broadly trust them to act fairly and even-handedly. That standing, more than any threat of punishment, is what gives a rule its hold on you. In Tyler's research this legitimacy-based motive is the strongest and steadiest source of everyday compliance, and it grows when authorities treat people with fairness and respect.

options.label: Personal conscience
options.desc: You obey because the law lines up with your own sense of right and wrong. A rule that matches your conscience needs no enforcement — you would keep to it anyway — while one you find genuinely unjust holds far less sway, and you may feel justified in challenging it. Here the law's authority is borrowed from your morals rather than from the state. Tyler groups this with legitimacy as a normative basis for compliance, and like legitimacy it predicts law-abiding behaviour more reliably than the fear of punishment does.

options.label: Risk and consequence
options.desc: You obey because breaking the law carries real costs. Compliance is a practical calculation — the chance of being caught set against the penalty, and weighed against what there is to gain — so the certainty and severity of enforcement matter most to you. This is the classical, instrumental view of law-abidingness, running from Beccaria and Bentham to modern deterrence theory. Tyler finds it genuinely shapes behaviour, but on its own less powerfully than people expect: where legitimacy and conscience are thin, the threat of punishment has to do all the work.

systems.name: Materialist or postmaterialist values
systems.statusNote: Inglehart's materialist–postmaterialist value index is a validated, widely used measure in comparative political science, introduced by Ronald Inglehart (1971) and developed across decades of the World Values Survey. The classic four-item index ranks the societal goals a person prioritises and sorts respondents into materialist, mixed, and postmaterialist groups (Inglehart, 1977; Inglehart & Abramson, 1994).
systems.blurb: Materialist and postmaterialist values describe which goals a society — and you — put first, a value dimension introduced by the political scientist Ronald Inglehart in 1971. It is not about loving possessions, which is consumer materialism; it is about priorities for the wider world. Materialist priorities place physical and economic security first — a strong economy, stable prices, order, safety and defence — the concerns of people who grew up when these could not be taken for granted. Postmaterialist priorities, more common among those raised in security and prosperity, place self-expression and quality of life first — a greater say in decisions, free speech, protecting the environment, and a more humane, less impersonal society. Inglehart's classic four-item index asks people to rank national goals and sorts them into three groups — materialist, mixed, and postmaterialist — and his 'silent revolution' thesis holds that as younger, more secure generations replace older ones, whole publics gradually shift toward the postmaterialist end. The dimension cuts across the old left–right divide and underpins the World Values Survey's map of cultural change, so neither pole is better: each reflects the conditions a generation grew up in.
systems.source: Inglehart's Materialist–Postmaterialist Values Index (Ronald Inglehart, 1971; World Values Survey)

options.label: Materialist
options.desc: You put physical and economic security first — a strong, stable economy, low inflation, order and safety. These are the foundations everything else depends on, so safeguarding them comes before more abstract aims. Inglehart found this outlook most common among people who grew up when security could not be taken for granted.

options.label: Mixed
options.desc: You hold a balance, wanting both security and self-expression, with the stronger pull depending on the circumstances. You might rank a sound economy alongside a greater say in decisions, refusing to treat order and freedom as a simple either-or. This is the largest group in most societies Inglehart studied.

options.label: Postmaterialist
options.desc: You put self-expression and quality of life first — a real say in decisions that affect you, free speech, protecting the environment, and a more humane society. With material security broadly in place, these are the goals you reach for next. Inglehart found this outlook spreading as more secure generations come of age.

systems.name: Hierarchy or equality between groups
systems.statusNote: Social Dominance Orientation is a validated, widely replicated individual-difference measure in political psychology. It was introduced by Pratto, Sidanius, Stallworth and Malle (1994) as part of Social Dominance Theory; the current two-factor SDO7 scale (Dominance and Anti-egalitarianism) was validated by Ho et al. (2015).
systems.blurb: Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) measures how much a person prefers society to be ordered as a hierarchy between groups rather than as equals. Developed by Pratto, Sidanius and colleagues in 1994 within Social Dominance Theory, it captures a general outlook — not a party or a single policy — that predicts attitudes to prejudice, immigration, welfare and conflict across the political spectrum. The current SDO7 scale separates two facets: endorsing active dominance of one group over another, and a subtler opposition to equality. This self-assessment places you on both, presented neutrally as a spectrum of social attitudes rather than a verdict.
systems.source: Felicia Pratto, Jim Sidanius, Lisa Stallworth and Bertram Malle, 1994 (SDO7 revision: Ho et al., 2015)

dimensions.name: Active dominance
dimensions.desc: How much you endorse powerful groups actively dominating weaker ones. A high score supports stronger groups asserting control by force; a low score rejects coercive dominance between groups.

dimensions.name: Opposition to equality
dimensions.desc: A subtler preference for keeping groups unequal — resistance to ideals and policies that level the playing field. A high score favours maintaining group differences; a low score supports greater equality between groups.

systems.name: How you relate to authority and tradition
systems.statusNote: Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) is a validated, heavily replicated individual-difference measure in political psychology, introduced by Bob Altemeyer (1981). Despite its name, 'right-wing' is a technical term for submission to established authority rather than a political party, and the trait is measured right across the political spectrum. Altemeyer described it as a covarying blend of three attitudinal clusters — authoritarian submission, authoritarian aggression and conventionalism — which Dunwoody and Funke (2016) operationalised and validated as three separable factors, the structure presented here. With Social Dominance Orientation it forms the dual-process motivational model of ideology and prejudice (Duckitt & Sibley, 2010).
systems.blurb: Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) measures how much a person defers to established authority, upholds traditional conventions, and supports firm sanctioning of those who break society's rules. Introduced by the psychologist Bob Altemeyer in 1981, it is among the most-studied dispositions in political psychology — and despite its name, 'right-wing' is a technical term for submission to the established order, not a political party, so the trait is found across the political spectrum. This self-assessment places you on the three facets Altemeyer identified and Dunwoody and Funke later validated as separable: submission to authority, aggression towards rule-breakers, and adherence to convention. Together with Social Dominance Orientation it forms the 'dual-process' model that political psychologists use to explain ideology and intergroup attitudes. It is presented neutrally as a spectrum of social attitudes rather than a verdict — neither pole is better or worse.
systems.source: Bob Altemeyer, 1981 (three-factor ASC validation: Dunwoody & Funke, 2016)

dimensions.name: Authoritarian submission
dimensions.desc: How readily you defer to established, legitimate authorities such as leaders, institutions and the law. A high score means trusting and following those in charge; a low score means questioning authority and reserving the right to disagree.

dimensions.name: Authoritarian aggression
dimensions.desc: How much you support firm, even harsh, sanctioning of people who break society's rules or whom recognised authorities condemn. A high score favours strong punishment to keep order; a low score prefers tolerance and leniency towards those who step out of line.

dimensions.name: Conventionalism
dimensions.desc: How strongly you uphold long-standing social conventions and the traditional norms endorsed by society. A high score means valuing tradition and shared standards of behaviour; a low score means being comfortable with nonconformity and changing norms.

systems.name: How you view hierarchy between groups
systems.statusNote: Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) is a validated psychometric scale introduced by Felicia Pratto, Jim Sidanius, Lisa Stallworth and Bertram Malle (1994) and revised into the two-facet SDO₇ scale by Arnold Ho and colleagues (2015). It measures a person's general preference for hierarchy versus equality between social groups; the SDO₇ revision distinguishes two empirically supported facets — group-based dominance (SDO-D) and opposition to equality, or anti-egalitarianism (SDO-E). The scale has been validated across many countries and large samples, and alongside Right-Wing Authoritarianism it is one of the two strongest individual-difference predictors of intergroup and political attitudes. This is a self-report of your own outlook, shown neutrally — neither a high nor a low score is treated as the right one.
systems.blurb: Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) is how far a person prefers society to be ordered by a hierarchy of groups rather than by equality between them. Introduced by Felicia Pratto, Jim Sidanius and colleagues in 1994, it is among the most studied attitudes in political psychology and the natural partner to Right-Wing Authoritarianism: together the two form the 'dual-process' model that explains much of where people stand politically. Where authoritarianism is about deferring to authority and tradition, SDO is about how you feel towards hierarchy and inequality between groups — nations, classes, ethnicities, genders, castes. The current SDO₇ scale (Ho and colleagues, 2015) measures it along two related strands. The first, group dominance, is the open belief that stronger groups may rightly lead and prevail over weaker ones. The second, opposition to equality, is the quieter preference for leaving group differences as they are rather than working to reduce them. This places you on both as a spectrum, each shown neutrally with no pole treated as the right one — people genuinely differ in whether they see group hierarchy as natural and orderly or as something to be levelled.
systems.source: Social Dominance Orientation (SDO₇) scale (Pratto, Sidanius, Stallworth & Malle, 1994; revised Ho et al., 2015)

dimensions.name: Group dominance
dimensions.desc: Support for some groups actively dominating others. A high score sees it as natural or acceptable for stronger or higher-status groups to lead, command and prevail over weaker ones; a low score holds that no group should dominate another and that groups should meet on an equal footing. This is the open, assertive face of the orientation — about power and who gets to be on top.

dimensions.name: Opposition to equality
dimensions.desc: How you regard efforts to even out differences between groups. A high score treats existing inequalities between groups as acceptable or simply how things are, and is unenthusiastic about policies or movements that try to reduce them; a low score actively wants to narrow group-based inequality and backs the measures that do. This is the quieter face of the orientation — less about domination than about whether equality is a goal worth pursuing.

systems.name: How you'd settle a dispute
systems.statusNote: The interests–rights–power framework is a foundational model of the dispute-systems-design field, introduced by William Ury, Jeanne Brett and Stephen Goldberg (1988). It is an analytical framework rather than a validated self-report scale; its central claim — that focusing a dispute on interests tends to cost less and satisfy more than contests over rights or power — has been examined empirically in studies of grievance and dispute-resolution procedures (Brett, Goldberg & Ury, 1990; Lytle, Brett & Shapiro, 1999).
systems.blurb: Every dispute can be approached in one of three ways, a framework set out by the negotiation scholars William Ury, Jeanne Brett and Stephen Goldberg in Getting Disputes Resolved (1988). You can reconcile interests — the underlying needs, concerns and priorities beneath each side's stated position — through negotiation or mediation, searching for an outcome that meets as much of what everyone actually wants as possible. You can turn to rights — an independent standard such as a law, a contract, a precedent or a shared principle of fairness — and let a court, an arbitrator or an agreed rule determine who is right. Or you can rely on power — leverage, costs and the capacity to impose consequences — so the outcome turns on who can compel whom, the logic of strikes, ultimatums and trials of strength. Ury and colleagues argue that interest-based resolution is usually the least costly and most durable, with rights and power better kept in reserve for when a precedent must be set or one side will not engage — yet each has its place, and most real disputes move between all three. This asks which you reach for first when a conflict is yours to settle.

options.label: Interests
options.desc: You look first for what each side actually needs beneath its stated position — the concerns, priorities and fears driving the dispute — and search for an outcome that satisfies as much of them as possible. This is the work of negotiation and mediation, which Ury and colleagues found is usually the least costly and most lasting way to settle a conflict.

options.label: Rights
options.desc: You appeal to an independent standard — a law, a contract, a precedent, an agreed principle of fairness — to decide who is right, handing the dispute to a court, an arbitrator or an accepted rule. This sets clear precedents and can protect a weaker party, though it tends to cost more in time and money and to leave a clear winner and loser.

options.label: Power
options.desc: You rely on leverage — the costs each side can impose and who is ultimately able to compel whom. Strength, deadlines and the threat of consequences decide the matter, as in a strike or an ultimatum. It can break a deadlock when the other side refuses to engage, but Ury and colleagues note it is usually the most costly route and the most likely to damage the relationship.

systems.name: How you communicate in conflict
systems.statusNote: The Intercultural Conflict Style (ICS) Inventory is a validated 36-item measure (18 items per dimension) developed by Mitchell Hammer (2005) and grounded in Stella Ting-Toomey's face-negotiation theory. It places conflict behaviour on two empirically supported dimensions — how directly people raise a disagreement, and how openly they show emotion while doing so — which in Hammer's confirmatory factor analysis formed a good-fitting two-factor model (directness scale Cronbach's alpha around .73; emotional expressiveness around .85). Crossing the two axes yields four styles. The patterns vary with cultural background and have been examined across cultural groups (Hammer, 2005; Oetzel & Ting-Toomey, 2003), and no style is more effective than another. This is a self-report of your own tendency, not a measure of skill.
systems.blurb: When a disagreement flares, two things shape how you handle it — and they sit apart from whether you stand firm or give way. The first is directness: do you name the problem plainly and say what you want, or work around it through hints, go-betweens, understatement and saving face? The second is emotional expressiveness: do you let feeling show in your voice and manner, treating visible passion as a sign of sincerity, or keep your emotions in check to stay calm and composed? The communication scholar Mitchell Hammer built the Intercultural Conflict Style model on exactly these two axes, drawing on Stella Ting-Toomey's research into how people across cultures manage 'face'. Crossing them gives four styles — Discussion, Engagement, Accommodation and Dynamic — each a different blend of plain-spokenness and shown emotion. The styles tend to run along cultural lines, yet everyone has their own and none is better than the rest: misunderstanding usually comes from reading another person's style through your own. This asks how directly you speak when a conflict is yours to handle, and how much emotion you let show.

options.label: Discussion
options.desc: You raise disagreements openly and in plain words, but keep your emotions level. You stick to the issue, value calm and precision, and trust a measured, on-the-record exchange to settle things — open confrontation is fine, visible heat is not. Others who share this style find it fair and businesslike; people who show more feeling can read your composure as coolness or indifference, when you intend focus and respect.

options.label: Engagement
options.desc: You name the disagreement directly and you let your feelings show while doing it. Intensity, animation and a raised voice are, for you, signs of sincerity and genuine care — the emotion is part of being honest, not a loss of control. People who share this style hear your passion as engagement; more restrained people can mistake it for anger or pressure, and may pull back just as you are leaning in.

options.label: Accommodation
options.desc: You handle disagreement carefully and indirectly, and you keep your emotions out of view. Rather than confront head-on you use hints, questions, pauses, a tactful third party or a softened word, working to protect everyone's dignity and the relationship — and you stay composed throughout. Others who share this style read your tact as considerate and wise; more direct people may miss the point you are making, or take your calm for agreement or evasion.

options.label: Dynamic
options.desc: You approach disagreement indirectly — through stories, third parties, hyperbole or circling around the point — while showing strong emotion as you go. The expressiveness signals how much the matter weighs on you, even as the indirectness leaves room to manoeuvre and save face. People who share this style follow both the feeling and the roundabout path; those used to plain, restrained talk can find it hard to read, unsure whether the emotion or the literal words carry the message.

systems.name: Your psychological contract at work
systems.statusNote: The psychological contract — the unwritten, perceived obligations an employee and employer each believe the other has taken on — is a long-established construct in organisational behaviour and employment relations, made measurable by the organisational psychologist Denise M. Rousseau (1989, 1995). Her Psychological Contract Inventory (2000) operationalises four types along two dimensions, time frame and performance terms, and the transactional, relational, balanced and transitional forms have been validated empirically across several national samples (e.g. Hui, Lee & Rousseau, 2004). It measures a person's perceived deal through self-report, not a legally binding agreement.
systems.blurb: The psychological contract is the unwritten set of mutual obligations a worker and an employer each believe the other has taken on — the felt 'deal' that runs alongside the formal, written employment contract. The organisational psychologist Denise Rousseau made these beliefs measurable and showed they fall into recognisable patterns along two axes: how long the relationship is meant to last (short-term or open-ended) and how clearly each side's performance is spelled out (specified or left broad). Crossing the two gives four types. A transactional contract is a short-term, narrowly defined economic exchange — a fair day's pay for a fair day's work, with little expected beyond the job description. A relational contract is open-ended and built on loyalty, security and mutual investment, where employer and employee look after one another over years. A balanced contract blends the two: a long-term partnership with clear, evolving performance goals and shared development. A transitional state is not really a contract at all but the uncertainty and eroded trust people feel during upheaval such as restructuring or layoffs, when the old deal has broken down and no new one is settled. Measured by Rousseau's Psychological Contract Inventory and studied across many countries, the framework helps explain why the same broken promise can feel trivial to one person and like a betrayal to another. This asks which deal best describes what you expect from working life — and neither security nor independence is the 'right' answer.
systems.source: Rousseau's psychological contract typology & Psychological Contract Inventory (Denise M. Rousseau, 1989–2000)

options.label: Transactional
options.desc: You see work as a clear economic exchange: specific duties for specific rewards, over a defined period. You give a fair effort for fair pay and expect little beyond what was agreed — and you offer the same in return, staying as long as the terms suit you. Rousseau links this short-term, well-specified deal with mobility and a focus on pay and conditions rather than long-term loyalty.

options.label: Relational
options.desc: You expect an open-ended relationship built on loyalty and mutual care: steady employment, support through good times and bad, and an employer invested in your wellbeing and growth — repaid with commitment and a willingness to go beyond your job description. Rousseau describes this long-term, broadly defined deal as the bond underlying lasting careers in one organisation.

options.label: Balanced
options.desc: You want the best of both: a long-term partnership with clear, evolving performance goals. The employer invests in your development and future employability while expecting you to keep raising your contribution as the business changes. Rousseau frames this as a dynamic deal that pairs relational commitment with transactional clarity, and finds it increasingly common in modern careers.

options.label: Transitional
options.desc: This is less a settled deal than one in flux — the uncertainty, mistrust and eroded expectations people feel when an organisation is in upheaval, such as during a merger, restructuring or layoffs. The old understanding has broken down and a new one has not yet formed, so obligations on both sides feel unclear. Rousseau treats it as a transitional state rather than a stable type.

systems.name: Why you stay in a job
systems.statusNote: Organisational commitment — the psychological bond that ties an employee to their employer — is a long-established construct in organisational behaviour. John P. Meyer and Natalie J. Allen (1990, 1991) showed it is not a single attitude but three separable, separately measurable components — affective, continuance and normative — each arising from different experiences and each predicting, in its own way, whether a person stays. Their scales (the Affective, Continuance and Normative Commitment Scales, later packaged as the TCM Employee Commitment Survey; Meyer, Allen & Smith, 1993) have been validated across many occupations and countries, and a meta-analysis of hundreds of samples (Meyer, Stanley, Herscovitch & Topolnytsky, 2002) confirmed the three components relate differently to outcomes such as staff turnover, attendance and wellbeing. This asks which of the three bonds you feel most strongly — not which is best.
systems.blurb: Organisational commitment is the psychological bond that keeps a person in their job — and the organisational psychologists John Meyer and Natalie Allen showed it is not one feeling but three. Affective commitment is wanting to stay: an emotional attachment to the organisation, a sense of belonging and shared identity. Continuance commitment is needing to stay: the awareness that leaving would cost too much — lost pay, benefits, seniority or pension, or simply too few alternatives. Normative commitment is feeling you ought to stay: a sense of duty or loyalty, perhaps because the employer invested in you, or because staying is what you believe a good employee does. Most people feel some blend of all three, but one tends to run strongest, and the difference matters: those who stay mainly because they want to tend to perform better and feel better than those held in place only by cost. Measured by Meyer and Allen's commitment scales and validated across many countries and occupations, this asks which of the three bonds best describes why you stay — and none of them is the 'right' reason.
systems.source: Meyer & Allen's Three-Component Model of organisational commitment & the TCM Employee Commitment Survey (John P. Meyer & Natalie J. Allen, 1990–1993)

options.label: Want to stay
options.desc: You stay because you want to. You feel a genuine emotional attachment to the organisation — you identify with what it stands for, feel you belong, and find meaning in being part of it. Meyer and Allen link this bond to the strongest outcomes: people committed this way tend to work harder, stay longer and feel better at work, because the relationship is one they have chosen rather than one they are stuck in.

options.label: Need to stay
options.desc: You stay because the cost of leaving is too high. Over time you have built up things you would lose by going — seniority, a pension, benefits, a familiar routine — or you sense there are few real alternatives elsewhere. The bond here is calculated rather than emotional: it keeps you in place, but Meyer and Allen find it does little to lift performance, since you remain out of necessity rather than desire.

options.label: Ought to stay
options.desc: You stay because you feel you should. A sense of duty or loyalty holds you in place — perhaps the employer trained you, supported you or took a chance on you, and leaving would feel like letting them down; or perhaps you simply believe that seeing things through is what a good employee does. Meyer and Allen describe this obligation-based bond as moral rather than economic, often shaped by upbringing and by what an organisation has invested in you.

systems.name: How much you trust people
systems.statusNote: Generalised (or interpersonal) trust is a long-validated individual difference: the default expectation that other people — including strangers — will behave honestly and fairly. It was first measured by Julian Rotter's Interpersonal Trust Scale (1967) and refined by Toshio and Midori Yamagishi (1994), who separated genuine trust in people from the security of committed relationships. Behavioural economists measure it directly with the trust game (Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe, 1995), and cross-country research links a society's level of trust to its economic performance (Knack & Keefer, 1997). How widely that trust reaches — its radius, from a close in-group out to strangers — is itself a validated dimension (Delhey, Newton & Welzel, 2011). Neither high nor low trust is treated here as the right answer.
systems.blurb: Generalised trust is your default belief about whether other people — including strangers — will deal with you honestly and fairly. Economists treat it as a kind of hidden currency: where it is high, people cooperate, lend, hire and trade with less friction, and societies with more of it tend to grow faster; where it is low, every dealing needs guarding, contracts and proof. This self-assessment places you on two validated dimensions rather than a single verdict. The first is how much you trust people in general — from guarded, where you assume it is wiser to protect yourself first, to trusting, where you extend goodwill before it is earned. The second is the radius of that trust: how far it reaches, from a close circle of family and friends you know well out to strangers, newcomers and people unlike you. The two are distinct — you can trust your inner circle deeply yet stay wary of outsiders, or extend an even-handed, moderate trust to almost anyone — and research finds that being trusting is not the same as being gullible, since people high in trust are often better, not worse, at spotting who cannot be relied on. Both ends are shown neutrally: broad trust lowers the cost of cooperation, while a narrower, more guarded trust can be a sensible response to an uncertain world.
systems.source: Rotter's Interpersonal Trust Scale (1967) and Yamagishi's general-trust measure (Yamagishi & Yamagishi, 1994)

dimensions.name: General trust
dimensions.desc: Your default expectation of other people. A high score extends goodwill before it is earned and assumes most people are honest and fair; a low score assumes it is wiser to protect yourself first and let trust be proven. Being trusting is not the same as being naive — people high in general trust are often better at telling who can be relied on.

dimensions.name: Radius of trust
dimensions.desc: How far your trust reaches. A low score concentrates trust in a close, known circle — family and long-standing friends — and stays wary beyond it; a high score extends trust outward to strangers, newcomers and people unlike you. The wider, generalised kind is what lets people deal with those they do not know, and economists link it to cooperation and growth; the narrower kind gives strong, secure bonds within your own group.

systems.name: Where you take risks
systems.statusNote: The Domain-Specific Risk-Taking (DOSPERT) scale is a validated psychometric instrument developed by Elke U. Weber, Ann-Renée Blais and Nancy Betz (2002) and revised into a shorter 30-item form by Blais and Weber (2006). It measures self-reported risk-taking in five content domains — financial, health and safety, recreational, ethical and social — and has been used in more than two thousand studies; a meta-analysis by Shou and Olney (2020) confirmed its reliability. Its defining result is that risk attitudes are domain-specific rather than one general trait: within a person, how much risk-taking varies across the five domains is about seven times larger than how much people differ from one another overall. Neither high nor low risk-taking is treated here as the right answer — each carries its own costs and benefits.
systems.blurb: Risk-taking is usually talked about as a single trait — you are either a risk-taker or you are cautious. The research says otherwise. The Domain-Specific Risk-Taking scale, built by Elke Weber and colleagues, measures how willing you are to take risks separately in five areas of life: financial decisions, health and safety, recreation, ethics, and social situations. Its central finding is that these barely move together — in large samples, how much a single person's risk-taking varies across the five domains is several times greater than how much people differ from one another overall. The same person can stake money on a volatile investment yet always wear a seatbelt, throw themselves off a cliff for fun yet never tell a white lie, or speak boldly against the crowd yet keep their savings locked away. So this self-assessment gives you a profile, not a verdict — a separate reading on each of the five domains rather than one score. Each domain is shown neutrally: more risk can mean opportunity, growth, thrill or honesty, while more caution can mean security, health, trust and peace of mind. There is no correct level, and the interesting thing is the shape — where you lean bold and where you hold back.
systems.source: The Domain-Specific Risk-Taking (DOSPERT) scale (Weber, Blais & Betz, 2002; revised Blais & Weber, 2006)

dimensions.name: Financial
dimensions.desc: Money decisions whose outcome is uncertain — investing a large share of your income, betting on a long shot, putting savings into something volatile, lending to a friend. A low score guards what you have and prefers the safe, known return; a high score will stake money for a larger but uncertain payoff. Economists read this as how readily you trade certainty for expected gain.

dimensions.name: Health & safety
dimensions.desc: Risks to your body and wellbeing — skipping the seatbelt, sunbathing without protection, riding without a helmet, ignoring a health warning. A low score plays it safe and avoids exposure; a high score accepts bodily risk for convenience, freedom or thrill. This is the domain most tightly tied to long-term health outcomes.

dimensions.name: Recreational
dimensions.desc: Risk taken for its own enjoyment — skydiving, whitewater rafting, climbing, fast skiing, heading somewhere unknown. A low score prefers calm, predictable leisure; a high score seeks out physical thrill and novelty. Of the five domains this is the one that many otherwise-cautious people will still embrace.

dimensions.name: Ethical
dimensions.desc: Bending rules or norms when there is something to gain — a questionable shortcut, a small dishonesty, cutting a corner others would not. A low score sticks closely to the rules even at a cost; a high score will accept moral or reputational risk for an advantage. Shown without judgement: where you sit is a description, not a verdict, and few people are uniformly high or low across all five domains.

dimensions.name: Social
dimensions.desc: Risks to your standing with other people — voicing an unpopular opinion, disagreeing with authority, starting a conversation with a stranger, admitting a mistake in public, choosing a path your circle disapproves of. A low score avoids social exposure and the chance of disapproval; a high score will risk standing out to be honest or to be seen. It is the domain least related to the physical ones.

systems.name: How you handle competition
systems.statusNote: Built on validated competitiveness research. Ryckman and colleagues constructed two psychometric scales that measure distinct competitive orientations — the Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale (1990) and the Personal-Development Competitive Attitude Scale (1996) — and showed the two are statistically independent rather than opposite ends of one trait. Separately, the behavioural-economics experiments of Niederle and Vesterlund (2007) established that people differ systematically in whether they will enter a competitive setting at all, independent of their actual ability. This self-assessment combines those findings into three orientations. It is a self-report, not an ability test, and no orientation is treated as the right one — each carries its own strengths and costs.
systems.blurb: Some people come alive the moment a situation turns into a contest; others do their best work when no one is keeping score. How you handle competition is one of the more stable differences in how people approach work, sport, study and play, and psychologists have built validated scales to measure it. This self-assessment draws on three research-grounded orientations. People high in hypercompetitiveness, measured by Ryckman and colleagues' Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale, treat a contest as a way to prove themselves: winning matters, losing stings, and where they stand relative to others is part of how they keep score. People high in personal-development competitiveness, a separate and statistically independent scale by the same team, use competition mainly to test and improve themselves, so the contest is a tool for mastery and beating others matters less than getting better. And a large group, highlighted by behavioural-economics experiments on who chooses to enter a tournament at all, simply prefer to step back from head-to-head contests and do better in cooperative, non-zero-sum settings. None of the three is the right answer here: each comes with its own strengths and its own costs. The interesting question is which one feels most like you.
systems.source: Competitiveness research — the Hypercompetitive and Personal-Development Competitive Attitude Scales (Ryckman et al., 1990, 1996) and the economics of competition entry (Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007)

options.label: Compete to win
options.desc: For you, competition is about coming out on top. A contest sharpens your focus, winning feels good and losing genuinely stings, and you naturally keep an eye on where you stand relative to other people. Psychologists call this a hypercompetitive orientation, measured by Ryckman and colleagues' Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale. Its strengths are drive, resilience under pressure and a refusal to coast; its costs can be strain and friction when winning crowds out other things you value. Recorded here as one honest orientation, not a verdict.

options.label: Compete to grow
options.desc: You welcome competition, but mainly as a way to test and stretch yourself. A strong opponent or a tough benchmark is useful because it reveals what you can do and pushes you to improve — the result matters less than the progress. This maps onto what researchers call personal-development competitiveness (Ryckman and colleagues, 1996), a measure shown to be statistically independent of the win-at-all-costs kind. Its strengths are steady growth and enjoyment of the process; you may simply care less about the scoreboard than the people around you expect.

options.label: Prefer cooperation
options.desc: You tend to step back from head-to-head contests and do your best where success is shared rather than won. Given the choice, you would rather build something together than race someone for it, and zero-sum pressure can sap you rather than spur you. Behavioural-economics experiments on who chooses to enter a tournament at all find this is a large and ordinary group — not a lack of ability, but a genuine preference for cooperation over rivalry. Its strengths are collaboration, trust and steadiness; recorded here without judgement.

systems.name: How you explain poverty
systems.statusNote: The three-way classification of poverty explanations — individualistic, structural and fatalistic — was introduced by the sociologist Joe R. Feagin (1972) and confirmed outside the United States by Adrian Furnham (1982), who found the same structure in Britain. It has since been measured with standard attribution scales across many countries (Bullock, 1999; Cozzarelli, Wilkinson & Tagler, 2001), and a person's dominant attribution reliably predicts their support for welfare and redistribution (Bullock, Williams & Limbert, 2003). No attribution is treated here as the correct one; the framework records where your emphasis falls, not which explanation is true.
systems.blurb: How you explain poverty is one of the most studied beliefs in the social sciences: when people are asked why some people are poor, their answers fall into a small number of recurring patterns. The sociologist Joe Feagin first mapped them in 1972 into three kinds of explanation, and researchers have measured them across dozens of countries ever since. An individualistic explanation puts the main weight on the person — effort, choices, skills and how money is managed. A structural explanation puts it on the surrounding system — wages, schooling, the job market, the cost of housing and healthcare, discrimination, and the circumstances people are born into. A fatalistic explanation puts it on chance — luck, illness, accident and forces no one controls. Most people hold a blend of all three but lean towards one emphasis, and which one tends to shape how they see welfare, taxation and opportunity. This is not a test of who is right: poverty is genuinely driven by all of these at once, and the instrument records where your own emphasis falls rather than ranking any explanation above another.
systems.source: Feagin's three-fold typology of poverty attributions (Feagin, 1972; Furnham, 1982)

options.label: Individual factors
options.desc: You see the main causes of poverty as lying mostly with the person — effort, decisions, skills, persistence and how money is managed. On this view, opportunities are broadly available and outcomes follow largely from what people do with them. Researchers call this an individualistic attribution; it is the most common pattern in strongly individualistic cultures. It is recorded here as one honest reading of a complex problem, not as a verdict on anyone.

options.label: Structural factors
options.desc: You see the main causes of poverty as lying mostly in the surrounding system — wages and the job market, the quality of schooling, the cost of housing and healthcare, discrimination, and the circumstances people are born into. On this view, the same person would fare very differently depending on the structures around them. Researchers call this a structural attribution; it tends to go with stronger support for collective and policy solutions.

options.label: Chance and circumstance
options.desc: You see the main causes of poverty as lying mostly in chance — luck, illness, accident, disability, and events no one chooses or controls. On this view, poverty can fall on anyone when circumstances turn against them, and is more a matter of misfortune than of either effort or system. Researchers call this a fatalistic attribution; it is the least common of the three but appears consistently across cultures.
