systems.name: The welfare state you believe in
systems.statusNote: Gøsta Esping-Andersen's empirically derived typology of welfare states (The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism, 1990), built from cross-national data on decommodification and social stratification; the Mediterranean (Ferrera, 1996) and East Asian productivist (Holliday, 2000) models are widely discussed extensions. A comparative classification of states, presented here as the model of social protection you most identify with.
systems.blurb: Every society decides how it shares risk and looks after its members, and political economists have found these settlements cluster into a handful of recognisable models — from the market-led liberal safety net to the universal social-democratic state. Building on Gøsta Esping-Andersen's classic three worlds of welfare capitalism, plus the Mediterranean and East Asian models later scholars added, this maps the great traditions of the welfare state. Which one matches how you think a society should care for its own?
systems.source: Esping-Andersen, G. (1990). The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism. Polity Press

options.label: Liberal welfare state
options.desc: A modest, means-tested safety net for those in real need, with most welfare left to the market and private provision; benefits are kept low to preserve the incentive to work. Seen in the United States, Canada and Australia.

options.label: Conservative (corporatist)
options.desc: Welfare earned through work and delivered by social insurance that preserves your existing status, with the family — not the state — as the first line of care. Seen in Germany, France and Austria.

options.label: Social democratic
options.desc: Welfare as a universal right of citizenship: generous, tax-funded services and benefits for everyone, designed to free people from depending on the market or the family. Seen in Sweden, Norway and Denmark.

options.label: Mediterranean (Southern)
options.desc: A patchwork of generous pensions alongside thin safety nets, leaning heavily on the extended family and informal networks to fill the gaps. Seen in Spain, Italy, Greece and Portugal.

options.label: East Asian (productivist)
options.desc: Social policy kept in the service of economic growth: welfare is targeted to support a productive workforce, with employers, the family and personal savings carrying much of the load. Seen in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

systems.name: Your investor type
systems.statusNote: Pompian's Behavioural Investor Types (2012) is a practitioner framework, widely taught in the CFA Program, that groups investors by their appetite for risk and by whether their decision-making blind spots are mainly emotional or mainly cognitive. It draws on documented behavioural-finance biases rather than being published as a validated psychometric scale, so it is offered here as a reflective self-identification — not a diagnosis, a measure of skill, or financial advice.
systems.blurb: Behavioural finance keeps finding that people fall into recognisable patterns as investors — defined less by how much they know than by how they actually decide when money is on the line. This self-identification draws on Michael Pompian's Behavioural Investor Types, a framework taught in the CFA Program that arranges investors along a rising scale of risk appetite and sorts them by whether their characteristic mistakes are emotional or analytical. At the cautious end the Preserver guards what they have and feels every loss; the Friendly Follower invests but leans on whatever is popular; the Independent Individualist forms strong, often contrarian views and backs them; and at the bold end the Active Accumulator chases growth with confidence and control. None is the right way to invest — each pairs a real strength with a characteristic trap. The useful question is which one sounds most like you.
systems.source: Pompian's Behavioural Investor Types (Behavioral Finance and Investor Types, Wiley, 2012)

options.label: Preserver
options.desc: You put financial security first. Protecting what you have matters more than chasing the next opportunity, a loss weighs on you more than an equal gain delights you, and you would rather hold steady than risk a setback. In Pompian's framework this is the Passive Preserver, the most cautious type, whose blind spots are mainly emotional — loss aversion, a pull toward the familiar, and treating money already held as worth more than money still to be made. Its strengths are discipline, patience and a level head in a downturn; its cost is missing growth by playing too safe. Recorded here as one honest pattern, not a verdict.

options.label: Follower
options.desc: You invest, but you tend to take your lead from others — friends, headlines, or whatever everyone seems to be buying. You may not hold strong views of your own, and you would rather be in a popular choice than an unconventional one. Pompian calls this the Friendly Follower, a passive type whose blind spots are mainly cognitive: chasing recent winners, overestimating your own appetite for risk, and being swayed by how a choice is framed. Its strengths are openness and a willingness to act; its cost is buying in late and drifting with the crowd. One pattern among several, recorded without judgement.

options.label: Independent
options.desc: You are hands-on and opinionated, happy to back your own analysis even when it cuts against the consensus. You research, form a view and act on it, with an above-average tolerance for risk. Pompian calls this the Independent Individualist, an active type whose blind spots are mainly cognitive: favouring evidence that confirms a view you already hold, over-weighting whatever comes easily to mind, and being slow to update when the facts change. Its strengths are conviction, originality and genuine engagement; its cost is mistaking a strong opinion for a correct one. Recorded as one orientation, not the right one.

options.label: Accumulator
options.desc: You invest to grow wealth and you back yourself to do it, often after success elsewhere in life. You are comfortable taking on risk, like to stay in control of your money, and trust that the path you have chosen is the right one. Pompian calls this the Active Accumulator, the boldest type, whose blind spots are mainly emotional: overconfidence, a belief you can steer outcomes you cannot, and a reluctance to rein yourself in. Its strengths are drive, decisiveness and an appetite for opportunity; its cost is over-trading and concentrated bets. Listed here as one honest pattern, without judgement.

systems.name: Organisational culture (Competing Values)
systems.statusNote: The Competing Values Framework (Cameron & Quinn) and its questionnaire, the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), are among the most widely used tools for diagnosing organisational culture, and the OCAI has been independently validated (Heritage, Pollock & Roberts, 2014), with adequate internal consistency reported for its four scales. That study also found it predicts outcomes such as job satisfaction more reliably when rating an organisation's current culture than its ideal one, so it is offered here as a structured reading of your workplace rather than a precise measurement.
systems.blurb: Organisations, like people, develop a recognisable character — a shared sense of how work gets done and what the place values. Kim Cameron and Robert Quinn's Competing Values Framework, drawn from research into what makes organisations effective, maps that character onto two tensions every organisation has to balance: whether it looks inward to its own people or outward to the market, and whether it leans towards flexibility or towards control. Crossing the two yields four cultures. A Clan runs on collaboration, mentoring and loyalty, and feels like a family. An Adhocracy thrives on innovation, moving fast and taking risks on new ideas. A Market is driven to compete and win, judged by results. A Hierarchy values order, clear procedure and dependable efficiency. Few workplaces are purely one — most blend all four — but usually one leads. Which one does yours actually feel like?
systems.source: Cameron & Quinn, Diagnosing and Changing Organizational Culture: Based on the Competing Values Framework (Jossey-Bass)

options.label: Clan
options.desc: Your workplace feels like an extended family. People know one another, decisions are made together, and the organisation invests in its members through mentoring, teamwork and a shared sense of belonging. Loyalty and morale hold it together, and it judges success partly by how well its people develop and get along. In the Competing Values Framework this is the collaborate quadrant — turned inward, and favouring flexibility over control. Its strength is commitment and cohesion; its risk is avoiding hard calls or growing inward-looking. One honest reading of a workplace, not a verdict on it.

options.label: Adhocracy
options.desc: Your workplace runs on new ideas. It moves quickly, encourages experiment and will back something unproven; people gather around a project, then regroup around the next. Initiative and originality count for more than following a rulebook, and leaders are happy to take a risk. In the Competing Values Framework this is the create quadrant — turned outward, and favouring flexibility over control. Its strength is innovation and adaptability; its risk is disorder, burnout or chasing novelty over follow-through. One pattern among four, recorded without judgement.

options.label: Market
options.desc: Your workplace is built to compete and win. Results, targets and measurable success — against rivals and in the market outside — drive it, and getting the job done matters more than process or comfort. People are demanding and goal-focused, and reputation is earned through performance. In the Competing Values Framework this is the compete quadrant — turned outward, and favouring control and stability. Its strength is drive and achievement; its risk is short-termism and a relentlessness that can wear people down. One orientation, not the right one.

options.label: Hierarchy
options.desc: Your workplace values order and dependability. Clear roles, procedures and lines of authority keep things running, and the organisation prizes efficiency, consistency and doing the job correctly. Stability is treated as a strength, not a failing: people know what is expected, and the same standards apply to everyone. In the Competing Values Framework this is the control quadrant — turned inward, and favouring control and stability. Its strength is reliability and fairness; its risk is rigidity and slowness to change. Listed here as one honest pattern, without judgement.

systems.name: How you see the people and the elite
systems.statusNote: Populist attitudes are measured by a validated survey scale developed by Akkerman, Mudde and Zaslove (Comparative Political Studies, 2014) and refined into three dimensions by Schulz and colleagues (2017): anti-elitism, the belief in popular sovereignty, and a view of the people as one virtuous whole. The scale is non-partisan — populist attitudes appear on the left and the right alike — and it is conventionally contrasted with two alternatives, pluralism and elitism. Presented here as the outlook you most identify with, not a verdict on it.
systems.blurb: Populism is less a left-or-right ideology than a way of seeing politics: a moral divide between an honest, ordinary people and a self-serving elite, paired with the demand that government simply carry out the people's will. Political scientists capture this outlook as a set of measurable attitudes — how far you distrust the establishment, how directly you think ordinary people should rule, and how much you see society as one virtuous people rather than many competing groups. Validated voter studies set it against two alternatives: pluralism, which trusts institutions to balance many legitimate interests, and elitism, which trusts experienced leaders to decide. Which comes closest to how you see the people and those in power?
systems.source: Akkerman, A., Mudde, C., & Zaslove, A. (2014). How Populist Are the People? Measuring Populist Attitudes in Voters. Comparative Political Studies, 47(9), 1324-1353

options.label: Populist
options.desc: You see a basic divide between ordinary, decent people and a self-serving elite, and you believe politics should faithfully carry out the people's will. Experts and established institutions count for little when they lose touch with what the public actually wants.

options.label: Pluralist
options.desc: You see society as many legitimate groups with competing interests and values, so there is no single 'will of the people' to enact. Good government balances those interests through institutions, negotiation, minority rights and checks on power.

options.label: Elitist
options.desc: You think the big questions are genuinely complex and best entrusted to experienced, knowledgeable leaders rather than settled by popular opinion. Sound judgement and expertise matter more than following the majority mood of the moment.

systems.name: How you relate to the tax office
systems.statusNote: Valerie Braithwaite's motivational postures come from large-scale survey research with Australian taxpayers and are measured by the Motivational Postures (Toward Taxes) Questionnaire, a validated instrument with five subscales (Braithwaite, 2003; Braithwaite, Murphy & Reinhart, 2007). Reported internal-consistency reliabilities run from about .63 to .82 across the five postures, and the questionnaire has since been adapted and re-validated in other countries (Kołodziej, 2021). It is offered here as a reflective self-identification, not a test of compliance, honesty, or character: the postures describe stances people take toward authority, most of us hold more than one, and which is uppermost shifts with circumstance and with how fairly the tax office is felt to act.
systems.blurb: Researchers who study why people pay tax keep finding that compliance is shaped less by the threat of an audit than by the stance a person takes toward the tax authority itself. This self-identification draws on Valerie Braithwaite's motivational postures, a set of five attitudes measured in large surveys of taxpayers and since validated in several countries. Two are postures of deference: commitment, a felt duty to pay because the system is seen as fair and worth supporting; and capitulation, going along with the rules without necessarily sharing the authority's aims. Three are postures of defiance: resistance, a wary, resentful compliance that still accepts the office's power to enforce; disengagement, a switched-off distance that grants the system neither authority nor purpose; and game playing, treating tax law as a puzzle to be worked to one's own advantage. The postures are not fixed traits or a measure of honesty — most people move between them depending on the issue and on how fairly they feel they are being treated. The question is which one best describes how you relate to the tax office.
systems.source: Braithwaite's Motivational Postures (Toward Taxes) Questionnaire (Taxing Democracy, Ashgate, 2003)

options.label: Commitment
options.desc: You pay your tax because you think you should. You see the system as broadly fair and worth supporting, accept that public goods have to be funded somehow, and feel a genuine obligation to contribute your share. In Braithwaite's framework this is commitment, the most positive posture toward the authority — cooperation that comes from agreeing with the system's aims rather than from fear of being caught. Its strength is a willing, low-friction relationship with the tax office; its blind spot can be assuming the system is fairer or better run than it always is. Recorded here as one honest stance, not a mark of virtue.

options.label: Capitulation
options.desc: You pay what you owe and follow the rules, but more because the tax office has the authority to require it than because you share its goals. You are not hostile — you accept the system and defer to it — yet your compliance is practical rather than heartfelt: you go along with what is asked. Braithwaite calls this capitulation, a posture of deference in which people accept an authority's power without necessarily endorsing its purpose. Its strength is steady, reliable cooperation; its cost is that the goodwill is thin and can erode if the relationship starts to feel one-sided. One stance among several, recorded without judgement.

options.label: Resistance
options.desc: You comply, but warily. You suspect the tax office of overreach or unfairness, dislike being pushed around, and watch closely for heavy-handed or arbitrary treatment — while still accepting that the authority has the power to enforce the rules. Braithwaite calls this resistance, a posture of defiance that pairs grudging cooperation with vocal mistrust. Its strength is that it holds authority to account and pushes back on unfair treatment; its cost is a tense, adversarial relationship that can harden if grievances go unanswered. Listed here as one honest stance, neither right nor wrong.

options.label: Disengagement
options.desc: You have largely tuned the tax system out. It feels distant and beside the point, and you grant it neither real authority nor much purpose — not so much fighting it as keeping your distance and not engaging. Braithwaite calls this disengagement, the most detached posture of defiance, marked by social distance rather than open conflict. Its strength can be a refusal to be drawn into a system one finds illegitimate; its cost is a disconnection that leaves little room for cooperation or recourse. Recorded as one orientation among several, without judgement.

options.label: Game playing
options.desc: You treat tax as a contest of wits. The law is something to be read closely, interpreted creatively and worked to your advantage, and you take a certain satisfaction in finding the angles others miss. Braithwaite calls this game playing, a posture of defiance in which the relationship with the tax office becomes a game with rules to be worked rather than simply followed. Its strength is sharp engagement with how the rules actually operate; its cost is a relationship built on manoeuvre that can shade into avoidance. Recorded here as one honest pattern, not a verdict on anyone's conduct.
